summary: deliverHTTPResponse can send on a channel that clearForward has already closed, panicking the serve goroutine and crashing the whole agent (leaving spawned children unreaped, breaking the doc's stream-close reap invariant).
evidence: deliverHTTPResponse loads ch under forwardMu, unlocks, then does `select { case ch <- resp: default: }` (local_http.go:97-108). clearForward (deferred in forwardHTTP, local_http.go:46, and reached on the 30s timeout branch) closes the channel under the lock (local_http.go:88-95). If an HttpResponse frame arrives concurrently with the timeout/return, the send hits a closed channel — send on a closed channel always panics, and the buffered cap-1 channel is ready so the select chooses it. deliverHTTPResponse runs synchronously on the serve goroutine (run.go:305-306), which is called on Run's main goroutine (run.go:168), so the panic kills the daemon without reapAllOrphans running.
verify_note: Confirmed: deliverHTTPResponse reads ch under forwardMu then releases before `ch <- resp` (local_http.go:98-105); clearForward (deferred on 30s timeout, line 46) can close(ch) in the gap. Send on closed channel panics even inside select+default. Caller runs synchronously in the sole stream-recv loop (run.go:288) with no recover, so it crashes the whole agent process and orphans spawned children. Window narrow (timeout racing a late/duplicate response) but real.
remediation: Serialize deliverHTTPResponse against clearForward (guard/close-once) so a response is never sent on a channel clearForward already closed.

summary: Store.Commit is not idempotent in the claim id: a retried Commit after a successful swap fails (the staging schema was consumed by the rename and the now-populated canonical blocks the drop), breaking the claim-producer invariant 'Terminal verbs (commit/abandon/release) must be idempotent in the claim identifier' that auto-terminal names as the sole mitigation for the verb-fires-before-rimsky-tx-commits leak path.
evidence: store.go:264-284 calls commitStagingSwap with no prior state check; server.go:174-178 passes the gRPC CommitRequest straight through; ledger.go:124-145 records ClaimStateCommitted only AFTER the swap and nothing ever reads it as a guard. concepts/claim-producer.md line 39 ('Terminal verbs ... must be idempotent in the claim identifier so the verb-then-transaction-fail leak path is recoverable') and concepts/auto-terminal.md invariant 3 ('the verb-then-tx-fail leak path is mitigated by requiring terminal verbs to be idempotent in the claim id') both depend on this. On retry, `ALTER SCHEMA rimsky_stg_<id> RENAME` fails (schema gone) so Commit returns pg/swap_failed and rimsky's resolution wedges in an errored state while the substrate is already committed. Note the interplay with the DROP-without-CASCADE finding: naively adding CASCADE would make a Commit retry DROP the just-published canonical data and then fail the rename — data loss; the correct fix needs an explicit committed-state idempotency guard.

Ledger records COMMITTED only after (ledger.go:140), never read as guard. Violates claim-producer.md:39 / auto-terminal.md:33 idempotency invariant. No data loss (single tx rolls back), config-gated to staged_async recovery path -> major not critical.

summary: The doc claims that in anonymous mode 'every request — including requests with no Authorization header — is admitted as a synthetic admin identity', but the middleware only substitutes the anonymous identity when the Authorization header is entirely absent; a request presenting a malformed, unknown, revoked, or expired bearer token is rejected 401 even with zero active keys.

summary: The invariant 'each (service, event) pair fires exactly once' overclaims: the code implements at-least-once delivery with retry-dedupe after a recorded success, and legitimately re-fires the same event on state re-transitions, so subscriber handlers must be idempotent — a reader building a subscriber from this doc would skip that.

The 'per-(service, event) ledger' phrasing at doc line 11 is likewise inaccurate — the key is (service, scope-kind, scope-id) with an overwritten state column (persistence.LifecycleIdempotencyRow fields at lifecycle.go:130-135).

summary: The claim-producer front is not the transparent forwarder invariant 7 requires: Capabilities is answered locally with a hardcoded response advertising all write semantics and SupportsSplitScope: true, while the SplitScope and ScopesConflict RPCs are not implemented at all (they fall through to UnimplementedClaimProducerServer), so the proxy advertises a capability that is guaranteed to fail.
evidence: claim_producer_handler.go:42-53 returns a canned CapabilitiesResponse with SupportsSplitScope: true and all four write semantics regardless of the spawned producer; the handler (lines 25-31 embed genv1.UnimplementedClaimProducerServer) implements only Capabilities/Open/Commit/Abandon/Release, but claim_producer.proto declares SplitScope (line 71) and ScopesConflict (line 77). host-agent-proxy.md invariant 7 states "A service that conforms to its own protocol works behind the proxy by construction" and "no per-protocol special-casing leaves some protocols unable to reach the spawn/forward path".
verify_note: host-agent-proxy claim_producer_handler.go:42-53 returns canned Capabilities SupportsSplitScope:true (not forwarded); SplitScope (proto :71) unimplemented -> UnimplementedClaimProducerServer returns Unimplemented, guaranteed failure. Violates host-agent-proxy.md:29 invariant 7 (transparent forwarder). ScopesConflict advertised false so moot; SplitScope is the defect -> major.
remediation: Forward Capabilities and every RPC (SplitScope/ScopesConflict, ListVersions/ListPartitions/GetVersionSchema, ListSubscriptions) to the spawned child instead of answering locally or leaving them Unimplemented.
phase1_note: The finding is half-refuted: the canned Capabilities response (full write-semantics envelope) is intentional per the dossier ('pure transport; any binding might realize any semantics'), not a bug. But claim-producer is a still-sanctioned late-bind protocol post-2026-07-14, and the handler advertises SupportsSplitScope:true while the SplitScope RPC falls through to codes.Unimplemented -- a real advertise/implement mismatch violating the still-live transparent-forwarder invariant. Fix: forward SplitScope (and ScopesConflict, or flip its advertised bit) to the spawned child; leave Capabilities canned as designed.

summary: The data-processing front violates invariant 7: ListVersions, ListPartitions, and GetVersionSchema are not forwarded (they fall through to UnimplementedDataProcessingServer and return codes.Unimplemented), and Capabilities returns a hardcoded {Materializations: ["full"]} instead of the spawned service's answer, so a conformant data-processing service does not work behind the proxy by construction.
evidence: data_processing_handler.go implements only Capabilities (canned, line 39-41), BeginCandidate, CommitCandidate, AbandonCandidate; data_processing.proto declares ListVersions (line 28), ListPartitions (line 29), GetVersionSchema (line 30), all of which rimsky's own client calls (lib/runtime/peer/data_processing_client.go:66,89,107). host-agent-proxy.md invariant 7: "The proxy is a transparent forwarder of every rimsky service protocol it fronts ... concept:data-processing ... No protocol ships as a registered-but-unimplemented stub."
verify_note: host-agent-proxy.md invariant 7 'transparent forwarder ... No protocol ships as a registered-but-unimplemented stub'. Violated: data_processing_handler.go embeds UnimplementedDataProcessingServer, implements only Capabilities (canned) + Begin/Commit/AbandonCandidate. proto declares ListVersions/ListPartitions/GetVersionSchema (data_processing.proto:28-30), all called by rimsky's client — fall through to codes.Unimplemented. A conformant data-processing service does not work behind the proxy -> major.
phase1_note: The finding's literal remediation (forward ListVersions/ListPartitions/GetVersionSchema) is now superseded intent -- per the 2026-07-14 user ruling, data-processing must not be late-bindable at all. The code has NOT caught up to that ruling either: the handler is still fully registered (not trimmed) and there is no registration/config-time rejection of late-binding a data-processing service, so the gap remains, just relocated. Fix: trim dataProcessingHandler entirely and add a loud registration-time rejection for late-binding non-(executor|claim-producer) protocol slots, per the RESOLVED conflict.

summary: resolveAndSpawn's lookup-then-spawn is not atomic, so two concurrent first dispatches for the same (run-scope, binding-name) both miss lookupSpawnByRunScopeBinding and both spawn a child process, breaking the doc's "One spawn per (run-scope, binding-name)" invariant; the second recordSpawn overwrites the routing key while the first child keeps running (and receiving its in-flight dispatch) until scope reap.
evidence: dispatch.go:115-124: `if spawnID, ok := state.lookupSpawnByRunScopeBinding(scopeID, name); ok {...}` followed by an unlocked spawnChild(...) and state.recordSpawn(...); state.go:280 recordSpawn does a plain map overwrite of runScopeBindings[key]. The same pattern repeats in resolveAndSpawnByService (dispatch.go:163-170). gRPC serves handlers concurrently, so two nodes in one run-scope binding the same service can hit this. host-agent-proxy.md invariant 2: "One spawn per (run-scope, binding-name)".
verify_note: REAL RACE: dispatch.go:115 lookupSpawnByRunScopeBinding (state.go:290-293 RLock) and spawnChild+recordSpawn (state.go:269-280 separate Lock, plain map overwrite) are not atomic; each state method locks independently, so concurrent first dispatches for one (scopeID,name) both miss and both spawn. gRPC serves concurrently. Repeated at dispatch.go:163-171. Breaks host-agent-proxy.md invariant 2 'One spawn per (run-scope, binding-name)' -> major.
remediation: Make lookup-then-spawn atomic per (run-scope, binding-name) via a lock or single-flight so only one child spawns.

summary: The per-protocol Capabilities responses the agent collects during the spawn readiness handshake and returns in SpawnAck.capabilities are discarded by the proxy — both recordSpawn call sites pass nil, spawnState.capabilities is never populated or read — so the advertised-capabilities handshake the adjacent host-agent concept doc describes dead-ends and the proxy's hardcoded Capabilities answers can never be replaced with real ones.

summary: The agent registers with the raw value of RIMSKY_API_KEY (the plaintext bearer token used everywhere else in the CLI), but owned-instance routing matches on the api-key ID (UUID), so an agent started with the documented env/flag never receives dispatches for owned instances — every dispatch fails host_agent_not_connected.
evidence: agent.go:57 flag help says "api-key presented to the proxy on Register (overrides $RIMSKY_API_KEY)" and hostagent/config.go:31 reads os.Getenv("RIMSKY_API_KEY") — the same env the CLI uses as the plaintext bearer (cli/run.go:157 common.ResolveAPIKey(os.Getenv("RIMSKY_API_KEY"))). But the routing key the proxy matches is the owner key ID UUID: dispatch.go:100 resolveOwnerRoutingKey(entry.ownerAPIKeyID) where ownerAPIKeyID comes from created_by_api_key_id (dispatch.go:326-329), set to ident.KeyID at instance creation (controlapi/instances.go:312). The e2e harness only passes because it works around this: test/scenarios/host_agent_harness_test.go:100 sets cfg.APIKey = ownerKeyID (the ID, not the key).
verify_note: REAL BUG: hostagent/run.go:241 sends Register ApiKey: cfg.APIKey (=RIMSKY_API_KEY plaintext); proxy agent_server.go:45-47 uses the presented value verbatim as routing key (no plaintext->ID resolution); dispatch.go:100 routes by ownerAPIKeyID=created_by_api_key_id=ident.KeyID. harness host_agent_harness_test.go:100 sets cfg.APIKey=ownerKeyID to work around. Documented flow yields host_agent_not_connected -> major.
remediation: Resolve the agent's Register identity from the CLI active-context config as the api-key ID, falling back to --api-key/$RIMSKY_API_KEY, instead of sending the raw bearer token or defaulting to anonymous.

summary: host-agent.md invariant (line 27) says the agent "reads auth from the CLI's active-context config", but `rimsky agent start` resolves the api-key only from --api-key/$RIMSKY_API_KEY and never reads the active context, so a user who ran `rimsky auth login` silently registers as "anonymous" and owner-routed dispatches miss their agent.
evidence: runAgentStart builds config via `hostagent.LoadConfigFromEnv()` plus the --api-key/--proxy flags (agent.go:52-77); LoadConfigFromEnv reads $RIMSKY_API_KEY (lib/runtime/hostagent/config.go:31). The active-context config exists and stores the key — `rimsky auth login` writes `current.APIKey = key` into ~/.rimsky/config.yml (auth_login.go:87), and Context has an APIKey field (config.go) — but no agent code calls LoadConfig/ResolveEndpoint. With no key, Run substitutes AnonymousRoutingIdentity (run.go:103-105). The config plumbing the invariant describes exists; the agent path never consumes it, so the code is the stale side.
verify_note: host-agent.md:27 says the agent 'reads auth from the CLI's active-context config', but agent.go:65 builds config via hostagent.LoadConfigFromEnv() + --api-key only (config.go:28 reads $RIMSKY_API_KEY); no call to the CLI active-context loader auth_login writes; run.go:103 falls back to AnonymousRoutingIdentity when empty. Code never consumes the documented plumbing -> major.
phase1_note: The design corpus has already been corrected by the remediation pass to explicitly say there is NO active-context config for the agent -- the exact opposite of what the finding's cited invariant said. Current code (LoadConfigFromEnv + --api-key/--proxy flags, no active-context read) now matches the corrected doc and the dossier exactly. The doc was the stale side and has already been fixed; the finding is refuted against current sources.

summary: The as-is story host-agent-control-plane's acceptance requires the status verb to report "the list of currently-spawned children (per run-scope, per binding)", but `rimsky agent status` reports only pid/proxy/since — the agent never records children in the status file at all.
evidence: runAgentStatus prints connected/disconnected with pid, proxy, since only (agent.go:167-206); statusSnapshot has just Connected/Proxy/Since fields (agent.go:286-290 and lib/runtime/hostagent/run.go:189-193), and writeStatusFile is called only with connection state (run.go:162-166) — no spawned-children data exists anywhere on the status surface, contradicting stories/host-agent-control-plane.md Acceptance.
verify_note: stories/host-agent-control-plane.md:22 requires status to report 'the list of currently-spawned children'; runAgentStatus (agent.go:167-206) reports only connected/proxy/since, statusSnapshot has no children fields, children (run.go:57) never written to status. Story acceptance unmet (dup family of 2320) -> major.

summary: AdvertiseInto unconditionally overwrites the discovery-cache entry for every bundled executor, so when a configured endpoint overrides a bundled executor (an explicitly supported scenario) the cache reports the in-proc handler's schema/tags for an executor actually dispatched to the remote endpoint, and Static:true means the real endpoint is never probed or refreshed.
evidence: lib/control/launch/supervisor.go:158-166 skips resolver.Register for overridden names (logging "bundled executor overridden by configured endpoint") but then calls bundledRegs.AdvertiseInto(disc) for ALL bundled names, clobbering the handshake-probed PeerEntry for the configured remote; lib/control/config/controlapi.go:180-182 has the same unconditional call after RunHandshake. Dispatch then validates against the bundled ExpectedAttributesSchema (via NewExpectedAttributesSchemaResolver) while executing against the remote executor.
verify_note: config/bundled.go:46-61 AdvertiseInto unconditionally SetExecutor(Static:true) with bundled schema for every advert; launch/supervisor.go:166 + config/controlapi.go:181 call it after RunHandshake even when a configured endpoint overrides a bundled executor. The handshake-probed remote PeerEntry is clobbered by the in-proc bundled schema, so dispatch validates against the wrong ExpectedAttributesSchema and Static:true blocks re-probe -> major.
remediation: Skip AdvertiseInto (or mark non-static/probeable) when a configured endpoint overrides a bundled executor so the cache reflects the real endpoint.

summary: Publishers cannot actually opt in as lifecycle subscribers even though the concept doc names publisher as a subscribing primary protocol and Purpose cites the publisher provision/teardown archetype: DialLifecycleSubscribers dials only claim-producers and executors, so a publisher declaring lifecycle_subscriber is silently ignored.
evidence: concepts/lifecycle-subscriber.md line 11 says opt-in works for 'claim-producer, executor, or publisher' and 'Any peer-service kind can subscribe'; line 15 names 'publishers that provision substrate at template-deploy and tear it down at undeploy' as an enabled archetype. But DialLifecycleSubscribers(ctx, stores RemoteClaimProducersConfig, execs ExecutorsConfig) (claim_producers.go:588-617) iterates only stores.ClaimProducers and execs.Executors — both call sites (config/controlapi.go:126, config/supervisor.go:106) pass no publishers. Meanwhile the config layer accepts lifecycle_subscriber in a publisher's protocol list (ValidProtocols at claim_producers.go:514 via validateProtocols call at :319) and the fan-out candidate set includes publisher names (peersReferencedBySpec at controlapi/lifecycle.go:445-450 walks spec.Publishers), so a subscribed publisher validates fine, is enumerated as a fan-out peer, then always misses the registry lookup (lifecycle.go:109-113 'not_subscribed' skip) and never receives an event. The candidate-set support and config acceptance show the code side is the incomplete half.
verify_note: claim_producers.go:588 DialLifecycleSubscribers takes only ClaimProducers+Executors; call sites (controlapi.go:126, supervisor.go:106) pass no publishers. validateProtocols accepts lifecycle_subscriber for publishers, so a subscribing publisher validates but is never dialed — silently dropped, contradicting lifecycle-subscriber.md:11,15 -> major.
remediation: Extend DialLifecycleSubscribers to also dial publishers declaring lifecycle_subscriber, matching the concept naming publisher as a subscribing primary protocol.
phase1_note: The 2026-06-19 fix only repaired the fan-out CANDIDATE set (peersReferencedBySpec now walks spec.Publishers); the dial/registration step (DialLifecycleSubscribers) was never extended to dial publishers, so a publisher declaring lifecycle_subscriber still validates at registration, is enumerated as a fan-out candidate, but is never in the lifecycle registry and is silently skipped as not_subscribed at fan-out time. Fix: extend DialLifecycleSubscribers to also dial publishers advertising lifecycle_subscriber (needs a publishers config param threaded through both call sites).

summary: config.StartSupervisor never wires runtime.Config.DeclaredTagsFor from the discovery cache (config.SupervisorConfig has no such field), so the supervisor's undeclared-tag rejection only ever sees builtin vocabularies and the invariant that undeclared tag emissions are rejected at the supervisor's terminal handler is silently unenforced for every out-of-process and bundled executor.
evidence: runtime.Config.DeclaredTagsFor exists (lib/runtime/supervisor.go:47) and gates validateTags' executor_protocol_violation rejection (lib/runtime/runner_dispatch.go:331-336: nil/!ok hook → tags accepted unvalidated), but the runtime.Start call at lib/control/config/supervisor.go:144-170 sets ExpectedAttributesSchemaFor and omits DeclaredTagsFor, and no call site anywhere sets it (only the builtin overlay at lib/runtime/supervisor.go:131-141 fires). Contradicts lib/protocols/proto/v1/executor_observability.proto:52-60 ("checks each emission's tags against declared_tags, and rejects emissions of undeclared names") and .ok-planner/design/concepts/terminal-tag.md:28 ("emissions of undeclared names are rejected at the supervisor's terminal handler").
verify_note: config/supervisor.go SupervisorConfig has no DeclaredTagsFor field; runtime.Start (supervisor.go:143-170) sets schema resolver but omits tags-resolver; only builtin overlay (runtime/supervisor.go:131-141) populates it. validateTags (runner_dispatch.go:331-336) returns unvalidated on !ok, so out-of-process/bundled executor tags never rejected — contradicts terminal-tag.md:28 -> major.
remediation: Add a DeclaredTagsFor source to SupervisorConfig and wire it in config.StartSupervisor so undeclared-tag rejection covers out-of-process and bundled executors, not just builtins.

summary: TestRegistryCoversRouter — the mechanical proof of the doc's load-bearing 'an unmapped operation is a wiring bug' invariant — rebuilds a parallel route list that has already drifted from NewApp: it omits registerDebugOverrideRoutes and registerFramesRoutes, so those route families escape the registry-coverage check.

summary: The held-frames diagnostics endpoint (and the held-frames gauge) surfaces only parked-state runs, while the concept doc defines a held frame as one with a node-run in `parked` OR `held` and explicitly says held-claim (holding-subgraph) work is surfaced there.
evidence: frame.md:28 says a frame is held when a run is 'parked ... or held (executor returned a held-claim terminal ...)' and 'Held frames are surfaced via a held-frames diagnostics endpoint'. handleAdminHeldFrames builds its response solely from listParkedDiagnostic, whose query is `WHERE d.state = 'parked'` (lib/foundation/persistence/postgres/queue_park.go:114, sqlite/queue_park.go equivalent); CountHeldFrames is likewise `WHERE f.ended_at IS NULL AND d.state = 'parked'` (postgres/frames.go:394-406, sqlite/frames.go:503-515). The route's own registered description agrees with the doc against the implementation: lib/control/controlapi/actions.go:384 'List frames held by holding-subgraph claims.' — yet a frame whose only in-flight run is in state 'held' never appears in the endpoint or the gauge.
verify_note: frame.md:28 defines held frame as node_run in 'held' OR 'parked' surfaced via the held-frames endpoint; handleAdminHeldFrames (admin_diagnostics.go:79) builds solely from ListParkedDiagnostic (queue_park.go:114 state='parked') and CountHeldFrames (frames.go:400 state='parked'). The route description actions.go:384 'List frames held by holding-subgraph claims' is the held-state case the query never returns -> major (functional gap).
remediation: admin_diagnostics.go: surface held (not only parked) node-runs in the held-frames endpoint and gauge, per the concept definition.
phase1_note: The design corpus has already been corrected to explicitly document that the held-frames diagnostic intentionally reports only the parked subset of held frames, not held-claim (state='held') holds -- exactly matching current code, and directly corroborated by the frame intent dossier's transcript-tier ruling. The finding's premise (that omitting held-state runs is a bug) is refuted. Adjacent nit not part of this finding's scope: actions.go:384's route description ('List frames held by holding-subgraph claims') still overclaims relative to the corrected doc and could use a wording fix, but that is a separate, much smaller issue than what was alleged here.

summary: GET /instances/{id}/assets/{alias} surfaces a committed-durable claim against a non-data-processing producer as an asset, contradicting the doc's invariant that such claims are "not surfaced as an asset" — and making the asset surface internally inconsistent, since the list endpoint filters those rows out.
evidence: handleListAssets (assets.go:103-111) applies buildDataProcessingPredicate and skips rows whose producer does not advertise "data_processing"; resolveAsset (assets.go:183-227), used by handleGetAsset (246), handleAssetVersions, and handleDeleteAsset, only filters by state=committed + lifetime=durable + node/producer match, with no capability check. So an alias absent from the list response is still returned by GET as an asset. claim-lifetime.md:22: "just not surfaced as an asset"; asset.md:12: "Assets are surfaced by querying claim handles that are committed and durable against data-processing-advertising producers." (Note: the DELETE path skipping the filter may be deliberate — claim-lifetime.md:14 routes ALL durable release through this endpoint — but GET vs LIST cannot both be right.)
verify_note: handleGetAsset via resolveAsset (assets.go:183-227,270,287) has NO data_processing capability check — returns a committed+durable claim against a non-data-processing producer as an asset — while handleListAssets applies buildDataProcessingPredicate (assets.go:108). Violates asset.md invariant 2; GET and LIST disagree on what an asset is -> major (real code bug).
remediation: Have resolveAsset (and the detail/history/delete endpoints) require the producer to advertise data-processing before surfacing a committed+durable claim as an asset, matching the list endpoint and the doc invariant.
phase1_note: Still true at dev tip: resolveAsset backs GET /instances/{id}/assets/{alias} with no data-processing capability check, while handleListAssets applies buildDataProcessingPredicate -- an alias absent from LIST is still returned by GET, contradicting the asset compound definition both the dossier and the concept doc agree on. Fix: apply the same data-processing capability check inside resolveAsset (or at its GET/history/delete call sites) as handleListAssets already does.

summary: resolveAsset never checks that the producer advertises data-processing, so the asset detail, materialization-history, and delete endpoints treat any committed+durable claim as an asset, contradicting the doc's invariant that such a claim 'is not an asset'.
evidence: resolveAsset (assets.go:183-227) matches only on ListByInstanceAndState(committed, durable) + producer-name lookup; handleGetAsset (line 287), handleAssetMaterializationHistory (line 411), and handleDeleteAsset (line 451) all serve/delete the result with no capability check. Only handleListAssets applies buildDataProcessingPredicate (line 108) and only handleAssetVersions gates via deps.DataProcessors (line 345). asset.md:22 ('A durable-lifetime claim against a producer lacking that capability is ... not an asset') and claim-lifetime.md ('just not surfaced as an asset') both say these endpoints must not resolve it — so GET /instances/{id}/assets/{alias} returns 200 and DELETE releases/deletes a non-asset durable claim.
verify_note: resolveAsset (assets.go:183-227) matches only committed+durable+producer-name, no data-processing capability check; handleGetAsset:287, handleAssetMaterializationHistory:411, handleDeleteAsset:451 serve/delete without check, violating asset.md:22 invariant; only list + versions gate. Same family as 96 -> major.
phase1_note: Same underlying gap as 96 (resolveAsset lacks the data-processing capability check), affecting detail, materialization-history, and delete in addition to GET. One fix (gating resolveAsset itself) closes both 96 and 97.

summary: The in-flight-run refusal in handleDeleteAsset is check-then-act: the active-holder check runs in one transaction, then Release and DeleteResolved run afterwards (Release outside any tx, delete in a second tx), so a run that co-holds the committed-durable claim in between is not refused and loses the claim under it.
evidence: assets.go:443-472 lists ClaimHolders and checks State==Active inside the first Transaction; producer.Release fires at line 509 and DeleteResolved in a fresh Transaction at line 515-517. postgres/claim_handles.go:290-305 DeleteResolved guards only `state IN ('committed','abandoned') AND holder_supervisor_id IS NULL` — committed-durable co-holding (claim-lifetime.md: 'available for future dispatches to co-hold') adds holder rows without changing handle state, so the delete succeeds despite a newly active holder, breaking asset.md:24's 'refuses if any in-flight run holds the claim'.
verify_note: REAL TOCTOU: handleDeleteAsset (assets.go) checks active holders in tx1 (~443-472), then producer.Release outside any tx (~509) and DeleteResolved in tx2 (~515). postgres/claim_handles.go:295-297 DeleteResolved guards only state IN('committed','abandoned') AND holder_supervisor_id IS NULL — no active-holder check. A committed-durable co-hold acquired in the window adds an active claim_holders row without changing handle state, so delete proceeds and cascade-strips the live co-holder, violating asset.md:24 -> major.
remediation: assets.go handleDeleteAsset: perform the active-holder check and Release/DeleteResolved atomically so a run co-holding the durable claim in between is refused.

summary: handleDeleteAsset silently skips the producer's release verb when deps.ClaimProducers is nil or the producer is not registered, then deletes the handle row anyway, violating the doc's invariant that delete 'releases the claim handle via the producer's release verb' and leaking producer-side state.
evidence: assets.go:507-514: `if deps.ClaimProducers != nil && row.ProducerName != nil { if producer, ok := deps.ClaimProducers.Get(...); ok { ...Release... } }` — every negative branch falls through to the DeleteResolved transaction at line 515 with no error, no log. asset.md:24 states the release verb is part of the delete contract; the producer-side durable resource is never released while rimsky's ledger row disappears.
verify_note: assets.go:507-514: producer Release runs only when ClaimProducers != nil AND producer registered; every negative branch falls through to DeleteResolved (:516) with no error/log, deleting the ledger row while the producer resource is never released. Violates asset.md:24 delete-release contract -> major (silent leak).
remediation: Do not delete the handle row when the producer is nil/unregistered; require the release verb to run first so producer-side state is not leaked.
phase1_note: Confirmed still present: Release is called only when deps.ClaimProducers != nil AND the producer is registered; every negative branch falls straight through to DeleteResolved with no error or log, deleting rimsky's ledger row while the producer-side durable resource is never released -- a silent leak against the delete contract both the dossier and the doc state as mandatory. Fix: fail the delete (don't proceed to DeleteResolved) when the producer can't be reached to Release, rather than silently skipping.

summary: The revoke last-key guard is a check-then-act outside any transaction: two concurrent revokes of the last two active keys each see ActiveCount=2 and both succeed, leaving zero active keys and silently flipping the deployment into anonymous (admit-all-as-admin) mode without the force_leave_anonymous flag — breaking the documented invariant in both api-key.md (Revoke bullet) and anonymous-mode.md (Revoke-the-last-key guard).
evidence: auth_handlers.go:211 active, err := keys.ActiveCount(ctx, now, nil) and :231 keys.MarkRevoked(ctx, row.ID, now, nil) run as separate statements with tx=nil (no Transaction wrapper, no row lock). The guard at :219 (thisRowActive && active <= 1 && !force) is evaluated on a stale count; MarkRevoked's WHERE clause only checks revoked_at IS NULL on the target row, so both concurrent revokes commit and IsAnonymousMode subsequently returns true.
verify_note: REAL TOCTOU: auth_handlers.go:211 keys.ActiveCount(...,nil) and :231 keys.MarkRevoked(...,nil) run as separate statements with tx=nil (no lock). Guard at :219 (thisRowActive && active<=1 && !force) is check-then-act: two concurrent revokes of the last two active keys each read active=2, both skip the guard, both commit -> zero active keys -> IsAnonymousMode flips to admit-all-as-admin without force_leave_anonymous. Breaks revoke-last-key invariant (confirms batch8 id 2177 by-omission) -> major.
remediation: Enforce the leave-anonymous guard atomically across all last-key removal paths (transactional/locked check on concurrent revoke, plus a guard on key expiry and rotation-grace revoke_at).

summary: The doc's invariants say operators 'cannot stay in anonymous mode after a key exists without explicitly revoking it' and 'returning the deployment to anonymous mode must do so explicitly' (force flag), but the code lets the deployment silently fall back into anonymous mode when the last active key expires or its rotation-grace revoke_at passes — no guard exists on those paths.
evidence: ActiveCount (lib/foundation/persistence/postgres/api_keys.go:127-130 and the sqlite twin) excludes rows where expires_at or revoke_at has passed, so the predicate flips to anonymous the instant the sole key's expiry lapses. handleCreateKey (auth_handlers.go:56-159) accepts an arbitrary ExpiresAt with no last-key or past-expiry validation, and handleRotateKey copies oldRow.ExpiresAt to the replacement. The force_leave_anonymous guard (auth_handlers.go:219) evaluates `active <= 1` only at revoke time, so rotate-then-revoke-the-new-key passes the guard (old key still active under grace) yet returns the deployment to anonymous mode when the grace expires. Net effect: an all-requests-are-admin state can be re-entered with no explicit operator confirmation, defeating the guard invariant documented at .ok-planner/design/concepts/anonymous-mode.md lines 26 and 29; only the 5-minute WARN banner mitigates. Ruling the code stale because the guard exists precisely to make return-to-anonymous explicit and the expiry/grace paths bypass it.
verify_note: postgres/api_keys.go:124-130 ActiveCount excludes expired/past-revoke_at rows, so the anonymous predicate flips the instant the sole key's expiry lapses. handleCreateKey (auth_handlers.go:56-159) accepts arbitrary ExpiresAt with no last-key/past-expiry guard; force_leave_anonymous (auth_handlers.go:219) fires only at revoke time. Deployment silently re-enters all-admin anonymous mode, contradicting anonymous-mode.md:26,29 -> major (security-relevant, banner-mitigated).
phase1_note: Confirmed still present: the explicit revoke path is guarded (force_leave_anonymous), but ActiveCount's predicate flips to zero the instant the sole active key's expires_at or rotation-grace revoke_at lapses, with no guard on those paths -- the deployment silently re-enters all-admin anonymous mode without any explicit operator action, contradicting the doc's unconditional invariant. Fix: refuse (or WARN-and-require-force) a create/rotate that would leave zero non-expiring active keys, or otherwise close the expiry/grace re-entry path.

summary: The doc invariant rejects notify-only mode combined with a blocking overflow policy, but the code only rejects block_dispatch; notify_only + auto_resume_after_ttl is accepted even though auto_resume_after_ttl also blocks the runner at overflow.
evidence: resolveOverflowPolicy (breakpoints.go:446-448) rejects only mode==notify_only && policy==block_dispatch. But handleOverflow (lib/runtime/breakpoint_eval.go:187-191) treats OverflowBlockDispatch and OverflowAutoResumeAfterTTL identically — both poll until the unresumed count drops below the 100-hit cap — so a notify_only breakpoint with auto_resume_after_ttl blocks dispatch once 100 unresumed notify hits accumulate (notify hits are only ever freed by the sweeper after hit_ttl). breakpoint.md:31 says "Notify-only mode combined with a blocking overflow policy is rejected at registration (the policy contradicts the mode's non-blocking semantics)" — auto_resume_after_ttl is a blocking policy, so the registration check under-enforces the documented invariant.
verify_note: breakpoint.md:31 rejects notify-only + any blocking overflow policy at registration; resolveOverflowPolicy (breakpoints.go:446-447) rejects only notify_only+block_dispatch. handleOverflow (breakpoint_eval.go:187-192) groups BlockDispatch and AutoResumeAfterTTL into the same block branch, so notify_only+auto_resume_after_ttl blocks at the 100-hit cap yet passes registration -> major.
remediation: Reject notify_only combined with auto_resume_after_ttl (not just block_dispatch), since auto_resume_after_ttl also blocks the runner at overflow.
phase1_note: The dossier (higher authority than the concept doc) explicitly ratifies notify_only+auto_resume_after_ttl as a legal combination, so the finding's literal remediation (reject that combination at registration) is wrong direction. But the underlying complaint is real: handleOverflow currently blocks the calling goroutine identically for BlockDispatch and AutoResumeAfterTTL, so a notify_only breakpoint with auto_resume_after_ttl genuinely blocks the runner once the 100-hit cap is reached -- violating the doc's non-blocking-notify_only invariant at the runtime level, not the registration level. Fix: make AutoResumeAfterTTL's overflow handling non-blocking for notify_only mode (or otherwise differentiate it from BlockDispatch) in handleOverflow, leaving resolveOverflowPolicy's registration check as-is.

summary: failHeldHolderClaims passes the sentinel string "instance-killed" as the claimant-guard supervisor id, so FailAllActiveByClaimHandle can never match and co-holder rows are silently never marked failed on instance termination.
evidence: instances.go:771 calls `deps.Persist.ClaimHolders().FailAllActiveByClaimHandle(ctx, h.ClaimHandleID, "instance-killed", tx)`. The implementation (lib/foundation/persistence/postgres/claim_holders.go:125-141) guards the UPDATE with `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM rimsky_claim_handles WHERE id = $1 AND holder_supervisor_id = $2)` — no supervisor is ever named "instance-killed", so the UPDATE matches zero rows every time. The sibling call sites pass a real supervisor id (runner_terminal_release.go:140 passes args.SupervisorID; sweep_parked.go:239 passes holderSupervisorID). Consequence: on force-terminate, held runs' co-holder rows stay 'active' forever while abandonInFlightClaims (instances.go:778-797) promotes the handle to abandoned with the row's real HolderSupervisorID; the doc's poison-rule invariant (claim-handle.md line 68: "every still-active holder's co-holder row is marked failed") is not upheld on this path.
verify_note: REAL BUG: instances.go:771 passes sentinel 'instance-killed' as supervisorID; claimantGuard (postgres/claim_handles.go) emits holder_supervisor_id = $2, so FailAllActiveByClaimHandle's EXISTS (claim_holders.go:125-141) never matches — co-holder rows never marked failed on force-terminate. Sentinel only at this call site; siblings pass real ids. Contradicts claim-handle.md:68 poison rule -> major.
remediation: Pass the real supervisor id (not the 'instance-killed' sentinel) to FailAllActiveByClaimHandle in failHeldHolderClaims, and add a scenario test for the instance-terminate held-claim path.

summary: handleMoveTag (PUT /v1/tags/{tag}) and handleDeleteTag (DELETE /v1/tags/{tag}, line 193) perform no compose-prefix check, so any non-compose client can retarget or delete a compose:-managed tag, violating the documented server-enforced reservation.
evidence: control-api.md:27 states 'requests originating outside compose are rejected when they target it', and rimsky.md:28 says the compose workflow relies on the prefix namespace to scan/diff/teardown project artifacts via the server's tag tables. The only compose check on the tag surface is in handleCreateTag (tags.go:65); handleMoveTag (tags.go:143-191) Upserts any existing tag — including compose:* — to a new template hash, and handleDeleteTag (tags.go:193-229) deletes it, both without consulting isComposeOrigin. A plain tag:set/tag:delete grant holder can therefore silently corrupt compose-managed project state out from under the compose flow. tag.md:26 documents create-only enforcement, so the concept catalog is also internally inconsistent about the invariant's scope; the enforcement gap on mutation/deletion defeats the reservation's stated purpose either way.
verify_note: control-api.md:27 says the compose prefix is server-enforced so outside-compose requests targeting it are rejected. Only handleCreateTag checks (tags.go:65); handleMoveTag (tags.go:143) and handleDeleteTag (tags.go:193) Upsert/Delete any tag incl compose:* with no compose check — a tag:set/tag:delete grant holder can retarget/delete compose-managed tags. Real enforcement gap; tag.md:26 correctly scopes to tag-create, so control-api.md is the drifting doc -> major.
remediation: Add the compose:-prefix reservation check to handleMoveTag, handleDeleteTag, and the tag upsert in template registration so non-compose clients cannot retarget/delete/create compose-managed tags.
phase1_note: Both intent dossiers (tag and control-api, independently distilled but tracing to the same 2026-06-06 session) and tag.md consistently scope the server-enforced compose-prefix reservation to CREATE only. Ordinary move/delete of an existing compose:-tagged tag by a caller holding the normal tag:set/tag:delete permission grant is not described anywhere as requiring an additional compose-origin check -- normal permission scoping governs it like any other tag. The finding's premise (that move/delete must also gate on compose-origin) is refuted by the create-only reading three independent artifacts agree on. Note: control-api.md:27's broader phrasing ('requests originating outside compose are rejected when they target it') is itself imprecise relative to tag.md and the dossiers and should eventually be narrowed to match -- but that is a doc-only fix outside this code-cluster row.

summary: Template registration with a tag parameter (POST /v1/templates) upserts the tag with no compose-prefix check, letting a non-compose client create or retarget a compose:-prefixed tag and bypass the reservation enforced on POST /v1/tags.
evidence: handleDeployTemplate validates the tag only with validTag() (templates.go:195), then Upserts it unconditionally at templates.go:288-295 (existing-template branch) and templates.go:331-333 (new-template branch). validTag's pattern (tags.go:20) admits ':' so 'compose:project:x' passes. The identical operation via POST /tags is rejected at tags.go:65 per control-api.md:27's invariant ('requests originating outside compose are rejected when they target it'), so the register path is an enforcement hole in the same namespace.
verify_note: control-api.md:27 says the compose: tag prefix is server-enforced. handleDeployTemplate validates tag only with validTag (templates.go:195; tagPattern admits ':'), then Upserts unconditionally (:289-291,331-333) with zero compose checks, while POST /tags rejects compose-prefixed tags from non-compose origin (tags.go:64-66). Enforcement hole in the same tag namespace via deploy -> major.
phase1_note: Same reasoning as 104: the create-only compose-prefix reservation, corroborated by two independently-distilled intent dossiers plus tag.md, does not require a compose-origin check on the template-registration tag-upsert path either, since template registration with an existing tag name is functionally a tag move/create by an ordinarily-permissioned caller, not a foreign-client compose impersonation attempt.

summary: computeCascadeGraph ignores its transaction error, so GET /v1/observability/instances/{id} returns a cascade_graph whose run summaries and last terminal events are all silently absent when the read fails.
evidence: cascade_graph.go line 39: `_ = deps.Tables.Transaction(ctx, func(...)` — if Events().LastTerminalByNodes or Nodes().GetRunSummary errors, `terminals` stays nil and `summaries` stays empty, and the handler (handler.go handleGetInstance, line 349) still writes 200 with a graph of nodes that appear to have never run.
verify_note: cascade_graph.go:39 '_ = deps.Tables.Transaction(...)' discards the read error; on read failure terminals stays nil and computeCascadeGraph still yields a graph the handler writes 200. Silent observability degradation on read failure only; no execution-path impact.

summary: handleGetNode discards the errors of three of its four transactions, so on a DB failure it returns HTTP 200 with silently empty holdings, events, and latest_attributes instead of an error.
evidence: handler.go lines 448, 454, 461 each read `_ = inTx(r.Context(), deps.Tables, ...)`; only the first ListByInstance transaction (line 428) checks its error. Same pattern at handleGetNodeRun line 571 (`_ = inTx(...)` around the claim-handle/node enrichment), which silently omits claim_id/instance_id/node_type on failure. An operator dashboard showing a node with an empty attribute bag and zero events during a transient DB error is wrong data presented as truth. The four separate transactions also mean the response is a non-atomic snapshot, which sits uneasily beside the concept doc's per-handler short-fresh-transaction invariant.
verify_note: observability/handler.go:447,453,461 '_ = inTx(...)' discard errors on holdings/events/latest-attributes enrichment; handleGetNodeRun:571 same. Returns 200 with silently-empty sections on transient DB error; observability-only, bounded -> minor.

summary: Shared blob handles are orphan-queued while still referenced: SnapshotBagForNewRun copies value_handle onto the new run's attribute row, then Upsert on the new run enrolls that copied handle as an orphan even though the older run's row still points at it, so the sweep reaps a still-referenced blob and the older row's bag silently reads as empty.
evidence: postgres/node_attributes.go:303-311 (and sqlite/node_attributes.go:351-358) INSERT the new run's row with the prior row's value_handle/value_handle_backend. postgres/node_attributes.go:147-153 then queues QueueBlobOrphan(priorHandle) whenever the new run's Upsert replaces it (priorHandle != newHandle), with no check that other rows reference the same handle. After the retention sweep deletes the blob, scanAttributeRow's ErrBlobNotFound branch (lines 60-63) returns an empty map with no error or log — silent loss of the persisted per-run record; and if the newer row is deleted by DeletePriorCascadeStales and a later SnapshotBagForNewRun re-copies the reaped handle, live carry-forward hydration reads an empty bag.
verify_note: REAL: SnapshotBagForNewRun (postgres/node_attributes.go:303) copies prior row's value_handle onto the new run (shared handle). Upsert:147 QueueBlobOrphan(priorHandle) when priorHandle!=newHandle with no refcount; blob_spill.go:30 unconditional; orphan_blobs.go:64 reapOneBlobOrphan deletes unconditionally; scanAttributeRow:60-63 then returns empty map with no error on ErrBlobNotFound — silent loss of still-referenced prior-run record. Narrow (spill+carry-forward+differing rewrite) but real -> major.

summary: Spilled scratch blobs are never enrolled in the orphan-blob ledger, violating the concept's invariant "Orphan blobs go to a persisted orphan-blob ledger and are swept after a retention window" — replaced or dropped scratch blobs leak permanently in the filesystem and pg-largeobject backends.
evidence: WriteScratchInTx (postgres/queue_park.go:369-375, sqlite/queue_park.go:364-391) overwrites scratch_handle/scratch_handle_backend without reading the prior handle or calling persistence.QueueBlobOrphan; the only callers of QueueBlobOrphan in the tree are the two node_attributes.Upsert impls (postgres/node_attributes.go:149, sqlite/node_attributes.go:166). Run-row deletion paths (postgres/nodes.go:888 DeletePriorCascadeStales, :936 DropPendingRun) likewise delete rimsky_node_runs rows carrying scratch_handle without enrollment. blob-backend.md line 26 states the invariant; the scratch spill surface bypasses it entirely.
verify_note: WriteScratchInTx (queue_park.go:369-375) overwrites scratch_handle via raw UPDATE without QueueBlobOrphan; node-run deletion paths (nodes.go:884 DeletePriorCascadeStales, :932 DropPendingRun) delete rows carrying scratch_handle with no enrollment. Spilled scratch blobs bypass the orphan-blob ledger, violating blob-backend.md:26 -> major (leak on fs/pg-largeobject).
remediation: On park, enroll replaced or dropped scratch blob handles into rimsky_blob_orphans so the sweep reclaims them instead of leaking on filesystem/pg-largeobject backends.
phase1_note: Confirmed on current tree: WriteScratchInTx overwrites scratch_handle/scratch_handle_backend via a raw UPDATE with no read-prior-handle-and-QueueBlobOrphan step (the only QueueBlobOrphan callers remain the two node_attributes.Upsert impls); DeletePriorCascadeStales and DropPendingRun still delete node-run rows carrying scratch_handle with no enrollment. blob-backend dossier requires 'SweepOrphanedBlobs: a dedicated foundation sweep removing orphaned handles (deleted rows, overwritten values)'. fix-code: enroll replaced/dropped scratch blob handles into rimsky_blob_orphans at both spill-overwrite and node-run-deletion sites on both backends.

summary: The template validator carries a rule rejecting `lifetime: durable` against a producer that does not advertise data-processing, directly contradicting the doc's invariant that such a claim is legal ("still durable, just not surfaced as an asset"), and the rule's hook is never wired in production so it is a dead, contradiction-encoding check.
evidence: template_validator.go:1101-1108 emits error "lifetime = %q requires store %q to advertise the data_processing protocol (asset pattern)" when hooks.StoreAdvertisesDataProcessing is non-nil; claim-lifetime.md:22 says "A `durable` claim against a non-DataProcessing producer is still durable (the row persists), just not surfaced as an asset", and asset.md:23 agrees ("is a held-durable claim, not an asset"). rg shows StoreAdvertisesDataProcessing is set only in template_validator_holds_test.go — the sole production RegistryHooks construction (lib/control/controlapi/templates.go:84-140) never sets it, so the rule can never fire at a real registration. Either the rule (plus TestValidateClaimProducers_DurableRequiresDataProcessing) must go, or the two concept docs are wrong; the coherent doc corpus (asset.md, claim-lifetime.md, attribute.md:23) says the code rule is the stale side.
verify_note: template_validator.go:1101-1108 rejects lifetime:durable against a producer not advertising data_processing, contradicting claim-lifetime.md:22 and asset.md:22 ('still durable, just not surfaced as an asset'). hooks.StoreAdvertisesDataProcessing is set only in *_test.go, never in production RegistryHooks (templates.go:84-144) — so the rule is dead in prod (prod matches docs) but a test locks in the wrong side. Rule + test should be removed -> major.
remediation: Remove the rule rejecting lifetime:durable against a non-data-processing producer (the doc invariant makes it legal); it is dead and encodes a contradiction.
phase1_note: Verified current design corpus is unambiguous: asset.md invariant 'A durable-lifetime claim against a producer lacking that capability remains durable but is not surfaced as an asset' and claim-lifetime.md invariant 'A durable claim against a non-DataProcessing producer is still durable (the row persists), just not surfaced as an asset' both directly contradict the validator's rejection rule. hooks.StoreAdvertisesDataProcessing is still set only in test code (grep confirms), so the rule is dead in production today (production behavior matches the docs) but the rule + its locking test assert the wrong side. fix-code: delete the rule at template_validator.go:1101-1108 and its test.

summary: The doc says the property-shape rule (source XOR default XOR read-only XOR unconstrained) is re-enforced at dispatch when the executor schema wasn't visible at registration, but the dispatch-side check function has zero production callers.
evidence: Doc line 53: "rejected at registration, or at dispatch if the executor's schema wasn't visible at registration time ... runtime dispatch reapplies the rule once the schema is visible. Enforced by the template validator at registration and at dispatch." Code: `code:lib/graph/node/template_validator.go::CheckEffectiveAttributesSchema#1711` is the exported dispatch-side variant — `rg CheckEffectiveAttributesSchema lib/ | grep -v _test` returns only the definition. The dispatch path (`lib/runtime/runner_dispatch.go:362-365`) blocks only on total schema invisibility (`executorSchemaUnavailableError`); once the schema is visible it never reapplies the shape rule, so a property that soft-failed the read-only fallback leg at registration is never re-checked.
verify_note: template_validator.go:1711 CheckEffectiveAttributesSchema has zero production callers (only definition + runner_dispatch_test.go). resolveAttributes (runner_dispatch.go:360-366) blocks only on total schema-invisibility and never reapplies the property-shape rule once schema is visible. attribute.md:53 'runtime dispatch reapplies the rule ... Enforced at dispatch' — dispatch-side enforcement is dead code -> major.
remediation: Decide whether the dispatch-time property-shape (source XOR default XOR read-only XOR unconstrained) re-check should be wired on the production path or the doc claim retired.

summary: The hardcoded 5-minute orphan-hit reap deletes unresumed pause-mode hits even while a live runner is blocked on them, silently converting every block_dispatch pause longer than 5 minutes into a forced no-overlay auto-resume and purging notify-only hit records after 5 minutes.
evidence: scheduler.go:254 sets orphanedHitCutoff := bpNow.Add(-5 * time.Minute) and line 270 calls SweepOrphanedUnresumed, whose SQL (postgres/breakpoint_hits.go:223-236, sqlite/breakpoint_hits.go:240-263) deletes ALL hits with resumed_at IS NULL and overflow_policy <> 'auto_resume_after_ttl' older than the cutoff — it cannot distinguish an orphaned hit (dead runner) from one an operator is actively inspecting. The blocked runner's poll (breakpoint_eval.go:220-221) treats the missing row as resume-with-no-overlay, so the dispatch proceeds without operator action; notify_only hits (never resumed by design) vanish from the ledger after 5 minutes. This contradicts breakpoint.md's model (pause until resume/deletion; "pause-mode hits cannot be silently dropped", line 30) and hit_ttl_seconds is ignored for block_dispatch pauses.

Force-resumes live pauses >5min and reaps notify-only records, contradicting breakpoint.md pause-until-resume. Name says 'orphaned', SQL is time-only -> major.
remediation: Exclude hits with a live blocked runner (and notify-only records) from the orphan-hit reap so a block_dispatch pause longer than 5 minutes is not force-resumed or purged.

summary: Two coexisting implementations of the byte-equal conflict fallback disagree on empty-scope semantics: ErrScopesConflictUnsupportedFallback returns true for two empty byte streams while locks.ClaimScopesByteEqual returns false, so the protocol-layer fallback violates the documented 'empty byte streams never conflict' invariant and duplicates logic that must change together.

DRY divergence + invariant violation -> major.
remediation: Collapse ErrScopesConflictUnsupportedFallback and locks.ClaimScopesByteEqual to one shared implementation that returns false for two empty byte streams (empty-never-conflicts).

summary: routeHeldClaimVerbError promotes the claim handle to abandoned without firing the deferred held cascade, so co-holder node-runs that settled earlier are left in state held permanently.
evidence: On a classified producer-verb error, CheckAndFireResolution (auto_terminal.go:117-123) calls routeHeldClaimVerbError, which emits an error-policy signal and calls promoteHandleState directly (auto_terminal.go:156-161), then returns nil. emitDeferredHeldCascade — the only code that transitions a handle's holder runs held→fresh/failed (terminal_decision.go:130, held_cascade_defer.go:186-219) — is reached only via ResolveClaimHandleTerminal's success path, which already errored. The currently-settling run is rescued by transitionThisHolderIfFullyResolved in applyTerminalComplete (runner_terminal.go:236), but co-holders that reached held at earlier terminals have no remaining trigger: transitionHolderIfFullyResolved fires only from emitDeferredHeldCascade or a run's own terminal, and no sweep re-evaluates held runs against resolved handles (rg NodeStateHeld shows no such consumer). Those runs violate the doc's own Commit/Abandon transition invariant and stay held forever. Additionally, after a failed Commit the handle is stamped abandoned without the producer's Abandon verb ever firing, leaving the producer-side claim opened-but-unresolved.
verify_note: auto_terminal.go:119-161 routeHeldClaimVerbError emits an error signal and promoteHandleState(abandon) then returns nil, skipping emitDeferredHeldCascade (held_cascade_defer.go:186-219) — the only path transitioning co-holder held runs; only the settling run is rescued (runner_terminal.go:236). Co-holders held at earlier terminals have no re-evaluation trigger. Also stamps the handle abandoned without firing producer Abandon (no fireProducerVerb) -> major.
remediation: auto_terminal.go routeHeldClaimVerbError: fire the deferred held cascade on abandon so co-holder node-runs leave held instead of stuck permanently.

summary: Begin-candidate idempotency key is a freshly-minted random UUID per acquisition attempt, so the producer-side idempotency the concept doc's invariant 1 relies on can never engage, and candidates begun in an aborted acquisition transaction are orphaned producer-side with no compensating abandon.
evidence: AcquireSubClaims mints `subID := shared.UUID(uuid.New())` then calls `dpClient.BeginCandidate(... ClaimHandleID: subID.String(), IdempotencyKey: subID.String())` — both halves of the doc's 'claim-handle plus idempotency-key pair' are new randomness on every attempt. If the tx aborts after k BeginCandidate RPCs (e.g. the overlapping-scope rejection at runner_subclaim.go:121, an Insert error at :160, or any later tryAcquire failure), no AbandonCandidate is issued and the retry begins brand-new candidates under new keys, so producer staging (e.g. S3 prefixes) leaks unboundedly. data_processing.proto:53-54 documents the key as 'rimsky-side run_id-derived' (stable across retries), which the code contradicts; the conformance-enforced idempotent path (lib/protocols/conformance/dataprocessing/runner.go::checkBeginCandidateIdempotent) is dead from rimsky's perspective.
verify_note: runner_subclaim.go:126 mints fresh uuid.New() used as both ClaimHandleID and IdempotencyKey (:131,133) per attempt; data_processing.proto BeginCandidateRequest says key is 'run_id-derived', contradicted. No AbandonCandidate on tx-abort paths (:121,160,164). Idempotency invariant data-processing.md:21 cannot engage; producer-side leak path -> major.
remediation: Use a stable idempotency key for BeginCandidate and issue AbandonCandidate compensation for already-begun descriptors when a later descriptor fails in AcquireSubClaims.

summary: The retry invariant says 'the persisted attribute bag stays unchanged' across the in-place retry loop, but applyTerminalError upserts the executor's attributes_delta into the persisted bag BEFORE the policy resolves, so an errored outcome carrying attributes_delta whose class maps to retry mutates the persisted bag mid-loop.

Outcome_Error carries AttributesDelta (runner_dispatch.go:279-281). error-policy.md:39 states 'Claims stay acquired, the persisted attribute bag stays unchanged, the dispatch id is preserved'; concepts/node-run.md:94-95 likewise says the bag is built at exactly one moment per row. The retry branch of errorPolicySignal also deliberately omits the delta from the signal (runner_error_policy.go:308-318), suggesting the delta was meant for settling outcomes only — the pre-policy upsert violates the documented invariant.
verify_note: runner_terminal_handlers.go:24-29 unconditionally upserts attributes_delta into the persisted bag before applyErrorPolicyWithScratch resolves retry-vs-settle; error-policy.md:39 states retry keeps the persisted bag unchanged; retry signal omits the delta (runner_error_policy.go:308-318). Invariant violation on the error+delta+retry path (narrow trigger) -> major.
remediation: Defer upserting attributes_delta into the persisted bag until the error policy resolves to a terminal (non-retry) outcome, honoring the 'attribute bag stays unchanged across retry' invariant.
phase1_note: Confirmed on current tree: applyTerminalError still merges and (post the 07-15 validation-gate fix, see finding 136) validates and upserts attributes_delta into the persisted bag unconditionally BEFORE calling applyErrorPolicyWithScratch, which is where retry-vs-settle is decided. error-policy dossier: 'Claims stay acquired, the persisted attribute bag stays unchanged' during retry, and 'the retry branch of errorPolicySignal also deliberately omits the delta from the signal' -- confirming the delta is meant only for settling (non-retry) verdicts. fix-code: defer the upsert until after applyErrorPolicyWithScratch resolves to a non-retry (settling) outcome.

summary: The doc's invariant that the sibling row-lock 'closes the race against a parallel worker on the same supervisor that may be terminating the sibling natively' is not actually delivered by the code: the native terminal path reads the sibling row without a lock and fires the producer verb before any claimant-guarded write, so conflicting Commit and Abandon verbs can both reach the producer for the same claim_id.
evidence: cancel-siblings.md line 24 claims the LockForUpdate in cancelInFlightSiblings (lib/runtime/terminal_decision_cancel.go:60) closes the same-supervisor race because 'producer-side claim-id idempotency cannot reconcile distinct verbs (Commit vs Abandon)'. But the native path that resolves the same sibling — resolveLinkedSubClaimsInTx, lib/runtime/runner_terminal_release.go:68 — gates on `row.State != spec.ClaimHandleStateActive` via a plain (non-locking) ListByNodeRun read, then ResolveClaimHandleTerminal fires the producer verb at lib/runtime/terminal_decision.go:102 (fireProducerVerb) BEFORE any row-guarded write; releaseClaim (runner_terminal_release.go:153-207) has no state check at all. Under Postgres read-committed a plain SELECT does not block on the walker's FOR UPDATE, so while the cancel walker's tx holds the sibling lock and has sent Abandon, a concurrently-terminating worker snapshot-reads the sibling as active and sends Commit; it only blocks later at promoteHandleState's guarded UPDATE (terminal_decision.go:224), whose ErrIllegalClaimHandleTransition is swallowed with a warn (terminal_decision.go:228-235), after which its SettleFromFanoutChild can additionally bump a 'commit' count for a child already counted as 'abandon' (child_execution.go:295). The row lock serializes DB state transitions but not the producer verbs, which is exactly the corruption the doc says the lock prevents.
verify_note: cancel-siblings.md:24 claims LockForUpdate closes the same-supervisor native-vs-cancel race. But the native path is unlocked: resolveLinkedSubClaimsInTx reads via plain ListByNodeRun (runner_terminal_release.go:54), releaseClaim plain Get (153); ResolveClaimHandleTerminal fires fireProducerVerb (terminal_decision.go:102) BEFORE promoteHandleState. Under read-committed a plain SELECT doesn't block on FOR UPDATE, so a concurrent native Commit + forced Abandon both reach the producer for one claim_id (guarded-transition error swallowed). SettleFromFanoutChild lacks per-child dedup -> double parent-counter bump -> major.
remediation: Take the sibling row-lock before the native terminal path fires the producer verb (claimant-guarded), closing the race the invariant claims is closed.
phase1_note: Confirmed on current tree: resolveLinkedSubClaimsInTx still reads sibling rows via a plain (non-locking) ListByNodeRun, gates only on row.State != Active, and calls ResolveClaimHandleTerminal (which fires the producer verb before any row-guarded write) with no lock; releaseClaim similarly has no state check. cancel-siblings dossier states the LockForUpdate in the cancel walk 'closes the race against a parallel worker on the same supervisor that may be terminating the sibling natively' -- but the native path it must close against remains unlocked, so a concurrent native Commit and a forced cancel-walk Abandon can both reach the producer for one claim_id under Postgres read-committed. fix-code: take the sibling row lock before the native terminal path fires the producer verb, so the two paths actually serialize as the invariant claims.

summary: Every caller of PropagateIfChildAfterTerminal discards the returned []CancelAction, so AggregateActionCancelNonWinners (the `first` policy) and the run-level cancel-siblings action are computed but never executed — under `first`, non-winner clones run to completion and the parent claim cannot resolve until all of them finish, degenerating `first` to best_effort at the claim level.

summary: Under staged_async write semantics, a selector that is not a valid schema identifier silently falls through to the in-place path (address = canonical selector, no staging schema) while still returning RealizedWriteSemantics = staged_async, so the supervisor's coexistence matrix grants reader×writer coexistence on a scope whose writes are actually in-place.

summary: The idempotent rows say the comparison target is 'the currently-queued stale row', but the code's prior-row lookup also matches a still-PENDING prior cascade row (resolving its bag on demand), so dedup can fire against a row that has not yet reached stale.

summary: 'Compared against the currently-queued stale row' (singular, definite article) hides that under the idempotent modes multiple queued rows can coexist and only the MOST RECENT prior (highest sequence) is compared — dedup is consecutive-duplicate suppression, not queue-wide dedup.
evidence: GetPriorCascadeStaleNotClaimed (postgres/nodes.go:903-912) is ORDER BY sequence DESC LIMIT 1. Failure of the queue-wide reading: rounds resolving to bags A, B, A under idempotent-queue queue all three (the third is compared only to B), so a reader who took 'the currently-queued stale row' to mean the whole queue would expect two rows. The story's own headline ('My executor never sees consecutive identical inputs') states the consecutive semantics; the concept doc should too.

summary: Invariant 4 defines the failure vocabulary only for the executor and claim-producer fronts ("executor-error / claim-producer-unavailable terminals") even though invariant 7 says the proxy fronts five protocols; the failure surface for publisher, validation, and data-processing dispatches is unstated in the doc.

summary: The doc unconditionally says the agent authenticates "with the user's api-key" and never mentions anonymous registration, but the code registers under a well-known anonymous routing identity whenever no key is configured — a first-class mode the adjacent host-agent-proxy doc documents.

summary: "Serves spawn / dispatch / reap / local-HTTP-forward requests against locally-running binaries" inverts the direction of the fourth verb: local-HTTP-forward requests originate FROM the locally-running binaries (hitting the agent's local listener) and are forwarded toward rimsky via the proxy, not served against the binaries.

Rewrote the sentence to state the agent relays child-raised local-HTTP callback requests on to the proxy, and dropped '/local-HTTP-forward' from the serve-against-binaries clause since it isn't a request served against the binary.

summary: The invariant "No capability config; the agent does not know in advance what binaries exist" omits the allow-paths glob allowlist, which is exactly an advance agent-side configuration bounding which binary paths may be spawned (spawns outside it are refused).

A fresh reader of the invariant would not expect any pre-declared binary-path boundary on the agent.
verify_note: host-agent.md:21 'No capability config; agent does not know in advance what binaries exist' omits the optional allow-paths allowlist (config.go:19 AllowPaths, spawn.go:100-102 pathAllowed->spawnFailed). Optional (default open), boundary imprecision -> minor.
phase1_note: The no-discovery invariant is correct but incomplete: it omits the optional allow-paths boundary the dossier treats as a first-class (if optional) trust control. Appended a clause naming it without contradicting the no-capability-config claim.

summary: "absolute, relative, and bare-name paths all work via the shell search path" is misleading: no shell is involved, only bare names consult a search path (the PATH env lookup at command construction), and relative paths resolve against the spawn's effective cwd, not any search path.
evidence: SpawnService execs directly via `exec.Command(params.BinaryPath, ...)` (spawn.go:60) — Go resolves bare names with exec.LookPath over $PATH when the Command is constructed; absolute paths are used as-is and relative paths resolve relative to cmd.Dir (set from the Spawn/binding cwd, spawn.go:61-63,105-108). Lumping all three forms under "the shell search path" would steer a reader to a wrong resolution model.
verify_note: host-agent.md:24 'absolute, relative, and bare-name paths all work via the shell search path'; spawn.go:60 execs via exec.Command (no shell); bare names use Go LookPath over $PATH. Misleading resolution model -> minor.
phase1_note: This is not a contested design choice (no dossier or transcript ever proposed shelling out) — it is a plain mechanism misdescription in an otherwise-uncontested invariant (all three path forms working at exec time is undisputed). Corrected the mechanism description without changing the invariant's substance.

summary: "The agent has no persistent state of its own" reads as false to anyone who finds the status file the agent itself writes to disk (plus the pid file its CLI wrapper writes); the invariant needs qualification, e.g. no state consulted across restarts.

phase1_note: Dossier intent (no state consulted across restarts) holds and is unchanged; the doc's literal wording was falsifiable by the informational status/pid markers. Qualified the claim to what the dossier actually means: no state that changes behavior across restarts.

summary: 'A uniform discipline applied across two overlapping lists' opens the definition with an unresolved referent — the reader must guess that the 'two lists' are the carrier-stream list and the sub-discipline list, and 'overlapping' misdescribes their relationship (the second partitions a subset of the first).

summary: permission.md's Boundaries glosses the adjacent dry-run concept as "(orthogonal — the request flag, not a grant property)", which contradicts both its own earlier clause in the same sentence and dry-run.md's definition that dry-run resolves from EITHER the flag OR the identity-bound grant mode.

summary: The adjacent supervisor doc's invariant "Candidate selection skips paused instances and dispatches matching pause-mode breakpoints with unresumed hits" is garbled and, on its most natural reading, false: candidate selection does not consult breakpoints or hits at all — pause-mode blocking happens in the runner after selection.

Pause-mode blocking is implemented by the runner polling waitForResume after the hit is created (breakpoint_eval.go:148, 210-232), post-selection — so a reader of the sentence would look for a selection-time hit filter that does not exist.
verify_note: candidate-selection SQL carries no breakpoint/hit filter; pause-mode blocking is post-selection in runner (breakpoint_eval.go); supervisor.md:31 garbles the two into one sentence -> minor.

summary: The per-instance bindings cache is never evicted — OnInstanceTerminated is a no-op and nothing else deletes from proxyState.instances — so the map grows unboundedly in a long-running proxy, and stale terminated-instance entries permanently break instance-less routing for any service name later reused by another instance (lookupInstanceByBinding requires exactly one match).

summary: stagingSchemaName lossily folds arbitrary claim ids into [a-z0-9_] (case-folded, punctuation collapsed to '_'), so two distinct concurrently-open claim ids that differ only in case or punctuation map to the same staging schema, and openStaging's CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS silently co-mingles their staged writes.
evidence: staging.go:51-63: 'A'..'Z' → lowercase, any other non-[a-z0-9_] rune → '_'; e.g. claim ids `abc-1` and `abc_1` (or `ABC` and `abc`) both yield `rimsky_stg_abc_1`/`rimsky_stg_abc`. openStaging (staging.go:72-73) uses IF NOT EXISTS so the second Open succeeds against the first claim's schema, and the first claim's Commit swaps both writers' data. Safe only if claim ids are guaranteed lowercase UUIDs, which the claim-producer protocol does not promise (claim_id is an opaque string).
verify_note: claim_producer.proto:14 promises claim_id is a client-generated UUID; distinct UUIDs cannot collide under the case-fold/[a-z0-9_] map. Asserted co-mingling bug unreachable for conforming clients -> refuted.

summary: Invariant claims the reconciliation worker retries mounting rows 'with backoff'; the steady-state reconciler retries at a fixed interval, not backoff.
evidence: Doc (line 35): 'A reconciliation worker drives the subscribe handshake for mounting rows with backoff and no attempt cap.' The continuous reconciler RunPublisherSubscriptionReconciler (`lib/runtime/publishers.go:114-129`) uses a fixed `time.NewTicker(interval)` (default 5s), and reconcileMountingSubscriptionsOnce (`:131-190`) makes a single client.Subscribe per mounting row per tick, leaving the row mounting on failure — a flat poll, not increasing backoff. The backoff helper callSubscribeWithRetry (pow28, `:221-248`) is invoked ONLY from ResyncPublisherSubscriptions startup (`:382`), never the steady-state reconciler. No per-row backoff/next-retry state is persisted (schema has no attempt/retry columns — `lib/foundation/persistence/postgres/migrations/001-initial.sql:521-533`). 'no attempt cap' is accurate; 'with backoff' is not. (concept:publisher invariant at publisher.md:34 repeats the same overclaim.)
verify_note: Invariant line 35 'with backoff and no attempt cap.' RunPublisherSubscriptionReconciler (publishers.go:114-129) uses fixed time.NewTicker(interval); reconcileMountingSubscriptionsOnce (:131-190) does one client.Subscribe per mounting row per tick, no backoff. pow28 exponential backoff (callSubscribeWithRetry :221-248) is invoked ONLY from ResyncPublisherSubscriptions startup (:382). 'no attempt cap' true for reconciler; 'with backoff' false. Confirmed.
phase1_note: Two dossiers state 'with backoff' for the steady-state reconciler, but both trace to one artifact whose own quoted evidence supports only 'no attempt cap', not backoff — the 'backoff' clause may be dossier distillation drift rather than an actual decision, or a real intent the code never implemented. Question for the human: was per-row exponential backoff ever a decided requirement for the continuous mounting reconciler specifically (as opposed to the startup resync path, which already has it), or should the doc's 'with backoff' be dropped to match the code's flat-interval retry-forever behavior?

summary: deliverDispatch blocks on the stream channel send while holding pendingMu, so one misbehaving spawn can wedge the entire agent connection
evidence: deliverDispatch takes pendingMu (defer unlock) and then does `select { case ch <- frame: case <-a.closed: }`. The per-stream channel is buffered at 16 (registerStream) and unary consumers (forwardUnary/forwardProxyUnary/Execute) read exactly ONE frame then clearStream. A spawned service that emits >16 frames on one stream_id fills the buffer; deliverDispatch then blocks on `ch <- frame` while still holding pendingMu. Because deliverDispatch is called only from the single per-connection readLoop, the whole readLoop stalls (no more Heartbeat/SpawnAck/Reaped/other-stream frames processed) and pendingMu stays locked, so registerStream/clearStream/registerSpawnPending for every other in-flight dispatch on that owner's connection block too — the connection wedges until a.closed. Contrast the sibling deliverSpawnAck (state.go:101) and deliverReaped (state.go:127), which deliberately release pendingMu before a `default:`-guarded non-blocking send. deliverDispatch should follow the same drop-on-full/lock-released discipline.
verify_note: Verified: readLoop (agent_server.go:96-120) is the single per-connection goroutine and calls conn.deliverDispatch synchronously (112). deliverDispatch (state.go:153-164) holds pendingMu via defer and blocks on `ch <- frame` (buffer 16) with only a.closed as escape. A spawn emitting >16 frames on one stream while a unary consumer reads only one wedges the readLoop and holds pendingMu, blocking registerStream/clearStream/deliverSpawnAck/deliverReaped for the whole connection until close. Sibling deliverSpawnAck/deliverReaped correctly release the lock and use a default: non-blocking send. Real wedge/robustness bug; major.
remediation: Release pendingMu before the blocking stream-channel send (or use a non-blocking/buffered send) so one stuck spawn cannot wedge the whole agent connection.

summary: A template hash shared by two tags gets undeployed and deleted when one sibling tag is removed/moved, orphaning the surviving tag

Reachable case: state has tags a@1.0->hashX and b@1.0->hashX (two distinct tags, identical spec bodies — Validate only rejects duplicate PATHS, not duplicate content, per TestValidate_DuplicatePath). Removing b@1.0 while keeping a@1.0 (still hashX) schedules ActionUndeploy + ActionTemplateDelete on hashX, tearing the template out from under the surviving a@1.0. Delete/undeploy must be filtered against hashes still referenced by any kept manifest tag.
verify_note: plan.go tag-move (169-172) and tag-removal (208-211) populate oldHashesNeedingUndeploy/Delete purely from the old hash with no check that a kept manifest tag still resolves to it. Validate (manifest.go 133/147) rejects only duplicate PATHS and duplicate TAGS, not duplicate CONTENT — so two distinct tags on distinct paths with identical spec bodies produce one shared hash (the registered[hash] dedup at 122-133 exists precisely for this). Removing one sibling schedules ActionUndeploy+ActionTemplateDelete on the shared hash; the deploys loop (183-185) skips re-deploy because the template is still 'deployed', so the surviving tag is left pointing at an undeployed/deleted template. Real correctness bug; requires the shared-hash precondition but impact is a torn-down live template.
