summary: Zero-run nodes make an instance never reach 'all settled' -> wait hangs (default timeout is unbounded)
evidence: isNodeSettled returns false for a node whose RunSummary is {Active:0,Pending:0,Fresh:0,Failed:0} (it requires Fresh>0||Failed>0). But every declared template node AND every message-receiver node is created as a NodeRow eagerly at instance creation (lib/control/controlapi/instances.go:930 and :951-960, one receiver per declared message type plus the empty-type root). GetRunSummary (lib/foundation/persistence/sqlite/nodes.go:483) counts by state over rimsky_node_runs, so a node with no runs reports all zeros. handleListInstanceNodes returns ALL such nodes with that summary (lib/control/controlapi/nodes.go:216-248). A message-receiver node for a declared-but-never-sent message type — or any node the cascade never reaches — therefore stays {0,0,0,0} forever, so allNodesSettled never returns true and WaitForInstancesTerminal loops until the timeout. Compose run's default timeout is 0 = unbounded (run_test.go:28), so such a run hangs forever — directly hitting the one-shot-to-terminal story falsifier ('stalls after the work is finished and has to be killed') and contradicting the ruling that an instance settles idle when there is no open frame and no pending message (a zero-run node contributes neither).
verify_note: Confirmed and reachable. isNodeSettled (wait.go:164) returns false for a {0,0,0,0} summary (requires Fresh>0||Failed>0); allNodesSettled requires every node settled. GetRunSummary (sqlite/nodes.go:483) GROUP BY state over rimsky_node_runs, so a node with zero runs reports all zeros. handleListInstanceNodes (controlapi/nodes.go:199-248) returns ALL node rows with no zero-run/receiver filter. Message-receiver nodes are created eagerly (instances.go:951-960: root '' + one per declared message type); a declared-but-never-sent message type's receiver — or any template node the cascade never reaches — stays {0,0,0,0} forever, so allNodesSettled never returns true. Compose run default timeout is 0=unbounded (run_test.go:28), so the wait hangs. Aggravating: WaitForInstancesTerminal never inspects inst.TerminatedAt (wait.go:120 discards it), relying solely on node settling, so even a server-side-terminated instance keeps looping. Directly falsifies one-shot-to-terminal and contradicts the settle-on-idle ruling.
remediation: Treat zero-run nodes as settled (and/or bound the wait timeout) so 'all settled' is reachable.

summary: Instance outcome uses cross-frame FailedCount, so a node that failed once but later ran fresh is misclassified as failure
evidence: classifyInstanceOutcome/mapNodeSummaryToOutcome key off RunSummary.FailedCount>0. GetRunSummary aggregates node-run states across ALL frames for a node_id (sqlite/nodes.go:483 GROUP BY state, no frame scoping). fresh/failed are terminal and stale-recovery/recalculate create a NEW node-run leaving the failed predecessor row in place (concept:node-run). So once any node-run fails, FailedCount stays >0 permanently; an instance that had a node fail in an earlier frame but converged to fresh in a later frame (iterative-workflows-converge) is still reported as failure and exits 1. Same aggregation drives the per-node NodeRunTerminal line.

GetRunSummary (sqlite/nodes.go:483) aggregates node-run states with no frame scoping (GROUP BY state over all runs for node_id). Per node-run.md, stale-recovery/recalculate create a NEW node-run row leaving the failed predecessor in place, and frames never share node-runs. So once any node-run fails, FailedCount stays >0 permanently; an instance whose node failed in an earlier frame but converged to fresh in a later frame is still classified failure and exits 1, and the per-node NodeRunTerminal line is likewise mislabeled. Contradicts iterative-workflows-converge. Minor.

summary: Commit is not idempotent in the claim id — a retried Commit errors instead of succeeding as a no-op

summary: Delete asset has a TOCTOU on active holders and no compensation if the post-release delete fails
evidence: The active-holder check runs in the read transaction (443-467), then producer.Release (509) and DeleteResolved (515-517) run in two later, separate transactions. A node run can register an active ClaimHolder between the check and the delete, so the refuse-if-in-flight guard (500-506) can be bypassed and an in-flight holder orphaned. Also, if Release succeeds but DeleteResolved errors, the producer-side claim is released while the committed row persists — no rollback/compensation, leaving an inconsistent asset.
verify_note: Verified assets.go: active-holder check runs in read tx (443-472), producer.Release (509) and DeleteResolved (515-517) run in two later separate txs. Real TOCTOU — a holder registered between check and delete escapes guard 500-506; and Release-success/DeleteResolved-failure leaves producer released while row persists, no compensation. Admin-path, pre-v1; minor is fair.

summary: isComposeOrigin fails OPEN when no identity is in context: any request stamping X-Rimsky-Compose-Origin: 1 is granted the compose-origin capability if the identity middleware is absent.
evidence: compose_prefix.go:24-27: `ident, ok := IdentityFromContextOK(r.Context()); if !ok { return true }`. This contradicts the fail-closed ruling for the permission surface. The branch is reachable in any NewApp construction with AppDeps.AuthState == nil (NewApp tolerates nil; app.go:80 only installs IdentityResolver when AuthState != nil) — and the package harness (app_test.go newHarness) builds exactly that. The safe form is `if !ok { return false }`; the grant check on line 28 (auth.CheckGrant(ident.Permissions, composeOriginAction, nil)) is the only intended allow path, and anonymous mode already passes it via AnonymousIdentity()'s `*` grant.
verify_note: compose_prefix.go:24-26 does `if !ok { return true }` — real fail-open. But the branch is reachable ONLY when AuthState==nil (app.go:80-81 installs IdentityResolver only when AuthState!=nil, and it always sets identity or 401s). In that mode the ENTIRE control API is ungated (gate() returns inner), and compose: is a cooperative namespace guard ('managed by the compose command', tags.go:66), not a security boundary. In any authed deployment the branch is dead. Real fail-closed-principle violation, trivial fix (`return false`), but near-zero practical impact — downgrade major→minor.

summary: The only allow-path test for compose-origin (TestCreateTag_ComposeOriginAllowed) passes through the identity-missing fail-open branch, and there is no test that a key WITHOUT the compose:origin grant is rejected when it stamps the header.
evidence: The harness (newHarness) has no AuthState, so no identity is ever in context; TestCreateTag_ComposeOriginAllowed succeeds via isComposeOrigin's `!ok -> true` branch, never exercising auth.CheckGrant(ident.Permissions, "compose:origin", nil). If gateByAction/CheckGrant enforcement of compose:origin were deleted entirely, no test would fail; conversely, fixing the fail-open branch to fail closed makes this test fail — the suite pins the wrong behavior. Needed: (a) identity present without compose:origin + header -> 400 reserved-prefix rejection; (b) identity with compose:origin grant + header -> 201.
verify_note: Confirmed: newHarness (app_test.go:55-71) builds AppDeps with no AuthState, so TestCreateTag_ComposeOriginAllowed (compose_prefix_test.go:93) succeeds via isComposeOrigin's `!ok->true` branch; CheckGrant(compose:origin) is never exercised, and no test covers identity-present-without-grant rejection. Fixing 736 to fail-closed would break this test, confirming it pins the fail-open path. Genuine gap, but subject is the same low-impact cooperative namespace guard as 736 — minor.

summary: gate() silently disables all permission gating when deps.AuthState is nil — a fail-open configuration switch on a fail-closed surface.
evidence: auth_middleware.go:339-344: `func gate(deps AppDeps, action string, inner http.HandlerFunc) http.HandlerFunc { if deps.AuthState == nil { return inner } ... }`. Combined with app.go:80 (IdentityResolver only installed when AuthState != nil), constructing NewApp without AuthState serves every route ungated and unaudited with no error, no warning log, and no startup refusal. Rimsky is explicitly embeddable (rules.md 'Project-agnostic'); an embedding consumer that builds AppDeps directly gets a fully open control API. Production wiring (lib/control/config/controlapi.go:192) happens to always set it, and the package test harness relies on the nil path — the ungated mode should at minimum be an explicit, named opt-in rather than the zero value of AppDeps.
verify_note: gate() (auth_middleware.go:339-342) does return inner when deps.AuthState==nil — real. But this is the intended no-auth mode: production wiring always sets AuthState (finding concedes controlapi.go:192) and the package harness deliberately relies on the nil path. It does not trigger in any real deployment; it's an embedder footgun (silent, no warning log) worth a guard, not a triggering bug. Downgrade major→minor.

summary: TOCTOU race in the last-active-key revoke guard: ActiveCount and MarkRevoked run in separate implicit transactions, so two concurrent revokes of the last two keys can both pass the guard and silently drop the deployment into anonymous mode (all requests admin) without force_leave_anonymous.
evidence: handleRevokeKey: `active, err := keys.ActiveCount(ctx, now, nil)` (line 211) then `changed, found, err := keys.MarkRevoked(ctx, row.ID, now, nil)` (line 231) — both with tx=nil, no shared transaction, no re-check. Two racing DELETE /v1/auth/keys/{a} and /{b} each observe active=2, both proceed, active count reaches 0, and anonymous mode (auth.AnonymousIdentity() = Grant{{Action:"*"}}) opens without the explicit confirmation the guard exists to require. Both APIKeyTable methods accept a Tx; the count + conditional revoke should be one transaction (with a re-count after MarkRevoked, or a serialized guard).
verify_note: Confirmed TOCTOU: handleRevokeKey reads ActiveCount (auth_handlers.go:211, tx=nil) then MarkRevoked (line 231, tx=nil) in separate transactions with no re-check. Two concurrent revokes of the last two active keys both observe active=2 (guard at line 219 requires active<=1), both proceed, and the deployment silently enters anonymous mode (AnonymousIdentity = `*` admin grant) without force_leave_anonymous — the exact confirmation the guard exists to require. Security-relevant; keep major.

summary: captureBody buffers up to 64MB of request body in memory per request BEFORE the permission check, for every gated action (including ones that never use the body), with no concurrency cap — a pre-authorization memory-amplification vector.
evidence: gateByAction calls captureBody (line 170) before requestTargets/CheckGrant (lines 175-191); captureBody does `io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(r.Body, auditBodyHandlerMaxBytes+1))` with auditBodyHandlerMaxBytes = 64MB (line 245). NewApp installs no request-size middleware (app.go: only RequestID, Recoverer, accessLog, AllowContentType). Any client holding the lowest-privilege valid key — or any client at all in anonymous mode — can POST N concurrent ~64MB bodies that are fully buffered before the 403 is computed. The audit copy is capped at 4MB (auditBodyCapBytes) and target extraction only needs bodies for 2 of ~40 actions; the 64MB full-buffer-before-authz window is much wider than either consumer needs.
verify_note: gateByAction calls captureBody (line 170) before requestTargets/CheckGrant (175-191); captureBody io.ReadAll's up to 64MB before authz, and NewApp installs no body-size middleware. Real. But it is NOT amplification: io.ReadAll only allocates what the client actually transmits (LimitReader caps at 64MB), so cost is 1:1 with bandwidth, and reaching gateByAction requires a valid credential (or anon mode, which is already fully open). A denied request still costs its full body in RAM — a legitimate hardening note, but 'memory-amplification vector' overstates it. Downgrade major→minor.

summary: captureBody swallows io.ReadAll errors and returns handlerRejected=false without restoring r.Body, so the handler proceeds against a partially-consumed body with no log and no error response.
evidence: Lines 252-255: `body, err := io.ReadAll(limited); if err != nil { return nil, nil, false }`. On a mid-read network error the original r.Body has been partially drained and is not replaced (the NopCloser reset on line 269 is skipped), the audit row silently loses request_params, and the handler sees a truncated stream — typically a confusing 400 from JSON decode rather than an honest request-read failure. The error should at least be logged, and the request failed.

summary: templateIDTargets swallows the persistence error when resolving template-hash -> tags and silently degrades to an empty target — fail-closed for scoped keys (good) but with zero observability.
evidence: Lines 51-58: `err := persist.Transaction(...); if err != nil || len(rows) == 0 { return []map[string]string{{}} }`. A transient DB failure during target derivation makes every template_tag-scoped key get 403 permission-denied on template:deploy/undeploy/deregister and instance:create, with no log line and no 500 — indistinguishable from a genuine grant mismatch for the operator debugging it. The error and the no-rows case deserve different handling (or at minimum a logged warning on err != nil).

summary: No test proves that non-auth operational events are EXCLUDED from GET /v1/audit — the KindIn allowlist (the boundary keeping audit:read from becoming a full event-log read that bypasses event:read) can regress with every test green.
evidence: TestAuditRoute_NoKindReturnsAllAuthRows seeds only the 5 auth.* events and asserts GreaterOrEqual(len(rows), 5); if `filter.KindIn = auditKinds` (audit_read.go:40) were dropped and /audit returned the whole event log, this test still passes. The scenario suite (test/scenarios/auth/audit_read_test.go) also never seeds a non-auth event and asserts absence. Needed: seed a state_transition (or any operational) event alongside the auth rows and assert it does not appear in the unfiltered /v1/audit page.

Missing test for a load-bearing security boundary — major.

summary: The ?kind= gate is prefix-based (auth.) while the error message and the KindIn filter promise the 5-entry auditKinds allowlist — a future sixth auth.* kind passes the prefix check but ANDs against the stale KindIn list and silently returns zero rows instead of either matching or 400ing.

summary: parseLimit has no upper bound, so ?limit=100000000 asks the store to materialize the entire audit table in one response page.
evidence: Line 101: `Limit: parseLimit(req, 100)`; app_util.go:18-27 rejects only non-positive/non-numeric values and passes any positive integer through. The MCP mirror of the same data enforces resourceReadMaxLimit (mcp_resources.go parseSinceLimit clamps `n > resourceReadMaxLimit`), so the two surfaces disagree. The uncapped parseLimit idiom is repo-wide, but this route is the security-audit feed and the cheapest to weaponize for a memory/latency spike by a key holding only audit:read.

summary: handleRotateKey silently swallows JSON decode errors on the request body, so a malformed body rotates the key with the default 24h grace instead of returning 400 — inconsistent with handleCreateKey, which 400s on invalid JSON.
evidence: Line 272: `_ = json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&body)`. A client that sends `{"grace": "1h"` (truncated) or a wrong content shape performs a real, plaintext-invalidating rotation with a grace it did not choose. handleCreateKey (lines 64-67) treats the identical failure as badRequest.

summary: handleRotateKey guards only RevokedAt, not RevokeAt: rotating a key already in rotation grace (addressed by ID) passes the guard and then fails inside the transaction with an unmapped ErrAPIKeyNameTaken, surfacing as a generic 500 instead of a 409.
evidence: Line 292 checks `oldRow.RevokedAt != nil` only. A prior rotation leaves the old row with revoke_at set plus an active same-name replacement (rimsky_api_keys_active_name_idx is unique on name WHERE revoked_at IS NULL AND revoke_at IS NULL). Rotating the graced row again (GetByID does not filter grace; GetByName does) reaches keys.Insert(newRow) which collides with the replacement -> persistence.ErrAPIKeyNameTaken -> writeError default branch -> 500 '...name already taken'. handleCreateKey maps the same sentinel to 409 (lines 128-131); rotate maps nothing. Either reject graced rows up front (mirroring the revoked check) or map the sentinel.

summary: Rotation grace accepts non-positive durations: {"grace":"-24h"} or "0s" yields revoke_at in the past, killing the old key immediately with no warning while the response still reads as a graceful rotation.
evidence: Lines 273-281 parse body.Grace with time.ParseDuration and use the value unchecked; revokeAt = now.Add(grace) (line 307). Elsewhere in-scope the same class of input is validated (breakpoints.go:137 'hit_ttl_seconds must be positive', 143 'ttl_seconds must be positive'). A `grace <= 0` request should 400 (or be an explicit immediate-revoke flag), not a silently-instant cutover.

summary: Rotation drops actor provenance from the audit trail: the new key row's CreatedByKeyID is never set and KeyRotatedPayload carries no rotated-by field, unlike create (CreatedByKeyID) and revoke (RevokedByKeyID).
evidence: newRow (lines 308-315) omits CreatedByKeyID even though the requesting identity is available via IdentityFromContextOK (used at lines 111-114 and 249-253 in the create/revoke paths); EmitKeyRotated's payload (lines 327-334, auth.KeyRotatedPayload) has no RotatedByKeyID. The api-key concept doc leans on the audit trail joining actions to keys ('auth-access audit rows carry the key id'); 'who rotated this key' is unanswerable from either the row or the auth.key_rotated event, only indirectly from the access_attempted row.

summary: EmitKeyRotated fills duplicate payload fields: KeyID==NewKeyID and KeyName==Name — the auth.KeyRotatedPayload shape carries the same value twice under two names.
evidence: Lines 327-334 set KeyID: newRow.ID and NewKeyID: newRow.ID, KeyName: oldRow.Name and Name: oldRow.Name. Consumers of the auth.key_rotated event get redundant keys; one pair should be dropped from the payload struct (foundation/auth/audit.go:92-99) and this call site.

summary: The wildcard-action predicate is duplicated between handleCreateKey and ActionRegistry.ValidateGrantScope — semantically identical logic in two places that must change together (Plumbline strict DRY).
evidence: auth_handlers.go:80 `if e.Action == "*" || strings.HasSuffix(e.Action, ":*") || strings.HasPrefix(e.Action, "*:")` and actions.go:118 (ValidateGrantScope) contain the same three-clause test. If the action grammar grows a new wildcard form, one site will be missed. Extract one named predicate (e.g. in foundation/auth next to ActionMatches) and use it in both.

summary: The key active-status predicate is hand-duplicated in Go twice (handleRevokeKey's thisRowActive and handleAuthStatus's admin loop) alongside the SQL ActiveCount definition — the api-key concept doc frames it as a single definition consulted everywhere.
evidence: auth_handlers.go:216-218 (`row.RevokedAt == nil && (row.ExpiresAt == nil || row.ExpiresAt.After(now)) && (row.RevokeAt == nil || row.RevokeAt.After(now))`) and 361-370 (three continue-guards in handleAuthStatus) restate the predicate that sqlite/postgres ActiveCount encodes in SQL. concept:api-key invariant 'Active-status predicate' says the middleware and the anonymous-mode predicate consult the same definition; three copies means a change to activeness (e.g. a new suspension state) silently diverges. A shared `func (k persistence.APIKey) ActiveAt(now time.Time) bool` would collapse the two Go copies.

summary: intToString hand-rolls strconv.Itoa, including an unreachable negative branch — Plumbline 'prefer plain over clever'.

Building the truncation marker via fmt.Sprintf or json.Marshal of a small struct would also remove the hand-assembled JSON string.

summary: IdentityFromContext (the panicking variant) is dead code — no call sites anywhere in the repo; only IdentityFromContextOK is used.

summary: Two idioms for the same dry-run mode check: breakpoints.go compares against the alias authModeDryRun while auth_handlers.go compares against auth.ModeDryRun directly — Plumbline one-idiom-per-job.

The alias exists only to save an import and creates a second spelling of the same comparison. Pick one form (drop the alias, or add an `IsDryRun(ctx) bool` helper next to ModeFromContext) and sweep.

summary: `_ = bpID` and the bpID variable it silences are dead residue in handleCreateBreakpoint — the id is only ever read via the `created` row.

summary: requestingKeyID returns the string literal "anonymous", duplicating auth.AnonymousKeyName.

summary: auth_routes handles nil AuthState by not registering the routes at all, while every other in-scope surface serves its routes ungated via gate() — two divergent nil-AuthState fail modes, and a second gating idiom (direct deps.AuthState.gateByAction vs the shared gate() helper).
evidence: auth_routes.go:13-15 `if deps.AuthState == nil { return }` then lines 16-27 call deps.AuthState.gateByAction directly; audit_read.go:33, breakpoints.go:29-38, and claims.go:37 all use gate(deps, action, handler), which degrades to ungated when AuthState is nil. With nil AuthState the API answers 404 on /v1/auth/keys but serves /v1/audit and /v1/instances/{...}/breakpoints wide open — an inconsistent boundary that also lets TestRegistryCoversRouter-style walks see different route sets depending on deps. One idiom (gate()) with one nil policy (ideally fail-closed, see the gate() finding) should cover both.

summary: Route path mixes retired lock vocabulary with claim vocabulary in a single URL: /v1/lock-holders/{claim_handle_id}/claim-holders — the concept catalog names this noun claim-handle, and the action/description/table all say claim.
evidence: claims.go:37 registers `GET /lock-holders/{claim_handle_id}/claim-holders` under action claim-holders:read whose registry description reads 'List claim-holder rows for a claim handle' (actions.go:362-365). The design catalog has concepts/claim-handle.md (advisory-lock and named-lock are separate concepts); the URL segment 'lock-holders' where a claim handle id goes is leftover from the locks->claims rename (also present in lib/control/observability/handler.go:54-55). Pre-v1 with no wire-compat guarantee (rules.md), the path can be renamed to /claim-handles/{claim_handle_id}/holders (or similar) and swept.

summary: Stray empty `//` comment line above the @concept citation block — cheatsheet allows only clean `// @<tag>: <slug>` lines in a citation block; the bare comment line is residue.
Same stray empty `//` line above the @concept citation block as auth_handlers.go.
The dry_run query flag is only honored for the exact string "true" — dry_run=1, dry_run=True, dry_run=yes silently EXECUTE, a dangerous failure direction for a preview flag on write actions.
evidence: Line 209: `if res.Mode == auth.ModeDryRun || r.URL.Query().Get("dry_run") == "true"`. A caller who intends a preview but writes ?dry_run=1 performs the real mutation (revoke, terminate, deregister...) with no signal that the flag was ignored. Unrecognized non-empty values should 400 (strict parse), matching how the entrypoint treats RIMSKY_ENTRYPOINT_MIGRATE ('any other non-empty value ... is a startup error', CLAUDE.md).

summary: IsAnonymousMode / InvalidateAnonCache race: a concurrent reader that computed the count before a key-mint commit can Store its stale isAnon=true entry AFTER InvalidateAnonCache runs, keeping anonymous-admin access alive for up to another cache TTL past the mutation.
evidence: Sequence: reader loads nil cache (line 55), runs ActiveCount seeing 0 keys (line 58); handleCreateKey's insert commits and calls InvalidateAnonCache (auth_handlers.go:143) storing nil; reader then executes line 63 `s.anonCache.Store(e)` with isAnon=true valid for anonCacheTTL. The invalidation exists precisely so 'committing it exits anonymous mode' takes local effect immediately (the dry-run note at auth_handlers.go:99 promises this), but the plain Store lets a pre-commit computation overwrite the invalidation. CompareAndSwap against the entry observed at the start of the computation (or a generation counter) closes it; impact is bounded (~TTL=1s) but it is unauthenticated-admin time.

summary: No test anywhere covers captureBody's two caps: the 64MB hard reject (413 + error body) and the 4MB audit truncation marker ({"_audit_truncated":true,...}) that substitutes for oversized request_params in audit rows.
evidence: grep for _audit_truncated / StatusRequestEntityTooLarge across lib/ and test/ finds no controlapi coverage (only graph/scratch/callback_test.go, a different surface). auth_middleware_test.go exercises dry-run modes, streaming Flush, and mode floors, but never a body >4MB or >64MB, so regressions in the truncation marker (audit fidelity) or the 413 path (including its early-return contract handlerRejected=true, which gates whether the handler runs at all) pass silently.

summary: No test covers the cross-instance ownership guard on delete/resume: a breakpoint that exists but belongs to a DIFFERENT instance must 404 (the bp.InstanceID != inst.ID branch), and no test covers resume with a hit belonging to a different breakpoint.
evidence: handleDeleteBreakpoint (breakpoints.go:310) and handleResumeBreakpointHit (breakpoints.go:367, 374) guard `bp == nil || bp.InstanceID != inst.ID` and `hit == nil || hit.BreakpointID != bpID`, but TestBreakpoint_DeleteNotFound uses a random nonexistent UUID and TestBreakpoint_ResumeMissingHitID a nonexistent hit — the mismatch (exists-but-wrong-parent) arms of both guards are never exercised. If either guard degraded to a bare nil check, deletion/resume of another instance's breakpoints via a guessed/leaked id would succeed and no test would fail.

summary: Run-scope-terminal delivery failures are permanently lost: CloseAndFanOutFrameRootRunScopesForInstance returns nothing, and a subsequent successful FanOutInstanceEvent deletes the instance-scope lifecycle rows, removing the instance from ListTerminatedWithLifecycleRows so the failed OnRunScopeTerminal is never retried.
evidence: tick() calls CloseAndFanOutFrameRootRunScopesForInstance with no return value; inside it FanOutRunScopeEvent 'continue's on a peer error (lifecycle.go:268-271) and the caller discards perPeerErr with `_, _, _ =` (lifecycle.go:336). tick then runs FanOutInstanceEvent (line 130) which deletes the instance-scope rows on success (lifecycle.go:204-211). Partial failure (peer errors OnRunScopeTerminal but succeeds OnInstanceTerminated) leaves the run_scope idempotency row un-terminal with no sweeper ever revisiting: the lifecycle-subscriber invariant 'each (service, event) pair fires exactly once' degrades to zero times.
verify_note: Confirmed. FanOutRunScopeEvent 'continue's on OnRunScopeTerminal error (lifecycle.go:268-270) WITHOUT upserting the terminal idempotency row, and CloseAndFanOutFrameRootRunScopesForInstance discards its return (`_,_,_=`, lifecycle.go:335) and is void. tick() then runs FanOutInstanceEvent which deletes instance-scope rows on success. ListTerminatedWithLifecycleRows (postgres/instances.go:279-283) keys ONLY on EXISTS instance-scope rows — no run-scope check — so once those are deleted the instance is never revisited. When a peer errors run-scope-terminal but succeeds instance-terminated in the same tick, that peer's run-scope terminal is permanently lost. Narrower than described (needs that partial-failure split) but a real break of the delivery invariant. Major.
remediation: Propagate OnRunScopeTerminal delivery failure out of CloseAndFanOutFrameRootRunScopesForInstance and gate instance-scope lifecycle-row deletion on success so a failed run-scope-terminal stays retryable.

summary: The template-missing fallback path never closes frame root run-scopes and never fires OnRunScopeTerminal — it only delivers OnInstanceTerminated — so a terminated instance whose template row is gone leaks open run-scopes and peers never see run-scope terminal.
evidence: if tpl == nil { fanOutFromLifecycleRows(...) } skips CloseAndFanOutFrameRootRunScopesForInstance entirely. RunScopes().Close needs no template spec, and the peer set is available from the instance's lifecycle rows, so the fallback could close scopes and fan out; it doesn't. TestInstanceTerminator_TemplateMissingFallsBackToLifecycleRows (instance_terminator_test.go:186-206) encodes the gap: `require.Len(t, calls, 1)` — no on_run_scope_terminal call expected. Per concept:run-scope a closed root scope is how the frame's end is materialized; claim producers keyed to scope terminal never release.
verify_note: Confirmed. instance_terminator.go: `if tpl == nil { fanOutFromLifecycleRows(...) }` and fanOutFromLifecycleRows (line 141-183) only fires OnInstanceTerminated + deletes instance-scope rows — never CloseAndFanOutFrameRootRunScopesForInstance, never OnRunScopeTerminal. RunScopes().Close needs no spec and peers are available from lifecycle rows, so it is implementable. TestInstanceTerminator_TemplateMissingFallsBackToLifecycleRows (line 186-206) encodes the gap (require.Len(calls,1), on_instance_terminated only). A terminated instance whose template row is gone leaks open root run-scopes; claims keyed to scope-terminal never release. Major.
remediation: In the template-missing terminator fallback, close frame root run-scopes and fire OnRunScopeTerminal, not just OnInstanceTerminated.

summary: Duplicate lifecycle delivery race: the idempotency ledger is consulted with separate get/dispatch/delete transactions and no row lock, so a terminator tick racing the DELETE-instance handler's FanOutInstanceEvent (or a concurrent CloseAndFanOut from the terminate handler) can dispatch OnInstanceTerminated / OnRunScopeTerminal twice to the same peer, violating the exactly-once invariant.
evidence: FanOutInstanceEvent runs Get, dispatch, Delete each under withOptionalTx with tx=nil — three independent transactions (lifecycle.go:178-211). handleDeleteInstance calls FanOutInstanceEvent (instances.go:567) and handleTerminateInstance calls CloseAndFanOutFrameRootRunScopesForInstance (instances.go:740) on request goroutines while the terminator tick does the same from its poll loop; both readers can observe state=created and both dispatch before either deletes/upserts. concept:lifecycle-subscriber: 'Idempotency at the rimsky side: each (service, event) pair fires exactly once.'
verify_note: Confirmed TOCTOU. FanOutInstanceEvent runs Get / dispatch / Delete each under withOptionalTx(tx=nil) — three independent transactions, no row lock/SELECT FOR UPDATE (lifecycle.go:178-224). handleDeleteInstance (instances.go:567) and the terminator tick (instance_terminator.go:130) both call it on the same terminated instance concurrently; both can Get a non-nil row and dispatch OnInstanceTerminated before either Deletes → double delivery to a peer, violating concept:lifecycle-subscriber exactly-once. Distinct mechanism from 766 (double-fire vs lost-fire). Major.
remediation: instance_terminator.go: consult the idempotency ledger under a row lock in one transaction so racing terminator/DELETE paths cannot double-dispatch OnInstanceTerminated/OnRunScopeTerminal.

summary: Stop() is not safe for concurrent callers: the select/default double-close guard is check-then-act, so two simultaneous Stop() calls can both take the default branch and both close(t.stop), panicking with close of closed channel.
evidence: Lines 78-82: `select { case <-t.stop: default: close(t.stop) }` executes after t.mu is released; nothing serializes two goroutines both reaching the default arm. A sync.Once or closing under t.mu would make the guard sound. Also Stop() before Run() returns without arming anything, so that Stop cannot terminate a later Run.

summary: errClaimProducersRegistryUnset has three mismatched vocabularies: the identifier says claim-producers registry, the message says 'store registry', and the condition it guards is deps.LifecycleSubs (the lifecycle-subscriber registry). 'store' is also the retired name for claim_producer.
evidence: var errClaimProducersRegistryUnset = errors.New("terminator: store registry not initialized") is returned from fanOutFromLifecycleRows when t.deps.LifecycleSubs == nil (line 152). FanOutInstanceEvent phrases the same condition as 'lifecycle subscriber registry not initialized' (lifecycle.go:194) — a third rendering of one condition.

summary: InstanceTerminator hardwires slog.Default() instead of the injected AppDeps.Logger used by every other consumer in the package, bypassing configured logging; tests wire shared.SilentLogger but terminator warnings still hit the process default logger.
evidence: NewInstanceTerminator sets logger: slog.Default() and ignores deps.Logger (foundationshared.Logger, app.go:31). summary: The state query filter silently collapses everything that is not 'running': ?state=failed and ?state=completed both return ALL ended frames (each other's rows included), and garbage values like ?state=bogus are accepted as 'ended' instead of being rejected with 400 — even though the response's state field advertises the three-value vocabulary running|completed|failed.

'running'/'failed'/'completed', postgres/frames.go:506-510) is never matched against the requested value, so a client filtering ?state=failed silently receives frames labeled state=completed, and invalid values pass validation that every sibling filter param (triggering_message_id, since/until on /events) performs.

summary: invalidate_node can create a run that spans two frames: it pairs the CURRENT running frame's ID with the run-scope of the node's LATEST run, which may belong to a PRIOR frame (paused instance, node not yet visited in the running frame). The inserted stale run lives in a prior frame's RunScope tree while being owned by the current frame, and its bag snapshot pulls prior-frame attribute data into current-frame cascade decisions.
evidence: applyDebugOverride: frameID := GetRunningFrameID(instance) but RunScopeID: latest.RunScopeID from GetLatestRunForNode, which falls back to terminal prior-frame runs when no in-flight run exists (postgres/nodes.go:797 ORDER BY in-flight-first). Prior frames' root scopes stay open until instance termination (only child_execution.go and the termination path call RunScopes().Close), so CreateNonCascadeStale succeeds and SnapshotBagForNewRun (postgres/nodes.go:1029) copies the prior frame's bag. Violates concept:run-scope 'A RunScope lives inside exactly one frame; RunScopes never span frames' and concept:frame 'Messages are the ONLY cross-frame carrier'; story debug-channel scopes the override to 'the running frame'.
verify_note: applyDebugOverride pairs GetRunningFrameID (current frame) with latest.RunScopeID from GetLatestRunForNode, which (nodes.go:797 in-flight-first ORDER BY) falls back to the newest TERMINAL run when no in-flight run exists — that run can belong to a prior frame. CreateNonCascadeStale (nodes.go:996) inserts with frame_id=current, run_scope_id=prior, guarded only by rs.closed_at IS NULL; it never checks frame/scope agreement. MarkFrameEnded (frames.go:69) stamps ended_at but does NOT close the root scope — only CloseAndFanOutFrameRootRunScopesForInstance (lifecycle.go, instance-termination) closes root scopes. So a prior frame's root scope stays open while a new frame runs. Reachable: paused/breakpoint instance, new frame running, node last ran in a prior (ended-but-open-scoped) frame. Creates a node-run whose frame_id and run_scope_id belong to different frames, violating run-scope invariant 'RunScopes never span frames'. Confirmed.
remediation: Fix debug_override invalidate_node so the created stale run's frame and run-scope are consistent — do not pair the current running frame with the node's latest (possibly prior-frame) run-scope.

summary: set_attribute on a paused instance with no in-flight run for the node writes into the latest PRIOR-frame terminal run's attribute row — rewriting persisted audit data that concept:frame declares immutable observability state, while having no effect on any future frame (frame isolation means no later frame reads it back).
evidence: setNodeAttributeForDebugOverride uses GetLatestRunForNode, which returns the newest terminal run when nothing is in flight, then Upsert/MergeDelta against latest.NodeRunID unconditionally; nothing checks latest.FrameID against the running frame (or that a frame is running at all — the frameID==nil case still counts touched=true and mutated++). concept:frame: persisted attribute rows of prior frames exist 'for external observability, not for the runtime to read back'; mutating them corrupts the audit trail and the override is silently ineffective. TestDebugOverride_SetAttributeNoInFlightRunIsNoOp covers only latest==nil, not latest-in-prior-frame.
verify_note: setNodeAttributeForDebugOverride (debug_override.go:236) uses GetLatestRunForNode which returns the newest terminal (possibly prior-frame) run when nothing is in flight, then Upsert/MergeDelta against latest.NodeRunID with no check that latest.FrameID == running frame; the call is made before the frameID!=nil block, so it also runs when no frame is running, still returning touched=true/mutated++. concept/frame.md:54 states prior-frame attribute rows exist for external observability, not to be read back or mutated. Mutating them corrupts audit state and the override never affects a future frame (frame isolation). TestDebugOverride_SetAttributeNoInFlightRunIsNoOp (debug_override_test.go:361) only asserts the latest==nil case; the latest-in-prior-frame case is untested. Confirmed.
remediation: debug_override.set_attribute must refuse to write into a prior-frame terminal run's attribute row (immutable per concept:frame) when no in-flight run exists.

summary: Message list advertises cursor pagination that is dead end to end: ?cursor= is silently ignored and next_cursor is always empty, so clients can never page past the first `limit` rows.
evidence: handleListInstanceMessages builds persistence.ListPagination{Limit: parseLimit(req, 100), Cursor: q.Get("cursor")} and returns page.NextCursor, but both backends' Messages().List never reference pag.Cursor and return PaginatedListResult{Rows: out} with no NextCursor (lib/foundation/persistence/postgres/messages.go List — `grep Cursor` over the file matches nothing; same for sqlite/messages.go). Cursor pagination is a live idiom elsewhere (postgres/events.go:152 returns NextCursor), so this endpoint's surface promises what its storage layer never delivers: a client that follows next_cursor terminates after one page with rows remaining, and a client that passes ?cursor= gets page 1 again.
verify_note: handleListInstanceMessages (messages.go:332) passes Cursor=q.Get("cursor") and returns page.NextCursor, but postgres Messages.List (messages.go:129) never references pag.Cursor and returns PaginatedListResult{Rows: out} with no NextCursor; sqlite/messages.go likewise has zero Cursor/NextCursor references. Cursor is a live idiom (events.go decodeEventCursor/encodeEventCursor). Result: next_cursor is always empty (client silently truncates at limit with rows remaining) and ?cursor= is ignored (re-serves page 1). Confirmed dead-end pagination.
remediation: Implement cursor decode + NextCursor emit in both postgres and sqlite Messages.List so the control route's advertised pagination actually pages.

summary: Publisher sends blank the dedup sender_subject instead of carrying the publisher-subscription identity, contradicting decision:message-sender-kind-discriminator.
evidence: The decision states the sender-subject field "carries the actor identity (api-key id, publisher subscription, or the `anonymous` sentinel)". handleCreateMessage sets `sender = row.PublisherName; senderSubject = ""` for the publisher path, so the dedup tuple is (instance, publisher, publisher_name, "", key): two live subscriptions of the same publisher name on one instance (or a subscription re-mounted with a new id) share a dedup namespace, and the subscription id is not recorded on the dedup row at all. Doc and code disagree; one of them is wrong.
phase1_note: The decision doc explicitly names 'publisher subscription' as one of the three things sender_subject is supposed to carry, but the publisher send path hardcodes senderSubject to empty string, so two live subscriptions of the same publisher name on one instance (or a re-mounted subscription) share a dedup namespace and the subscription id is not recorded on the dedup row at all. The 2026-07-14 dossier ruling describes dedup as 'publishers by name' but doesn't address subscription-level granularity, so it doesn't retract the decision doc's more specific claim. Fix: set senderSubject to the publisher-subscription id (row.ID.String()) on the publisher send path.

summary: postMessageRequest.Sender is accepted and silently discarded while DisallowUnknownFields rejects every other unknown field; the MCP message_send schema advertises the field with no hint it is ignored.

summary: MCP message_send has no way to carry a caller idempotency key — the catalog synthesizes a fresh random Idempotency-Key per invocation, so an MCP client retry duplicates the message, defeating decision:idempotency-key-header-universal.
evidence: concept:message says "The idempotency feature is universal — operator retries, publisher sends, and lifecycle handlers all use the same idempotency-key surface", and decision:idempotency-key-header-universal's rationale is "replay-safe by construction". The message_send inputSchema here exposes only id/type/payload/sender/publisher_subscription_id; mcp/catalog.go:127 then sets `inner.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "mcp-"+uuid.NewString())` on every POST, so two invocations of the same tool call with identical args mint distinct dedup tuples and enqueue two messages. An MCP client that retries after a timeout — the exact scenario the mandatory header exists for — double-sends. The schema needs an idempotency_key argument mapped to the header (with the random key as fallback).
verify_note: message_send inputSchema (mcp_route.go:88) exposes only id/type/payload/sender/publisher_subscription_id — no idempotency key. mcp/catalog.go sets inner.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "mcp-"+uuid.NewString()) on every POST/PUT, so identical retries mint distinct dedup tuples. concept/message.md:17-19 mandates a required idempotency key and calls the feature 'universal'; decision:idempotency-key-header-universal exists for replay-safety. An MCP client retry after timeout double-sends the message (and triggers a duplicate frame). Confirmed design-conformance gap.
remediation: Thread a caller-supplied Idempotency-Key through MCP message_send instead of synthesizing a fresh random one per invocation.
phase1_note: Confirmed still present: message_send's MCP schema exposes only id/type/payload/sender/publisher_subscription_id and the catalog synthesizes a fresh random Idempotency-Key on every POST, so an MCP client retry after a timeout double-sends the message -- exactly the scenario the mandatory header exists to prevent, and a violation of the documented MCP/HTTP transport-parity invariant. Fix: add an idempotency_key argument to the message_send tool schema and thread it through to the Idempotency-Key header, falling back to a random key only when the caller omits it.

summary: Descendants and ancestors walk two different relations: ancestors follow substitution_refs (data lineage) while descendants follow parent_run_id (run-tree spawn parentage), so a consumer that substituted from run X appears in its own /ancestors but never in X's /descendants — story:lineage-exploration's falsifier.
evidence: walkLineageRuns dir==ancestors expands via extractSubstitutionRefRunIDs(fr.Record) (the {{nodes.X.attribute.Y}} citations concept:lineage defines as the data dependency), but dir==descendants expands via Lineage().QueryByParentNodeRunID, whose SQL matches record->>'parent_run_id' — the fan-out/sub-graph spawn parent written by the runtime (lib/runtime/lineage_writer.go:45), not the inverse of substitution refs. A standard cascade subscriber that read attributes from run X carries a source_kind="run" substitution ref to X but a different (or absent) parent_run_id, so GET /lineage/runs/{Y}/ancestors returns X while GET /lineage/runs/{X}/descendants omits Y. story:lineage-exploration falsifier: "a real downstream consumer is missing from the descendant walk". The reverse-substitution-ref lookup already exists in-file (recordMentionsSource with kind "run") — descendants just doesn't use it. lineage_test.go masks this by hand-seeding parent_run_id records.
verify_note: walkLineageRuns ancestors expands via extractSubstitutionRefRunIDs (substitution_refs = data lineage, lineage.go:211) while descendants expands via QueryByParentNodeRunID whose SQL matches record->>'parent_run_id' (lineage.go:114 SQL; parent_run_id is spawn/fan-out/subgraph parentage set at child_execution.go:94, state_propagation aggregation tree). The two directions traverse non-inverse relations: a run that read attributes from X carries a substitution_ref to X but a different/absent parent_run_id, so X's /descendants omits it while it appears in its own /ancestors. story/lineage-exploration.md falsifier: 'a real downstream consumer is missing from the descendant walk.' The reverse-substitution lookup recordMentionsSource(record,"run",id) already exists in-file (used by by-source pivot) but descendants doesn't use it. Confirmed.
remediation: Make descendants and ancestors traverse the same relation (substitution_refs) so /descendants mirrors /ancestors per story:lineage-exploration's falsifier.

summary: by-source and by-producer reverse lookups scan only the 500 most-recent records of the kind and filter in memory — once the projection exceeds 500 leaf_run / claim_terminal rows (a handful of instance runs), older matches are silently omitted with no truncation signal.
evidence: handleLineageBySource (lines 369-371) and handleLineageByProducer (lines 417-419) issue a single Lineage().Query with ListPagination{Limit: 500} — the postgres impl orders observed_at DESC and applies the LIMIT with no cursor loop — then JSON-decode-filter the page via recordMentionsSource/recordMentionsProducer. Every leaf-run terminal writes a record, so any aged deployment blows past 500 quickly, after which these endpoints return only matches from the newest 500 rows while responding 200 with a plain "records" array (no truncated flag, no next_cursor, no limit/cursor params accepted). story:lineage-exploration acceptance: "the source-pivot and producer-pivot return the records they should".
verify_note: handleLineageBySource (lineage.go:369) and handleLineageByProducer (lineage.go:417) issue a single Lineage().Query with ListPagination{Limit:500}; the postgres Query (lineage.go:74) orders observed_at DESC and applies LIMIT with no cursor loop, then filters in-memory via recordMentionsSource/recordMentionsProducer. by-source doesn't even scope by instance. Every leaf_run/claim_terminal writes a record, so once the projection exceeds 500 rows older matches are silently dropped; responses return a plain {"records":...} with no truncated flag, no next_cursor, and no cursor/limit params accepted. story acceptance: 'the source-pivot and producer-pivot return the records they should.' Confirmed silent incompleteness.
remediation: Push the by-source/by-producer filter into the query (or paginate) instead of scanning the 500 most-recent records and filtering in memory; surface a truncation signal if a cap remains.

summary: extractSubstitutionRefRunIDs decodes SourceKind and then ignores it: any substitution ref whose source_version_or_id parses as a UUID is walked as an ancestor run regardless of kind.

summary: handleLineageClaimAncestors semantics diverge from the run-ancestors walk: the seed's own records are included in "ancestors", every historical record per claim is returned (runs dedupe to the latest), and depth counts from the seed rather than from the first ancestor generation.

summary: Dotted params_redact entries are silently skipped, and nested secrets cannot be redacted at all
evidence: ApplyParamsRedact does `if strings.Contains(key, ".") { continue }` — a template author writing params_redact: ["credentials.token"] gets zero redaction with no error. No register-time validation rejects dotted entries (ParamsRedact in lib/foundation/spec/template.go:18 is never validated anywhere; grep shows the only readers are controlapi). Redaction is also strictly top-level: a secret nested under a non-redacted map key (params: {db: {password: ...}}) has no redaction path whatsoever. The declared redaction surface silently misses these fields and the secrets ship in GET /instances responses.
verify_note: ApplyParamsRedact (redact.go:18) does `if strings.Contains(key, ".") { continue }` — dotted params_redact entries are silently skipped with no error; redaction is strictly top-level (only out[key] for top-level keys), so nested secrets (params.db.password) are unredactable. ParamsRedact (spec/template.go:18) is never validated anywhere — grep confirms the only readers are controlapi/instances.go; no register-time rejection of dotted entries. Declared redaction silently misses these fields and the secret ships in GET /instances. Confirmed.
remediation: Support dotted params_redact paths so nested secrets are actually redacted.

summary: Redaction fails open: empty/nil redact list returns params verbatim, and call sites pass nil on template-load errors

A transient DB/template-load failure therefore exposes every secret param unredacted in the instance read surface. Fail-closed (omit params or error) is the safe default for a secret-redaction path.
verify_note: ApplyParamsRedact (redact.go:10) returns params verbatim when len(redact)==0. Both callers fail open on template-load error: handleListInstances (instances.go:457-466) logs 'load template for params_redact failed; skipping redaction' and leaves redact=nil; instanceRedact (instances.go:483-491) returns nil on error. A transient template/DB load failure therefore exposes every secret param unredacted in the instance read surface. Fail-closed (omit params or error) would be the safe default. Confirmed.
remediation: Make redaction fail closed: nil/empty redact list on a template-load error should redact all params rather than return them verbatim.

summary: tagPattern admits '/', but slash-containing tags are unaddressable via every {tag}/{id} path route — create succeeds, then the tag can never be moved, deleted, or resolved
evidence: tagPattern `^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9._:@/-]{0,254}$` accepts e.g. 'env/prod'; POST /v1/tags creates it. But PUT/DELETE /v1/tags/{tag} and GET/DELETE /v1/templates/{id} carry the tag as a single chi path segment: a literal '/' never matches `{tag}`, and a percent-encoded '/' isn't decoded — chi v5 routes on r.URL.RawPath when set (mux.go routeHTTP) and URLParam returns the still-escaped 'env%2Fprod', so TemplateTags().Get misses → 404. The CLI even escapes it (cmd/rimsky/cli/client.go:339 url.PathEscape). Either strip '/' from the grammar or decode params; today it mints unmanageable resources.
verify_note: tagPattern `^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9._:@/-]{0,254}$` (tags.go:20) admits '/'. POST /v1/tags takes the tag from the JSON body so 'env/prod' is creatable, but PUT/DELETE /tags/{tag} (tags.go:50-51) and GET/DELETE /templates/{id} (templates.go:69-70) carry it as a single chi path segment. A literal '/' yields two segments -> route miss (404); the CLI url.PathEscape's it (client.go:339,351,235,271) to %2F which chi's URLParam returns still-escaped, so TemplateTags().Get('env%2Fprod') misses the row stored as 'env/prod'. Either way the tag is unaddressable after creation. Real fail-open grammar defect; edge-triggered (needs a slash in the tag), major stands.
remediation: Disallow '/' in tagPattern (or make routes handle it) so a created tag can be moved/deleted/resolved.

summary: compose: reserved-prefix guard exists only on create — move and delete freely mutate compose-managed tags
evidence: handleCreateTag rejects `compose:`-prefixed tags without isComposeOrigin (tags.go:65-68, 'managed by the compose command'), but handleMoveTag (143) and handleDeleteTag (193) have no such check: any holder of tag:set / tag:delete can repoint or remove a compose-owned pointer, which is exactly the mutation the create guard exists to reserve. DELETE /v1/templates/{tag} (templates.go:616,625) deletes compose tags unguarded too. Tests cover none of this (tags_test.go has no compose-prefix cases).
verify_note: handleCreateTag guards composeReservedPrefix (tags.go:65) but handleMoveTag (143) and handleDeleteTag (193) have no such check; handleDeleteTemplate deletes compose tags unguarded (templates.go:616,625). isComposeOrigin gates create on the compose:origin permission (compose_prefix.go), yet a holder of only tag:set / tag:delete can repoint or remove a compose-managed pointer, nullifying the reservation the create guard exists to enforce. No compose-prefix cases in tags_test.go (grep empty). Confirmed.
remediation: Apply the reserved-prefix guard to tag move and delete, not just create.

summary: Create/move tag use check-then-act across separate transactions — duplicate-create 409 contract is racy and move can resurrect a concurrently-deleted tag
evidence: handleCreateTag runs the TemplateTags().Get existence check in one Transaction (79-86) and the Upsert in another (97-102); two concurrent creates of the same tag both pass the check, both get 201, and the loser's binding is silently overwritten — a create acting as an unrequested move. handleMoveTag similarly Gets (147-153) then Upserts (180-185) in separate txs, so a tag deleted in between is recreated rather than 404ing. A single tx with a conditional insert (or unique-violation mapping to 409) closes both.

summary: RFC3339 layout literal instead of time.RFC3339, and timestamps serialized as pre-formatted strings unlike sibling responses
evidence: tags.go:133, templates.go:475, templates.go:514 all spell out "2006-01-02T15:04:05Z07:00" — which is exactly time.RFC3339 — instead of the named constant. tagItem.UpdatedAt / templateListItem.RegisteredAt are string fields, while nodeResponse.CreatedAt and messageItem.ReceivedAt let encoding/json marshal time.Time; two idioms for one job.

summary: Register-with-tag Upserts unconditionally: silently moves existing tags under template:register permission, bypassing the tag:set gate, the duplicate-409 contract, and the compose: prefix guard
evidence: handleDeployTemplate only checks validTag(tag) (195); both the existing-template path (288-294) and the fresh-insert tx (331-333) call TemplateTags().Upsert. Consequences: (1) POST /v1/templates with tag=X where X already points at another template repoints X — a tag move performed with only template:register, while PUT /v1/tags/{tag} requires tag:set; (2) POST /v1/tags returns 409 on duplicate but this path silently overwrites; (3) the composeReservedPrefix check in handleCreateTag (tags.go:65) is absent, so 'compose:*' tags can be created/moved here by anyone. templates_test.go never exercises register-with-tag against a pre-existing tag.
verify_note: handleDeployTemplate (gated only by template:register) calls TemplateTags().Upsert unconditionally on both the existing-template path (templates.go:290) and fresh-insert tx (332), after only validTag(). Confirmed consequences: (1) repoints an existing tag with template:register, bypassing the tag:set gate on PUT /tags/{tag} (tags.go:50); (2) silently overwrites where POST /tags returns 409 (tags.go:87-90); (3) no composeReservedPrefix guard, so compose:* tags are creatable/movable here. Strongest of the set — a genuine permission-gate bypass.
remediation: Reject register-with-tag when the tag already points elsewhere; route tag movement through the tag:set gate, duplicate-409 contract, and compose: prefix guard.

summary: Registered/deregistered lifecycle fan-out fires before (and outside) the persistence transaction — subscribers can receive events for state changes that never commit

summary: pickCanonicalRoute misroutes tools whose action maps multiple sibling routes: auth_status invokes GET /v1/auth/keys, asset_versions and asset_materialization_history invoke GET /v1/instances/{id}/assets/{alias}, and lineage_get can never reach the ancestors/descendants routes.
evidence: The heuristic (placeholders-satisfied -> item-vs-list by `_list` suffix -> shortest path) cannot discriminate sibling routes sharing the same placeholders. Traced against v1Actions in lib/control/controlapi/actions.go: (1) auth_status (action auth:read, routes /v1/auth/keys, /v1/auth/keys/{nameOrID}, /v1/auth/status; args {}): placeholder filter keeps [/v1/auth/keys, /v1/auth/status], neither is an item route so the item filter is a no-op, shortest-path picks /v1/auth/keys (13 < 15) — the tool returns the API-key list instead of auth status. (2) asset_versions / asset_materialization_history (action asset:read; args id+alias): all four routes placeholder-satisfied; wantItem=true keeps only /v1/instances/{id}/assets/{alias} (the only route ending in a placeholder) — both tools return the asset itself, never /versions or /materialization-history. (3) lineage_get with run_id: wantItem=true always shadows /runs/{run_id}/ancestors and /runs/{run_id}/descendants behind /runs/{run_id} (same for /claims/{claim_handle_id}/ancestors) — those documented reads are unreachable through the MCP skin. The registry maps tools to actions, not routes (ActionEntry.MCPTools has no per-tool route), so the heuristic has no discriminator to recover with.

Traced against actions.go v1Actions: (1) auth_status (auth:read, args {}): placeholder filter keeps /v1/auth/keys + /v1/auth/status, neither item, shortest picks /v1/auth/keys (len 13 < 15) -> returns key list not auth status. (2) asset_versions & asset_materialization_history (asset:read, args id+alias): all four routes placeholder-satisfied, wantItem=true keeps only .../{alias} -> both return the asset item, never /versions or /materialization-history. (3) lineage_get (single tool for 7 routes, args run_id): wantItem=true keeps only runs/{run_id}, shadowing /ancestors and /descendants permanently. Multiple documented reads silently misroute. Internal route test only covers 2-route item/list cases; the sibling-collision cases are untested.
remediation: Fix MCP catalog route selection so auth_status, asset_versions, asset_materialization_history, and lineage_get ancestors/descendants map to their correct routes.

summary: tools/call never sets the MCP-level CallToolResult.isError flag; REST 4xx/5xx failures from Catalog.Invoke are flattened into content[0].text, so MCP clients see every failed tool call as a success.
evidence: catalog.go:139-146 returns `map[string]any{"status":…, "error":true, "body":…, "isError":true}` with a nil *Error for any resp.StatusCode >= 400 — the isError key is clearly intended to reach the protocol level. handleToolsCall (server.go:178-187) marshals whatever Invoke returns and wraps it as `{"content":[{"type":"text","text":string(bs)}]}` — the result object carries no top-level "isError" field. Per MCP 2025-06-18, tool execution errors must be reported via CallToolResult.isError=true; embedding it inside a text blob means conformant clients (and agent frameworks that branch on isError) treat permission-denied, not-found, and validation failures as successful calls.
verify_note: catalog.go:139-146 returns a plain map with embedded isError:true and a nil *Error for status>=400, so Invoke takes the success return. handleToolsCall (server.go:178-187) marshals it into content[0].text and never sets a top-level CallToolResult.isError. Per MCP 2025-06-18 tool errors must set isError=true; spec-conformant clients read isError=false and treat permission-denied/not-found/validation failures as successful. Genuine protocol conformance gap.
remediation: Set CallToolResult.isError when Catalog.Invoke returns a 4xx/5xx so MCP clients see failures as failures.

summary: The admin-route de-preference filter in pickCanonicalRoute tests strings.HasPrefix(r.Path, "/admin/") but every registered route path is prefixed /v1 (e.g. /v1/admin/diagnostics/parked-nodes), so the filter never fires in production.

(lineage:prune, parked-node:read, waitset:read, diagnostics:read); HasPrefix("/v1/admin/...", "/admin/") is always false, making hasNonAdmin/candidate-skipping dead code against real registry data. parked_node_list currently lands on /v1/diagnostics/parked only because the shortest-path tiebreak happens to agree (22 < 35 chars) — the intended preference is unenforced and will silently break if a shorter admin sibling is ever registered. TestPickCanonicalRoute uses no /v1/admin paths, so the mismatch is untested.

summary: url4QueryFromRemaining silently drops object- and array-valued arguments when mapping remaining args onto GET/DELETE query strings; the caller gets a success with the filter ignored instead of an invalid-params error.
evidence: catalog.go:183-189: `if trim[0] == '{' || trim[0] == '[' { continue }`. A model calling e.g. event_list or lineage_get with a structured filter argument (the schemas advertise additionalProperties or object-typed fields) has that argument dropped without any diagnostic — the tool returns unfiltered data and the client cannot tell. Returning CodeInvalidParams naming the unencodable key would fail loudly instead.

summary: Filtered evaluates CheckGrant with a nil target, so an API key holding only scope-restricted grants cannot discover tools it is in fact permitted to invoke — tools/list and tools/call disagree.
evidence: catalog.go:48 `auth.CheckGrant(ident.Permissions, entry.Action, nil)`. auth.ScopeMatches (lib/foundation/auth/scope.go:7-18) returns false for any scoped grant entry when target is nil (the target lookup misses), so a key granted e.g. instance:create scoped to template_tag=X sees no instance_create tool in tools/list, while Invoke succeeds for matching targets because the inner gateByAction computes requestTargets from the real request. The tool catalog under-reports capability for exactly the least-privileged keys; agentic clients that plan from tools/list will never attempt calls they are entitled to make.

summary: Invoke synthesizes a fresh Idempotency-Key (mcp-<uuid>) on every POST/PUT and offers no client pass-through, so retried tools/call requests are never deduplicated — a retried message_send produces a duplicate message (and hence a duplicate frame).
evidence: catalog.go:126-128 stamps `"mcp-"+uuid.NewString()` unconditionally. The header exists because POST /v1/instances/{id}/messages requires it precisely for dedup (lib/control/controlapi/messages.go:129-131,205 persists it as IdempotencyKey), but the MCP surface defeats that purpose: neither the message_send input schema nor Invoke lets the caller supply a stable key, and the JSON-RPC request id/session (which could seed a deterministic key) is ignored. Since only a message runs a frame, an MCP client retry after a network timeout double-runs work.

summary: handleInitialize ignores the initialize params entirely — the client's requested protocolVersion is never read, and the server unconditionally answers 2025-06-18.
evidence: server.go:143-156 takes only (w, req) and never unmarshals req.Params. Per the MCP lifecycle spec, if the server supports the client's requested version it must respond with that same version; a client requesting an older supported revision gets 2025-06-18 back and may legitimately disconnect. Client capabilities/clientInfo are likewise discarded without validation.

summary: The server issues an Mcp-Session-Id on initialize but keeps no session state and never validates the header on subsequent requests; serveStream just echoes back whatever the client sent.
evidence: handleInitialize (server.go:144) mints newSessionID() per initialize; servePost never reads sessionHeader, and serveStream (server.go:104-106) reflects any client-supplied value verbatim. Per MCP streamable-HTTP, a server that assigns a session ID should reject non-initialize requests lacking it (400) and terminated/unknown IDs (404); a stateless server should not issue one at all. Issuing-but-ignoring advertises stateful semantics the server does not honor — clients that rotate or fabricate session IDs observe no difference, and session termination (DELETE) is unsupported while the ID is still handed out.

summary: Response.ID carries omitempty, so parse-error responses omit the id field where JSON-RPC 2.0 requires "id": null.
evidence: types.go:19 `ID json.RawMessage \`json:"id,omitempty"\``. writeRPCError(w, nil, CodeParseError, …) at server.go:63 and :68 passes a nil RawMessage, producing `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","error":{…}}` with no id member. JSON-RPC 2.0 §5: when the id cannot be detected (Parse error / Invalid Request), the Response id MUST be Null. Strict clients keyed on the id member fail to correlate or reject the reply.

summary: RegistryEntry.IsWrite is dead within the mcp package — populated by the actionRegistryAdapter and by test fixtures but never read by any mcp code path.
evidence: grep across lib/control/controlapi/mcp: IsWrite appears only in the types.go:51 declaration; catalog.go and server.go never consult it (the write/read distinction is enforced downstream by gateByAction via the controlapi ActionRegistry, auth_middleware.go:215). Per Plumbline dead-code rules the field (and its copy in mcp_route.go's adapter and the test fixtures) should be deleted until something in the package needs it.

summary: Function name url4QueryFromRemaining reads as a typo/leetism ("url4Query") — non-idiomatic Go naming; should be urlQueryFromRemaining or queryFromRemaining.
evidence: catalog.go:180 `func url4QueryFromRemaining(m map[string]json.RawMessage) string`. Single call site at catalog.go:96. No other identifier in the package uses a digit-infix style; one idiom per job favors the plain name.

summary: writeRPCResult/writeRPCErrorObj encode-failure fallback appends a bare {"error":"encode: …"} object after a possibly partially-written response body, yielding malformed, non-JSON-RPC output.
evidence: server.go:239-241 and :251-253: after json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(resp) fails midway (headers and a body prefix already flushed), fmt.Fprintf writes a second JSON object onto the same body; the concatenation is invalid JSON and the fallback object is not a JSON-RPC Response (no jsonrpc/id/error.code members). Logging and abandoning the write would be strictly better than emitting garbage.

summary: TEST GAP: route-picking tests cover only the four well-behaved tool families (node/message/instance/template); none of the sibling-route families that actually misroute (auth_status, asset_versions, asset_materialization_history, lineage_get) nor the /v1/admin prefix behavior are exercised.
