summary: Data race in unified startup: each role runner calls config.OpenBlobBackend -> db.SetBlobBackend on the shared driver while earlier roles' background goroutines are already reading the blob fields
evidence: StartUnifiedStack starts runners sequentially: RunScheduler (scheduler.go:76) opens the blob backend and config.StartScheduler spawns background loops (lib/control/config/scheduler.go:81 runAuthSweepLoop, :83 scheduler.Start) that read tables' blob wiring on row writes (lib/foundation/persistence/postgres/node_attributes.go:107 reads si.blob/si.blobThreshold). Then RunSupervisor (supervisor.go:140) and RunControlAPI (controlapi.go:47) each call OpenBlobBackend again on the SAME driver, and SetBlobBackend is a plain unsynchronized field write in both drivers (lib/foundation/persistence/postgres/backend.go:47-51 's.blob = bb; s.blobThreshold = threshold', sqlite/backend.go:42 same shape). Concurrent unsynchronized interface-value write while another goroutine reads is a Go data race (torn interface possible); with the filesystem backend the three writes are three distinct backend pointers. Per-role processes are unaffected (single write before serving), so this is specific to the unified composition. Fix: open the blob backend once before starting any role (e.g. in StartUnifiedStack) and pass it down, or synchronize SetBlobBackend/readers.
verify_note: StartUnifiedStack (unified.go:53,56,59) passes the SAME driver to all three runners started sequentially. Each Run* calls config.OpenBlobBackend -> db.SetBlobBackend (blob.go:33/37/44/51), which is an unsynchronized field write (postgres/backend.go:47-51 s.blob/s.blobThreshold/s.blobRetention; sqlite same). Scheduler's background loops start in RunScheduler (config/scheduler.go:81 auth sweep, :83 scheduler.Start ticking) before supervisor/control-api call SetBlobBackend again on the shared driver; node_attributes.go:107 reads si.blob/si.blobThreshold on writes. Concurrent unsynchronized interface-value write while another goroutine reads = Go data race (torn interface possible; filesystem backend yields three distinct pointers). Specific to the unified composition; -race on that path would flag it.
remediation: Open/Set the blob backend once before spawning any role goroutine, or guard db.SetBlobBackend with synchronization, so earlier roles' background readers never race the write.

summary: control-api metrics server binds on the control-API host instead of metricsHostFromEnv(); RIMSKY_METRICS_HOST is silently ignored for this role
evidence: controlapi.go:82 'startMetricsServer(host, "control-api", ...)' passes the RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_HOST value (default 127.0.0.1), whereas scheduler.go:117 and supervisor.go:217 both pass metricsHostFromEnv() (env:RIMSKY_METRICS_HOST). Consequences: setting RIMSKY_METRICS_HOST has no effect on the control-api role's metrics listener, and setting RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_HOST=0.0.0.0 silently exposes the metrics endpoint on all interfaces regardless of RIMSKY_METRICS_HOST. One of three roles diverging from the shared env contract with no error or log.
verify_note: controlapi.go:82 passes host (RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_HOST, default 127.0.0.1) to startMetricsServer, whereas scheduler.go:117 and supervisor.go:217 pass metricsHostFromEnv() (RIMSKY_METRICS_HOST). Divergence confirmed: RIMSKY_METRICS_HOST is silently ignored for control-api, and RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_HOST=0.0.0.0 exposes its metrics on all interfaces. Real bug; downgraded to medium — metrics endpoint, low-sensitivity data, config inconsistency.

summary: OpenBlobBackend return value discarded — reads as validation but carries the load-bearing side effect db.SetBlobBackend
evidence: controlapi.go:47 'if _, err := config.OpenBlobBackend(rimskyCfg.Blob, driver); err != nil'. OpenBlobBackend (lib/control/config/blob.go:26) is not a pure validator: every success branch calls db.SetBlobBackend on the shared driver, so the control-api role's blob wiring happens through a discarded return value. Violates the explicit-code rule (hidden mutation behind an apparent validation call) and is the third redundant SetBlobBackend write feeding the unified-startup race. If only validation is intended, call persistence.ValidateBlobConfig; if wiring is intended, keep the handle and make the side effect visible.

summary: Dead fields on UnifiedStack: failBufN is written and never read; names is appended and never read in production code
evidence: failBufN set at unified.go:65 and in unified_test.go:41/60/125 but no code reads it (grep for failBufN finds only assignments). names appended at unified.go:75 and populated in unified_test.go:39 but never read anywhere — Drain does not use it for logging or ordering. Plumbline: dead code is deleted, not carried.

summary: RunSupervisor writes errors to os.Stderr with a hardcoded 'rimsky-supervisor:' binary prefix — idiom drift from the package's slog-based error reporting, and the prefix is wrong in unified mode
evidence: supervisor.go:45, :58, :63, :118 use fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "rimsky-supervisor: %v\n", err) while every other error path in the package (scheduler.go:72/78/107, controlapi.go:33/43/48/71, and supervisor.go's own :52/:142/:204) uses the slog-backed log.Error. In the unified stack and the compose verb this code runs inside a process that is not the rimsky-supervisor binary, so the stderr prefix misidentifies the source; the errors are also double-reported (stderr write + returned error that the caller logs again). One idiom per job: report via the passed logger and return.

summary: Inconsistent env-parse policy in the same file: non-numeric RIMSKY_SCHEDULER_TICK_MS is silently swallowed (defaults to 250) while non-numeric metrics ports are startup-fatal
evidence: scheduler.go:67 'tickMs := atoiDefault(os.Getenv("RIMSKY_SCHEDULER_TICK_MS"), 250)' — atoiDefault (scheduler.go:209) returns the default on any parse error, so a typo like RIMSKY_SCHEDULER_TICK_MS=25O silently runs at 250ms. metricsPortFor (scheduler.go:151-175) treats the same class of typo as a startup-fatal error, a policy the tests pin down explicitly (launch_test.go:171 'non-numeric RIMSKY_METRICS_PORT should error, not silently disable metrics'). Two policies for one job.

summary: RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_PORT=0 silently falls back to default 8080, and negative values are accepted and passed through to the listener
evidence: controlapi.go:36-38 'if n != 0 { port = n }' — an explicit "0" is silently treated as "use default 8080" (contrast metricsPortFor where <=0 means disabled), and a negative value (e.g. "-1") sets port=-1 which only fails later inside config.StartControlAPI with a bind error that does not name the env var. Non-numeric values are startup-fatal with a clear message (line 32), so the validation is half-done: numeric-but-invalid values escape it.

summary: Raw "RIMSKY_PROCESS_ROLE" string literal duplicates the exported persistence.ProcessRoleEnv constant
evidence: scheduler.go:171 'if os.Getenv("RIMSKY_PROCESS_ROLE") == "unified"' — lib/foundation/persistence/blob_config.go:51 declares 'const ProcessRoleEnv = "RIMSKY_PROCESS_ROLE"' and the memory-blob gate (blob_config.go:68) uses it. The launch package already imports persistence. Strict DRY: the env-var name should resolve to the one named symbol so a rename cannot desynchronize the port-offset check from the blob gate.

summary: defaultRimskyConfigPath is declared in scheduler.go but used only by open_driver.go
evidence: scheduler.go:30 'const defaultRimskyConfigPath = "/etc/rimsky/rimsky.yml"' — its sole consumer is OpenDriverFromEnv (open_driver.go:20). One-feature-per-file placement: the constant belongs with the driver/config-opening feature, not the scheduler runner.

summary: Vocabulary confusion: the scheduler's identity env var RIMSKY_SCHEDULER_ID populates a local named supervisorID with fallback values 'scheduler-<hostname>'
evidence: scheduler.go:82-89 'supervisorID := os.Getenv("RIMSKY_SCHEDULER_ID")' then 'supervisorID = "scheduler-" + hostname'. A variable named supervisorID holding scheduler-prefixed identities read from a SCHEDULER env var forces the reader to untangle three vocabularies for one value. The config field name (config.SchedulerConfig.SupervisorID, lib/control/config/scheduler.go:27) is the upstream source of the confusion, but the launch-local variable could at least be named for what it is (schedulerID / claimantID) with the field assignment making the mapping explicit.

summary: Cancelling the ctx passed to StartUnifiedStack does not stop or drain any role — ctx is startup-scoped only, and two of three runners ignore it entirely
evidence: RunScheduler and RunControlAPI never reference their ctx parameter; RunSupervisor uses it only for the startup observability handshake (supervisor.go:156). All background lifetimes are anchored to context.Background() (scheduler.go:111, supervisor.go:209, controlapi.go:76) and torn down only via the returned StopFunc/Drain. A caller that cancels the StartUnifiedStack ctx expecting teardown gets a silently still-running stack. Nothing in the signature, a type, or a test pins down this 'ctx is for startup only' contract.

summary: StartUnifiedStack's failure-forwarding goroutine and its startup-failure drain path are untested
evidence: The goroutine at unified.go:76-85 (reads the runner's error channel, forwards a RoleFailure to failCh, ignores nil errors and closed channels) is never exercised: TestUnifiedStack_FailChDeliversFailure (unified_test.go:122) writes directly into stack.failCh, bypassing the forwarding logic entirely. Likewise the startup-failure path (unified.go:70-73: runner N fails -> already-started roles drained in reverse, error wrapped 'start <role>') has no test, even though the package already has the runner-stub seam (runSchedulerFn/runSupervisorFn/runControlAPIFn) used by TestStartUnifiedStack_OneDriverAcrossRunners, making both tests cheap.

summary: startMetricsServer's bind-failure and serve-error reporting paths and metricsHostFromEnv are untested
evidence: startMetricsServer (scheduler.go:177-207) reports a bind failure to the failureReporter and returns nil (startup continues, failure surfaces asynchronously via FailCh), and reports async serve errors from the Serve goroutine — neither path has a test, though both are trivially exercisable by occupying a port on 127.0.0.1. metricsHostFromEnv (scheduler.go:137) is also untested. Note the resulting policy asymmetry is unpinned: a non-numeric port is synchronously startup-fatal (tested) while a port-in-use is an asynchronous role failure after StartUnifiedStack has already returned success (untested, undocumented).

summary: RunSupervisor's config-resolution logic — advertise-host precedence, YAML default clamps, env expansion — has no unit tests
evidence: The advertise host/port precedence chain (supervisor.go:103-124: env RIMSKY_SUPERVISOR_CALLBACK_ADVERTISE_HOST > yaml callback.advertise_host > unset-with-loopback-warning; env port with parse-fatal on non-numeric), the silent clamps (concurrency<1 -> 4, livenessMs<100 -> 5000, claimPollMs<50 -> 1000, supervisor.go:75-86), and loadSupervisorYAML's os.ExpandEnv behavior (supervisor.go:243-254) are all pure config-resolution logic with zero test coverage in this package — the CLAUDE.md-level gotcha about callback.advertise_host rests on untested code. Extracting the resolution into a testable function would cover it without any server startup.

summary: Supervisor ID fallback ignores the os.Hostname error, unlike the scheduler's fallback in the same package
evidence: supervisor.go:71-72 'hostname, _ := os.Hostname(); supID = fmt.Sprintf("%s-%d", hostname, os.Getpid())' — on Hostname failure this yields an ID like "-1234". scheduler.go:84-88 handles the same case explicitly ('if hostname, err := os.Hostname(); err == nil && hostname != ""' with a 'scheduler-default' fallback). Two idioms for one job (derive a default role identity), one of which can produce a degenerate ID.

summary: Two watcher idioms for the same serve-error-to-reporter job: supervisor blocks bare on CallbackServeErr, control-api needs a stopped-channel select
evidence: supervisor.go:219-223 blocks directly on h.CallbackServeErr() because the callback server closes its serveErr channel on shutdown (lib/runtime/callback.go:163), while controlapi.go:84-94 needs the stopped channel + sync.Once machinery because controlAPIHandle.serveErr is never closed (lib/control/config/controlapi.go — buffered send at :274, no close). The asymmetry is correct today but load-bearing and invisible: if controlAPIHandle ever closes its channel the stopped machinery becomes dead weight, and if CallbackServer ever stops closing its channel the supervisor watcher becomes a goroutine leak. Uniform close-on-shutdown semantics upstream would collapse both to one idiom.

summary: frames ?state= filter conflates failed and completed and silently accepts unknown values
evidence: handleListFrames maps `s == "running"` to Unresolved=true and EVERY other value (failed, completed, typos) to Unresolved=false. The read model exposes a derived tri-state (running/failed/completed via the CASE in Frames().ListForObservability), so `?state=failed` returns all ended frames including rows whose returned state field says "completed", and `?state=bogus` returns ended frames instead of a 400. No validation against the three legal derived values.
verify_note: handler.go:373-376 maps s=='running' to Unresolved=true and every other value to Unresolved=false with no validation. Read model derives tri-state via CASE (frames.go:283-285 running/failed/completed on ended_at IS NULL / failed exists / else). Confirmed: ?state=failed returns Unresolved=false = all ended frames including completed (conflation), and ?state=bogus returns ended frames instead of 400. Downgraded to medium — observability read filter.

summary: handleGetNode swallows errors from three of its four transactions, serving fabricated-empty data on DB failure
evidence: Lines 448, 454, 461: `_ = inTx(...)` for holdings (ClaimHandles.ListByHolderNode), events (Events().List), and the latest-attributes/run-summary block. A failing query yields HTTP 200 with holdings=[], events=null, latest_attributes={}, run_summary zero — indistinguishable from a genuinely idle node. Contrast with the first block (lines 428-434) which correctly returns 500.
verify_note: handleGetNode uses `_ = inTx(...)` at lines 448 (holdings), 454 (events), 461 (latest attrs + run summary), discarding errors, while the first block (428-434) correctly returns internalErr. On a failing query the handler serves HTTP 200 with holdings=[], events=null, latest_attributes={}, zero run_summary — indistinguishable from an idle node. Confirmed; medium (observability read surface, misleading not corrupting).

summary: computeCascadeGraph discards the Transaction error; graph served with silently-missing summaries and terminal events
evidence: `_ = deps.Tables.Transaction(ctx, func(...)` — if Events().LastTerminalByNodes or Nodes().GetRunSummary fails, terminals is nil and summaries partial/empty, and handleGetInstance still returns 200 with a cascade_graph whose every node shows run_summary: null / no last_terminal_event. Operators cannot distinguish a never-run graph from a read failure.
verify_note: cascade_graph.go:39 `_ = deps.Tables.Transaction(...)` discards the error; on LastTerminalByNodes or GetRunSummary failure, terminals is nil and summaries partial, yet handleGetInstance still returns 200 with cascade_graph nodes showing run_summary:null / no last_terminal_event. Operators cannot distinguish never-run from read failure. Confirmed; medium.

summary: rimsky_parked_nodes_by_reason gauge never returns to zero: vanished reasons keep their last non-zero value forever
evidence: refreshGauges sets only reasons present in queue.CountParkedByReason(ctx), whose SQL (`WHERE state = 'parked' GROUP BY parked_reason`) returns no row for a reason that drained to zero. The GaugeVec is never Reset() and absent labels never zeroed, so once all rate_limit parks resume, rimsky_parked_nodes_by_reason{reason="rate_limit"} stays at its old count indefinitely — alerts on parked-by-reason never clear. NodesByState avoids this only because CountByState pre-seeds all seven states to 0.
verify_note: refreshGauges (metrics_hook.go:122-128) sets ParkedByReason only for reasons returned by CountParkedByReason, whose SQL (queue.go:620-640, WHERE state='parked' GROUP BY reason) omits drained reasons. SetParkedByReason (metrics_hook.go:66-67) is a bare GaugeVec.WithLabelValues().Set with no Reset(), so a drained reason keeps its last value forever. Contrast CountByState (nodes.go:263-271) which pre-seeds all seven states to 0, why NodesByState clears correctly. Confirmed stale-gauge bug; medium (alerting never clears).

summary: handleGetNodeRun swallows enrichment errors twice over
evidence: `_ = inTx(...)` discards the transaction error, and inside, `if holder, err := ...; err == nil && holder != nil` / `if nodeRow, err := ...; err == nil && nodeRow != nil` silently drop query errors. On DB failure the response is 200 with claim_id, instance_id, node_type silently null/empty rather than 500.

summary: handleGetInstance swallows Templates().GetByHash error
evidence: `t, _ := deps.Tables.Templates().GetByHash(ctx, row.TemplateHash, tx)` — on a transient DB error template is nil, so computeCascadeGraph takes the template==nil branch and renders the graph with edges_in/edges_out all empty, returned as 200. Every other query in the same transaction propagates its error.

summary: 404 message "dispatch not found (terminal-deleted)" misstates the model; terminal runs are retained, not deleted
evidence: Queue.GetByID filters `d.state IN ('pending','stale','running','held','parked')` — terminal rows (fresh/failed) remain in rimsky_node_runs until the retention sweep; the frames failed-state derivation (`EXISTS ... r.state = 'failed'`) and GetRunSummary depend on their retention. A run that just settled 404s here with a message claiming it was deleted, and nothing signposts that /node-runs is a live-queue-only view (terminal runs are readable via the lineage surface).

summary: node-runs read model collapses five live run states into derived pending/claimed; parked and held runs are indistinguishable
evidence: Both handleListNodeRuns (lines 521-524) and handleGetNodeRun (lines 564-567) derive `state` solely from `row.ClaimedBy != nil`, and ListLive/GetByID never select d.state. An operator listing /node-runs cannot tell a parked or held run from one actively running or awaiting claim, even though /system/summary and the metrics surface expose the full five-state vocabulary. The identical two-line derivation is also duplicated across the two handlers.

summary: node-runs ?state= filter silently ignores values other than pending/claimed
evidence: filter.State is passed verbatim; queueImpl.ListLive/CountLive `switch filter.State` only recognizes "pending"/"claimed", leaving stateClaimed nil for anything else — `?state=parked` or `?state=running` returns the entire live queue with no 400 and no filtering.

summary: peerListResponse omitempty drops empty arrays despite handlers deliberately building non-nil slices
evidence: `ClaimProducers []PeerEntry \`json:"claim_producers,omitempty"\`` (and Executors) — encoding/json omits zero-length slices whether nil or not, so GET /claim-producers with none configured returns `{}` rather than `{"claim_producers": []}`. The handlers' `entries := []PeerEntry{}` initialization shows the empty array was intended.

summary: get-by-name peer handlers serve a zero-value PeerEntry for declared-but-uncached peers
evidence: handleGetExecutor (204-208) and handleGetClaimProducer (151-155): when `!ok` from the discovery cache but peerExists(deps...) is true, the zero-value `cached` is written as `"peer": {name:"", endpoint:"", reachability_status:"", ...}`. The list handlers synthesize an unreachable fallback entry from the PeerSpec for exactly this case; the get handlers should do the same.

summary: system/health hardcodes "postgres_status" though the backend is config-selected (postgres|sqlite)
evidence: handleSystemHealth pings deps.Driver (persistence.Database, backend-agnostic) and reports the result under `"postgres_status"`. On an all-in-one SQLite deployment the health payload claims a postgres status for a database that isn't postgres.

summary: system/summary node_counts mixes per-run-row counts with a per-node count in one map
evidence: Nodes().CountByState counts ALL retained rimsky_node_runs rows grouped by state (a node accumulates one fresh row per frame until retention prunes), while the "no_runs" key in the same nodeCounts map is nodesTotal - nodesWithRuns, a per-node quantity. The map's entries are not commensurable: node_counts.fresh can exceed nodes_total. The response also labels them node_counts while node_runs_total is the sum of the same numbers.

summary: rimsky_nodes_by_state help text says "Count of nodes" but the refresher feeds it run-row counts
evidence: refreshGauges feeds SetNodesByState from Nodes().CountByState, whose SQL is `SELECT state, count(*) FROM rimsky_node_runs GROUP BY state` — all retained run rows, not nodes. The fresh series grows with retained history rather than tracking the node population, contradicting Help: "Count of nodes in each state."

summary: rimsky_node_runs_pending help text describes the wrong predicate
evidence: Help says "state='stale' and claimed_by IS NULL" but the feeding query, queue.CountLive(State: "pending"), counts `state IN ('pending','stale','running','held','parked') AND claimed_by IS NULL` — it includes cascade-waiting 'pending' runs and unclaimed parked/held runs, not just dispatch-awaiting stale rows.

summary: multi-transaction handlers violate the cascade-graph short-fresh-transaction invariant and produce torn reads

summary: Fake's default Open returns the wire zero RealizedWriteSemantics, violating the producer contract it exists to model
evidence: fake.go:105-114 builds OpenOutcome{Available:true, Result:{Address, ClaimScope}} with RealizedWriteSemantics unset (WriteSemanticsUnknown). The write-semantics concept invariant says the wire zero value must not be returned by producers (both real client layers reject it: lib/runtime/claimproducer/inproc_client.go:42, lib/runtime/peer/client.go:47), and the Fake ignores the caps it was constructed with (NewFake takes WriteSemanticsAllowed but default Open never realizes one). No consumer sets OpenFunc (grep: 0 hits in lib/runtime + lib/control tests), so every fake-backed acquisition persists a holder row with empty realized semantics; a subsequent conflict evaluation against such a holder feeds "" to locks.ModeCoexists and panics in mvccPassThrough (conflict.go:38) — the conflict matrix is untestable through the fake's default path. Default Open should return a realized value from f.caps.WriteSemanticsAllowed.

summary: mvccPassThrough panics on unknown write-semantics fed straight from a persisted DB string — one corrupt/NULL ledger row crashes the supervisor

summary: ModeCoexists silently classifies any non-"rw" Intent (including empty/corrupt) as a reader, weakening conflicts — inconsistent with the panic on unknown WriteSemantics

summary: Evaluate fails open on malformed values: a non-map attrs silently matches everything, and non-string values for string keys coerce to "" (the child_key non-fan-out sentinel)

summary: attrs paths with empty segments ("a..b", "a.", " a") pass Validate but can never match

The claim-rollback half of the atomicity contract is only protected incidentally, by the unchecked `cands[0]` panic in the second transaction (line 111). summary: Lock-acquisition ordering rests on a 50ms sleep; if goroutine 2 wins the lock first the test fails spuriously
evidence: The test assumes tx1 has acquired LockForUpdate within 50ms of goroutine launch. On a loaded CI machine, goroutine 1 may not have reached LockForUpdate when goroutine 2 starts; if tx2 acquires first, tx1 blocks behind it and the final assertion `t2 < c1` fires as a false serialization failure. Nothing enforces the intended ordering (e.g. a channel signal after tx1 stores firstHoldStart, or a retry that tolerates either acquisition order while still asserting non-overlap of the two hold windows).

summary: testHeldClaimAutoTerminalSerialization name overpromises: no auto-terminal behavior is exercised
evidence: The file is auto_terminal.go and the test/suite name says 'HeldClaimAutoTerminalSerialization', but the body only proves ClaimHandles().LockForUpdate row-lock mutual exclusion between two transactions. Nothing about held-claim resolution or the terminal-decision engine (the single audited producer-verb site per concept:auto-terminal) is touched, and the file carries no @concept: auto-terminal citation. Name it for what it proves (LockForUpdate serialization) or extend it to the auto-terminal read-decide-write sequence it is presumably standing in for.

summary: ReleaseClaim guard test never asserts run state; partial wrong-claimant mutation and the owner-release running→stale flip are both unproven
evidence: ReleaseClaim in both backends sets `claimed_by = NULL, claimed_at = NULL, state = 'stale'` under the claimant predicate (postgres/queue.go:367-384). testClaimantGuardRunReleaseClaim asserts only claimed_by (via GetClaimedBy) and last_progress_at after the wrong-claimant call, and only Kind == "unclaimed" after the owner call. A backend that flipped state to 'stale' for the wrong claimant while retaining claimed_by would pass, and a backend that cleared claimed_by on owner release without restoring state='stale' would also pass — the state column, half of what ReleaseClaim writes, is outside the cross-backend contract this test establishes.

summary: Complete guard test asserts only claimed_by; the active_terminal_at stamp is unproven in either direction
evidence: Queue.Complete sets `claimed_by = NULL, active_terminal_at = NOW()` under the claimant predicate (postgres/queue.go:278-289). testClaimantGuardRunComplete checks ownership retained after the wrong-claimant call and Kind == "unclaimed" after the owner call, but never reads active_terminal_at. A wrong-claimant Complete that stamped active_terminal_at without touching claimed_by passes, and an owner Complete that never stamped it also passes — so the two backends are free to diverge on the terminal timestamp.

summary: Empty-claimant guard bypass is enshrined as cross-backend contract with no design artifact blessing it
evidence: testClaimantGuardRunEmptyClaimantCarveOut proves that expectedClaimedBy == "" releases, completes, and removes another supervisor's claimed rows — a deliberate bypass of the claimant guard (the ruling and invariant 4 in concept:claim-handle are 'claimant-guarded release'). Grep of .ok-planner/design/{concepts,decisions} finds no mention of an empty-claimant carve-out (the only documented carve-outs are the acquire-unavailable path in concept:auto-terminal/terminal-resolution, which is different), and unlike its sibling tests the function carries no @decision citation. Runtime callers exist only for RemoveForNodeInTx (lib/graph/scheduler/pure_cascade.go:73, lib/runtime/sweep_parked.go:190); the empty-claimant ReleaseClaim and Complete legs appear caller-less, so the conformance suite may be locking in unused bypass surface. Either document the carve-out as a decision and cite it here, or narrow the bypass to the verbs that need it.
phase1_note: Confirmed factually: testClaimantGuardRunEmptyClaimantCarveOut proves expectedClaimedBy=="" bypasses the guard on Queue.ReleaseClaim/Complete/RemoveForNodeInTx; only RemoveForNodeInTx has real production callers (both passing ""), and Queue.Complete has zero production callers at all, ReleaseClaim's one caller passes a real claimant. Neither claim-handle.md's invariant-4 guard nor advisory-lock.md's two-guard-shape model (both about the separate rimsky_claim_handles table) address this Queue/node-run-level claimed_by guard, and no concept/decision doc mentions an empty-claimant carve-out for it. Design-call: is the empty-claimant bypass on ReleaseClaim/Complete intentional scaffolding that should be narrowed to RemoveForNodeInTx only (its sole live caller shape) and documented as a decision, or should the conformance test itself be narrowed to stop asserting unused bypass surface?

summary: Wrong-claimant ParkActiveInTx asserts only 'some error', unlike the sentinel-checked Promote/Reassign guards

summary: claimed_at ordering established via time.Sleep(20ms) between inserts

summary: Post-delete orphan sweep omits rows the fixture demonstrably seeds: rimsky_frames, rimsky_messages, and rimsky_nodes are never counted after Instances().Delete, so the exact sqlite FK bug class the test targets (cascade silently not firing) would pass undetected for those tables.

Real coverage gap. Severity downgraded: the general cascade IS proven via run_scopes/node_runs (a global sqlite FK-off or blanket regression trips those); the leaf-table gap only slips a narrow per-table FK-removal regression, not the broad 'cascade not firing' class claimed.

evidence: testMessageIdempotencyInsertOrLookup performs first-then-replay in strictly sequential transactions (lines 49-64). dispatch.go establishes the suite's idiom for two-goroutine races; message idempotency, an explicitly ruled invariant ('message idempotency dedups by key'), has no equivalent.

Adding GetByRun(runA) == {which:A} after the runB upsert would prove two per-run rows coexist. No other in-scope test seeds two runs for one node, and the out-of-scope run_state_writes_isolated_by_scope.go variant only proves cross-scope (two scopes), not two-runs-in-one-scope coexistence.

A backend that pre-populates or leaks another scope's bag into a fresh scope is not caught by these files.

summary: The test codifies a state that violates concept:run-scope's never-span-frames invariant: the rebound run keeps its old scope while pointing at a new frame with a different root scope
evidence: Lines 36-51: the second frame is minted with a fresh main scope (seedMainRunScopeForInstance), then the run — created under fix.MainRunScopeID in fix.FrameID — is rebound to newFrameID. RebindRunFrameInTx (sqlite/queue_park.go:253) updates frame_id only, so the run now binds fix.MainRunScopeID (frame 1's root scope) into frame 2, i.e. the scope spans frames. concept:run-scope invariant: 'A RunScope lives inside exactly one frame; RunScopes never span frames.' Contradicts concept:blob-backend invariant 'Orphan blobs go to a persisted orphan-blob ledger and are swept after a retention window' — the ledger covers replacement-side orphans only, not write-side failures. Fix shape: ledger the new handle (write-ahead) in the enclosing tx before/with the attribute row, or delete-on-error compensation.

summary: SelectCandidates does not exclude terminated instances; queued runs on a terminated instance remain dispatchable
evidence: The candidate WHERE clause checks only `i.paused = false` — there is no `i.terminated_at IS NULL`. The terminate handler (lib/control/controlapi/instances.go:657) fails only killStates {running, parked, held}; 'stale' and 'pending' runs are left untouched, and pending runs later transition to stale via the gate evaluator when their failed senders drain. Run-scope closing happens after the terminate tx, best-effort with warn-and-continue (lib/control/controlapi/lifecycle.go:324-334), and only gates Enqueue, not selection of existing rows. The messages sibling query has the guard (postgres/messages.go:209 `AND i.terminated_at IS NULL`), and the ruling states candidate selection excludes paused/terminated. Result: supervisors claim and execute work for terminated instances. Test gap: conformance has select_candidates_paused.go but no terminated-instance selection test. Same gap in sqlite/queue.go:181.
verify_note: queue.go:153-155 WHERE has i.paused=false but no i.terminated_at IS NULL; sqlite:179-181 same. Sibling messages.go pickPendingForIdleInstances has `i.terminated_at IS NULL`. Terminate handler (instances.go:657-704) fails only killStates {running,parked,held}, leaves stale/pending. RunScopes.Close (run_scopes.go:73) only sets closed_at; SelectCandidates never joins run_scopes, so closure doesn't gate existing rows. No terminated guard in ClaimDispatchRow or runtime dispatch either. Result: stale runs on a terminated instance stay selectable and execute. Instance concept:29 makes an instance inert after force-terminate. Trigger is race/drain-dependent but reliably reachable via pending->stale. Executing work after explicit operator kill = critical.
remediation: Add a terminated_at IS NULL predicate to SelectCandidates in both postgres/queue.go and sqlite/queue.go so runs of terminated instances stop dispatching.

summary: Keyset cursor (enqueued_at, id) does not match ORDER BY (enqueued_at, sequence, id): equal-timestamp pages can skip and duplicate candidates
evidence: Cursor predicate at line 174 is `(d.enqueued_at > $6 OR (d.enqueued_at = $6 AND d.id > $7))` but ordering is `ORDER BY d.enqueued_at, d.sequence, d.id`. For equal enqueued_at rows with differing sequence (re-dispatches enqueued in the same cascade wave as first runs), a row sorting after the page's last (cursor) row but with a smaller id is skipped for the rest of the pass, and a row sorting before it with a larger id is returned again. The conformance test (conformance/select_candidates_cursor.go:87-92) pins strict id-tiebreak for equal timestamps but only seeds fresh nodes where every sequence is 1, so the mismatch is untested. Either the cursor must include sequence or the ORDER BY must drop it. sqlite/queue.go:190,282-290 has the identical mismatch.
verify_note: Real keyset mismatch: cursor predicate queue.go:174 is (enqueued_at,id) but ORDER BY:187 is (enqueued_at,sequence,id); sqlite:190 + 282-290 identical. Equal-timestamp rows with differing sequence can be skipped or re-returned within a paged pass. Conformance select_candidates_cursor.go seeds fresh nodes (sequence=1) so ORDER BY sequence is a no-op tiebreak -> mismatch untested. But impact is bounded: cursor resets to zero each pass so skipped rows self-heal next poll, and duplicates are harmless (SKIP LOCKED + idempotent claim). One-cycle latency, not data loss -> downgrade to minor.

summary: Late-bind store clause is all-or-nothing: a required_stores set mixing statically-accepted and late-bound stores is never selectable
evidence: The store filter is `d.required_stores <@ $1::text[] OR ($5 <> '' AND $5 = ANY($1) AND (SELECT COALESCE(bool_and(i.service_bindings ? rs.name), false) FROM unnest(d.required_stores) AS rs(name)))`. With required_stores = {a, b}, accepted = {a, proxy}, service_bindings = {b}: branch 1 fails (b not accepted) and branch 2 fails (bool_and requires ALL stores in service_bindings, but a is not a binding). concept:supervisor describes the extension per store ('a node-run whose ... required store is NOT in the static accept-lists is still selectable when the proxy IS accepted AND the catalog carries the named binding'); the correct predicate is per-store: each required store in (accepted-set ∪ bindings). No conformance test covers the late-bind clause at all.
verify_note: Store late-bind branch queue.go:161 uses bool_and(i.service_bindings ? rs.name) over ALL required_stores, so a mixed set {static-accepted a, bound b} fails: branch1 (subset) fails on b, branch2 fails because a is not a binding. concept:supervisor:29 documents a per-store extension (each required store selectable via static accept-list OR proxy+binding). Correct predicate is per-store union. A valid mixed-store node is never dispatchable. No conformance test exercises the late-bind clause. Major stands.
remediation: Make the queue selectable when required_stores mixes statically-accepted and late-bound stores.

summary: Backend divergence: sqlite SelectCandidates implements no late-bind acceptance at all — late-bound services never dispatch on the sqlite backend
evidence: Postgres carries the late-bind executor clause (lines 167-171, `$4 = ANY($2) AND i.service_bindings ? d.executor_name`) and store clause (lines 158-162). The sqlite sibling (sqlite/queue.go:198-223) filters in Go via executorAccepted/storeAccepted closures that check only the static accept-lists and ignore req.LateBindExecutorProxy / req.LateBindClaimProducerProxy and i.service_bindings entirely (executorAccepted's `required` parameter is also dead). The all-in-one image — the documented `rimsky run --service` local-dev flow — runs sqlite, so host-agent late binding silently never matches there. concept:supervisor documents the late-bind clause as part of candidate selection with no backend carve-out.
verify_note: sqlite SelectCandidates (queue.go:198-223) filters via executorAccepted/storeAccepted closures checking only static accept-lists; the `required` param on executorAccepted is dead, and neither req.LateBindExecutorProxy/LateBindClaimProducerProxy nor i.service_bindings are consulted (the sqlite query doesn't even reference service_bindings). Postgres carries the late-bind clauses (167-171). all-in-one image runs sqlite = the documented `rimsky run --service` local-dev flow, so host-agent late binding silently never matches there. Backend divergence from concept:supervisor:29 with no carve-out. Major stands.
remediation: Port the postgres late-bind acceptance clause into sqlite SelectCandidates so late-bound services dispatch on the sqlite backend.

summary: Postgres-only wait-set NOT EXISTS predicate at dispatch time contradicts concept:wait-set and diverges from sqlite
evidence: Lines 182-186 exclude candidates with undrained rimsky_wait_set rows. concept:wait-set states: 'The dispatcher then claims stale rows by sequence, gated only by the serialization constraint ... The upstream-dependency predicate no longer lives at dispatch time; it is fully resolved by the row being in stale at all.' Since wait-set rows exist only on cascade-driven pending runs and pending→stale happens only after all rows drain, the clause is dead when the invariant holds — and if the invariant ever breaks, postgres and sqlite (which has no such clause, sqlite/queue.go:173-191) silently behave differently. Either delete the clause or add it to sqlite plus a conformance test; per Plumbline, one idiom repo-wide.
phase1_note: Confirmed on current tree: postgres's SelectCandidates carries an extra 'AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM rimsky_wait_set w WHERE ... drained_at IS NULL)' clause that sqlite's SelectCandidates lacks entirely (sqlite candidate query has no wait-set predicate at all). wait-set dossier states the upstream-dependency predicate 'is fully resolved by the row being in stale at all' and dispatch eligibility is 'checked once at that transition' (pending->stale), not re-checked at dispatch-time SELECT. Since a stale row is guaranteed drained, the postgres clause is redundant when the invariant holds but creates a silent cross-backend behavioral asymmetry if it ever doesn't (Plumbline: one idiom repo-wide). fix-code: delete the postgres clause (or add the same guard plus a conformance test to sqlite) to restore parity.

summary: Insert maps a duplicate content-hash to ErrTemplateInUse (409), violating the documented persistence-layer idempotent re-registration
evidence: concept:template states: 'Idempotent re-registration is a persistence-layer property: re-registering an identical spec is a no-op rather than a conflict.' Templates are content-addressed (id = hash), so a unique violation on id means the identical spec is already registered — yet lines 43-46 wrap it as shared.ErrTemplateInUse ('template already registered'), which the control API maps to HTTP 409 (app.go:198). The register handler's pre-check narrows this to a race between two concurrent identical registers, but the persistence layer itself breaks the named invariant. sqlite/templates.go:40-43 has the identical mapping. Should be ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING (or an already-exists no-op signal).
verify_note: templates.go:43-46 (and sqlite:40-43) map a unique-violation on the content-hash id to shared.ErrTemplateInUse -> HTTP 409, contradicting concept:template:16 'Idempotent re-registration is a persistence-layer property: re-registering an identical spec is a no-op rather than a conflict.' The persistence layer does break the named property. But register handler (templates.go:277-303) pre-checks GetByHash and returns 200 for an existing template, so 409 only surfaces on a concurrent identical-register race, is recoverable, and causes no data corruption. Real drift but narrow -> downgrade to minor.
phase1_note: Confirmed on current tree: both backends still map a unique-violation on the content-hash id to shared.ErrTemplateInUse -> HTTP 409. template dossier's Net position states 'Re-registering the same spec is idempotent' as a persistence-layer property. The register handler's GetByHash pre-check masks this in the common case (200 for an already-registered identical spec), narrowing real-world impact to a concurrent identical-register race -- hence minor, not major. fix-code: switch the insert to ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING / an already-exists no-op signal at the persistence layer so the property holds unconditionally, not just when the handler happens to pre-check.

summary: rimsky_node_runs.frame_id ON DELETE CASCADE (and node_attributes cascading off node_runs) lets the frame retention prune delete rows carrying blob handles without ever enqueuing them in rimsky_blob_orphans, permanently leaking spilled blobs.

The only QueueBlobOrphan call sites are the attribute-overwrite paths (postgres/node_attributes.go:149, sqlite/node_attributes.go:166), so handles held by pruned runs never reach the ledger, violating blob-backend.md's invariant 'Orphan blobs go to a persisted orphan-blob ledger and are swept'. Postgres large objects are not covered by row cascades. Code side (schema + prune path) is inconsistent with the reaper design.
verify_note: PruneTraceForRetention is a bare DELETE; cascades remove rows carrying blob handles with no QueueBlobOrphan — spilled blobs leak, violating blob-backend.md orphan-ledger invariant.
remediation: Enqueue blob handles from node_runs/node_attributes into rimsky_blob_orphans as part of frame prune rather than relying on ON DELETE CASCADE; extend the prune e2e test to seed spilled blobs and assert ledger enrollment.

summary: Per-frame root run-scope rows have no FK linkage to their frame and no reaper, so the frame retention sweep leaves one orphaned rimsky_run_scopes row per pruned frame, growing unboundedly on long-lived instances.
evidence: 015 makes every frame open create a fresh root run scope (lib/graph/frame/producer.go:29-38) but adds rimsky_frames.root_run_scope_id with no FK and no reverse cleanup. Child scopes die via parent_run_id -> rimsky_node_runs(id) ON DELETE CASCADE when the frame's runs cascade away, but the root scope has parent_run_id NULL; PruneTraceForRetention deletes only rimsky_frames, and no DELETE FROM rimsky_run_scopes exists anywhere in lib/. Only instance deletion reclaims them. The missing FK also permits dangling root_run_scope_id values (015 itself backfills a zero-UUID placeholder).
verify_note: 015 adds root_run_scope_id with no FK; root scopes have parent_run_id NULL so no cascade fires; no DELETE FROM rimsky_run_scopes exists — one stranded row per pruned frame.
remediation: Link per-frame root rimsky_run_scopes rows to their frame (FK cascade) or add a reaper so the frame-retention sweep removes them instead of leaking one row per pruned frame.

summary: rimsky_messages has no index on frame_id, so the per-dispatch ListDeliveredForFrame query and the FK ON DELETE SET NULL maintenance during frame pruning both seq-scan the ever-growing messages table.

No DELETE FROM rimsky_messages exists, so the table grows monotonically. The sqlite migrations have the identical gap, so this is a schema-design omission, not a dialect drift.
verify_note: No frame_id index on rimsky_messages; listDeliveredForFrameSQL is on the dispatch path and frame-prune FK maintenance seq-scans a monotonically growing table.
remediation: Add an index on rimsky_messages.frame_id (new migration) to back ListDeliveredForFrame and FK ON DELETE SET NULL pruning.

summary: The consolidation reused ordinals 014 and 015 that previously belonged to different migrations, breaking append-only numbering and enabling silent misapplication on pre-consolidation dev databases.
evidence: git commit 12243806 deleted 014-drop-publisher-target-node.sql and 015-node-run-resuming-state.sql when 001-013 (plus old 014/015) were collapsed into 001-initial.sql; the new post-consolidation migrations were then numbered 014/015 again with different filenames. Because the runner keys idempotency on full filename (persistence/migrations.go:57), a dev DB carrying the old rows would apply the new 014/015 on the old schema without error — a franken-schema instead of a loud failure. Pre-v1 drop-and-recreate stance mitigates but new numbers should have started at 016.

summary: No index leads with rimsky_events.occurred_at, so the retention sweep's DeleteOlderThan seq-scans the event log on every sweep.

summary: ListParkedOverdue applies LIMIT in SQL before the overdue/resume predicates (which run in Go), so overdue rows beyond the first limit parked rows are invisible and can be starved indefinitely, unlike postgres which filters then limits.
evidence: sqlite fetches WHERE state='parked' AND max_park_duration_seconds IS NOT NULL AND parked_at IS NOT NULL ... LIMIT ? then filters deadline/resume_at in Go (lines 108-122); postgres/queue_park.go:88-89 pushes parked_at + max_park * INTERVAL <= $1 AND (resume_at IS NULL OR resume_at > $1) into SQL before LIMIT. With >=limit not-yet-overdue (or resume-pending) rows ordered first by parked_at ASC, sqlite returns a short/empty page while genuinely overdue rows exist; repeated calls rescan the same window. Code (sqlite) is the stale side.
verify_note: sqlite ListParkedOverdue LIMITs in SQL before the overdue/resume predicates run in Go; postgres pushes both into SQL — overdue rows beyond the first page starve.
remediation: Move the overdue/resume predicate into the SQL WHERE clause (as postgres does) so LIMIT is applied after filtering, not before.

summary: CapturingLogger.With returns a child that aliases the parent's records slice under a separate mutex, so records logged through a With-derived logger are invisible to the parent's Records() and concurrent parent/child appends race on the same backing-array slot.

Production code derives loggers via With (e.g. lib/control/launch/unified.go:69 logger.With("role", r.name)), so any test asserting on CapturingLogger records silently misses everything logged through the derived logger. No logger_test.go exists in lib/foundation/shared/ to catch this.
verify_note: CapturingLogger.With aliases the parent's records slice under a separate mutex — child appends invisible to parent, concurrent appends race on the same backing slot.
remediation: Share a single synchronized records sink between parent and With-derived children (shared pointer + one mutex).

verify_note: walkPath decodes numbers to float64 without UseNumber and stringify uses %v: integers >=1e7 render scientific in embedded mode, int64 >2^53 lose precision; map/slice arm renders correctly — inconsistent.
remediation: Use json.Decoder.UseNumber in walkPath and render numbers without %v scientific-notation/precision loss in stringify.

summary: Confirmed prior lead: the pure-cascade claim-only path enqueues a NEW stale node_run every tick while leaving the original stale run untouched, violating the at-most-one-past-pending invariant and re-executing the node (re-acquiring claims) indefinitely.

ListPureCascadeReady (postgres/nodes.go:171-200, sqlite/nodes.go:173-186) selects ALL runs with state='stale' and empty node.executor with no claimed_by/duplicate guard, so the next tick returns BOTH the original run and the sweep's own enqueued run and enqueues again for each — compounding per tick. Terminal completion only clears rows claimed by the completing supervisor (RemoveForNodeInTx updates only claimed_by IS NOT NULL / = supervisor rows), so unclaimed stale duplicates survive settle and the sweep regenerates forever: the node re-executes and re-acquires claims (e.g. an items-queue producer pops a new item per cycle), and the frame never reaches ListRunningFramesNoPendingNodes settle. Violates node-run.md:71 'At most one node-run per (node, run-scope) is in a state past pending at any moment' — the code side is wrong. TestProcessPureCascade_NativeClaimOnly_Enqueues (pure_cascade_test.go:393-443) proves the source run stays 'stale' after the enqueue but uses a fakeQueue that inserts no rows, so the compounding across ticks is untested and invisible.
verify_note: Traced end to end: fresh stale row per tick, source row never consumed, no duplicate guard in ListPureCascadeReady, RemoveForNodeInTx clears only claimed rows — duplicates compound, claims re-acquired indefinitely, frame never settles; only test uses a fakeQueue and cannot see it.
remediation: pure_cascade.go: the claim-only pure-cascade path must reuse the existing stale run, not enqueue a new stale node_run every tick (violates at-most-one-past-pending).

remediation: Unlink the in_progress sentinel before (or atomically with) removing/renaming the payload folder, and have popOne/tryRenameClaim stat the folder so a crash cannot leave a claim addressing a nonexistent folder.

summary: Open validates req.Intent then discards it — store.Open(ctx, claimID, selector) has no intent parameter, so under staged_async (the default) an intent='r' open on a schema selector creates and returns a fresh empty staging schema as the address instead of the canonical pre-stage snapshot, breaking staged-async read semantics that rimsky's reader-writer coexistence gate relies on.

remediation: Thread req.Intent into store.Open so intent='r' returns the canonical pre-stage snapshot (not a fresh staging schema), and branch Commit on intent for read-only vs write-back; then the fanout-intent-inheritance story's proof is non-vacuous.

summary: Commit is not idempotent in the claim id for staged claims: a second Commit for the same claim fails with pg/swap_failed (staging schema no longer exists), violating concept:claim-producer's idempotency invariant; no idempotency test exists in the postgres producer (filesystem has TestCommit_Idempotent).

summary: itemsQueueView counts rows WHERE state = 'queued', but the store's item state vocabulary is 'available'/'in_progress', so queued_count is always 0 and the admin view is wrong.

summary: commitStagingSwap drops the canonical schema without CASCADE, so every Commit over a canonical schema that already contains objects (every re-materialization after the first commit) fails with 'schema is not empty', breaking the staged-async story for repeat runs.
evidence: DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS canonicalID has no CASCADE; Postgres RESTRICT-drops non-empty schemas. After a first successful swap the canonical schema contains the staged tables. The test masks this: atomic_staging_test.go:128-132 resets canonical to an EMPTY schema before Commit. Contradicts story:store-postgres.
verify_note: commitStagingSwap DROPs the canonical schema without CASCADE, so every commit over a canonical schema already holding objects fails pg/swap_failed — and the test masks it by resetting canonical to empty before Commit, hiding the repeat-materialization breakage.
remediation: Rework commitStagingSwap to atomically replace the canonical schema (DROP ... CASCADE or rename-swap) so re-publish succeeds, and make Commit detect an already-consumed staging schema and return success (idempotent in claim id); add store tests for re-publish and terminal-verb retry.

summary: Commit is not idempotent for staged claims: a retry after a successful swap fails with pg/swap_failed because the staging schema no longer exists, misreporting a committed claim as failed. (Store-side confirmation of C074's terminal-idempotency-broken.)
evidence: commitStagingSwap re-runs DROP canonical + ALTER SCHEMA staging RENAME on retry; staging was consumed by the first swap so ALTER fails and the whole tx rolls back. Abandon (DROP IF EXISTS) and Release are idempotent; Commit is the one terminal verb that turns a supervisor retry into a spurious failure.
verify_note: commitStagingSwap re-runs DROP+ALTER with nothing gating an already-committed claim, so a retry after a successful swap fails pg/swap_failed — violates terminal-verb idempotency (Abandon/Release use IF EXISTS and are fine).

summary: openPickPolicy is not idempotent per claim_id: a retried Open claims a second row under the same claim_token, and the Pop action's DELETE WHERE claim_token=$1 later deletes both rows, silently destroying an unprocessed item.
evidence: The UPDATE always picks a fresh 'available' row and stamps claim_token=$1 without first checking for an existing row with that token; claim_id is threaded through every subsequent verb so a client retry reuses it. applyPickAction's Pop and Recycle act on ALL rows matching the token, so the first-picked item (whose payload the executor never saw on the retry path) is popped unprocessed.
verify_note: the contract requires idempotency only for terminal verbs; the client generates a fresh UUID per acquisition attempt so no path retries Open with a reused claim_id, and an Open-then-tx-fail orphan is recycled by the visibility sweep — the double-claim scenario is unrealizable.

summary: canonicalRowID/normalizePolicyValue only special-case string and []byte, so partition policies over uuid (or numeric) id columns emit JSON number-array partition keys and row payloads — garbage claim scopes for the most common PK type.
evidence: pgx v5 returns [16]uint8 for a uuid column and pgtype.Numeric for numeric; canonicalRowID falls through to json.Marshal producing a number array as the PolicyRow.ID (and thus PartitionKey and claim scope). Only string/[]byte/int paths are covered by tests; no DB-backed RunPartitionPolicy test exists.
verify_note: canonicalRowID handles only string/[]byte before json.Marshal, and pgx v5 yields [16]uint8 for uuid, so uuid PKs produce number-array partition keys/scopes/payloads — garbage scopes for the most common PK type, untested.
remediation: Extend canonicalRowID/normalizePolicyValue to canonicalize uuid and numeric id columns to stable string keys instead of JSON number arrays.

summary: listarray.Unmarshal accepts duplicate element keys, so siblings get byte-equal ClaimScopeData, violating concept:fan-out's requirement that a producer reject overlapping partitions. (Confirms C072's fs-side finding at the shared helper.)
evidence: The validation loop only rejects empty keys; {'list':[{'key':'a'},{'key':'a'}]} passes, and ToSubScopes plus the pg server's claimScopeForElement yields two identical-scope descriptors. No duplicate-key test in listarray_test.go.
verify_note: listarray.Unmarshal accepts duplicate keys, yielding byte-equal sibling scopes via claimScopeForElement — violates concept:fan-out's must-reject-overlap invariant; no duplicate-key test.

summary: RunPartitionPolicy does not reject duplicate row ids, so a partition-policy SELECT that returns repeated ids emits overlapping (byte-equal) sub-claim scopes instead of rejecting the request.
evidence: The rows.Next() loop appends every row keyed by vals[0] with no uniqueness check; server.go turns each ID directly into ClaimScopeData via json.Marshal(r.ID). concept:fan-out requires distinct scopes and rejection on overlap.
verify_note: RunPartitionPolicy appends every row with no id-uniqueness check and maps each id straight to ClaimScopeData, so repeated ids emit byte-equal overlapping sub-scopes instead of rejecting — distinct path from 1805.
remediation: Reject a partition-policy SELECT that returns repeated ids so sub-claim scopes are disjoint.

summary: Under staged_async, a selector that is not a valid schema identifier silently falls through to the no-staging path (address == scope == selector) while still returning realized staged_async — a staged-async no-op, exactly what story:store-postgres forbids.
evidence: stagedScopeBytes returns false for e.g. 'Analytics-Prod', so Open returns Available with Address==ClaimScope==selector and RealizedWriteSemantics=staged_async; the executor writes in place with no staging area. concept:write-semantics honesty requirement and story:store-postgres both forbid the no-op.
verify_note: under staged_async a selector failing schemaIdentRegex falls through to address==scope==selector yet still reports realized staged_async, and Abandon is then a no-op — the staged-async no-op the story and concept:write-semantics forbid.

summary: evictIfNeeded falls back to evicting the OLDEST record even when it is still OPEN, and the cap is hardcoded to 1024, so >1024 concurrently open claims silently drop live records — SplitScope on an evicted (or post-restart) parent then fails NotFound.
evidence: ledger.go:313-320 deletes l.order[0] regardless of State when no non-open record exists; NewClaimLedger(1024) is not configurable. SplitScope routes through LookupClaim backed only by this in-memory map, so an evicted-but-open parent (or a parent opened on another replica / before restart) fails with unknown claim_handle_id. No eviction test exists.
verify_note: evictIfNeeded deletes the oldest record even when OPEN once no non-open record exists, the cap is hardcoded 1024, and SplitScope's LookupClaim is backed only by this in-memory map, so >1024 open claims (or a restart) turn live parents into NotFound; no eviction test.
remediation: Never evict OPEN ledger records (skip/extend), make the cap configurable, so SplitScope on a live parent cannot fail NotFound.

summary: ClaimLedger is a near-verbatim copy of the filesystem store's ledger (plus one extra method), violating strict DRY — semantically identical claim-ledger logic in two places that must change together.
evidence: diff of the two ledger.go files shows only gofmt-level differences and the pg-only Subscribe method; shared/ (home of listarray) already exists for cross-producer helpers.

evidence: wc -l reports 723; the file mixes Open/terminal verbs, pick actions, partition-policy execution, validators, and items-table verification.

summary: Query/scan failures are folded into Result{Pass:false} with no error-vs-check-failure distinction, so infrastructure errors surface as data-quality failures.

verify_note: runOne folds Query/Scan errors into Result{Pass:false} with no error discriminator, and the consumer maps any !Pass to pg/verifier_check_failed/<kind>, so a dropped connection mid-check is reported as a data-quality failure.
remediation: Distinguish query/scan infrastructure errors from check failures in sql-checks Result rather than collapsing both into Pass:false.

summary: The check-kind vocabulary (kinds, config keys, defaults, helpers) is implemented twice — here and in lib/services/executors/verifier-shape-checks/checks/checks.go — with already-diverged semantics and no shared conformance suite.

A user moving a check spec between the two bundled verifiers gets silently different behavior.
verify_note: the check-kind vocabulary is copy-pasted between sql-checks and verifier-shape-checks with verified drift (threshold honored in one, ignored in the other) and no shared conformance suite — strict-DRY violation.
remediation: Extract the check-kind vocabulary (kinds, config keys, defaults, helpers) into one shared package with a conformance suite; remove the diverged copy in verifier-shape-checks.

summary: pk_unique's Interpret fails open (Pass=true) when called with no arguments or a non-bool, unlike every other kind which fails closed on a malformed scan.

summary: row_count_ratio is the only check kind with zero coverage in the package's isolated unit suite, and its low/high bounds are never sanity-validated (low > high compiles to an always-fail check).

summary: BuildClaudeCliResumeArgs never passes --session-id, yet resumed runs still report session_token = opts.SessionID, so the second park/resume or self-edge resume in a RunScope targets a nonexistent CLI session.
evidence: Spawn binds via --session-id opts.SessionID; the Resume path has no --session-id but OnComplete/OnPark still write SessionToken: opts.SessionID — decision:claude-agent-session-attribute promises the next dispatch resumes the prior CLI conversation; the chain breaks at generation two.

remediation: Have BuildClaudeCliResumeArgs pass --session-id (matching the reported session_token) so a second park/resume or self-edge resume targets the correct CLI session.

summary: The clean-exit-without-report reminder retry always resumes SessionID: opts.SessionID, which is wrong when the run itself started via Resume(opts.SessionToken) — the retry resumes a session that does not exist and the dispatch errors instead of recovering.
evidence: runAgentReal launches via Resume(SessionID: opts.SessionToken) when SessionToken!='' so no CLI session named opts.SessionID exists; the clean-exit retry at 753 hardcodes SessionID: opts.SessionID → 'No conversation found'.
verify_note: The clean-exit reminder retry hardcodes SessionID:opts.SessionID; in a resume-launched dispatch the live CLI session is opts.SessionToken, so --resume opts.SessionID targets an unbound session and the recovery errors instead of resuming.
remediation: Resume the reminder retry via the session the run actually started with (SessionToken when Resume was used), not always opts.SessionID.

summary: While any tool_use is open, the silence watchdog is skipped entirely, so with the default tool_use_timeout of 0 a tool that hangs without emitting stdout stalls the dispatch forever even when silence_timeout is configured.

verify_note: The silence check sits in the else-of oldest!=nil, so while any tool_use is open and tool_use_timeout<=0 (default 0) neither branch fires; a hung/unclosed tool defeats a configured silence_timeout — largely an intended don't-kill-running-tools tradeoff with a missing default cap.

summary: BuildCliEnv leaks the freshly created tmpDir (containing the written API key file) on every error path after MkdirTemp.

summary: registerStream replays buffered history outside the mutex while the pump may concurrently deliver newer chunks to the just-registered callback, so a late-registered OnStdout can observe chunks out of order and corrupt stream-json parsing.
evidence: registerStream snapshots hist, appends cb, unlocks, then invokes cb(replay); pump independently snapshots cbs under lock and calls them after unlocking — a chunk read between the windows is delivered before the older replayed chunk finishes.

summary: The _missing_url reserved-attribute rejection has no producer anywhere in the repo — only _invalid is exercised — so it is dead validation that silently reserves a key in real dispatches.

summary: BuildClaudeCliArgs reads RIMSKY_DISPATCH_MAX_USD from process env inside the otherwise-pure arg builder, and the env fallback is silently absent on the resume path.

summary: CliConfigError.ErrorClass() is never called; server.go re-derives the same agent/attribute_invalid literal after IsCliConfigError, duplicating the mapping in two places.

summary: No test exercises the tool_use timeout path (agent/tool_use_timeout) or the open-tool-use/silence interaction, while the sibling silence timeout is tested.

summary: A syntactically valid cron expression that never fires (e.g. 0 0 31 2 *) makes robfig Next() return the zero time, which the due-check treats as permanently due, so the sensor posts a bogus fire_at=0001-01-01 message and re-fires every tick (1/sec) forever.

summary: The window-deterministic idempotency key (subscriptionID + NextFireAt) makes N independent replicas' fires collapse to one enqueued message at the control API, contradicting the sensor-cron story's documented posture that two replicas post exactly two per window — the story/replica-posture claim (and the in-package tests) are stale.
evidence: idemKey = subscriptionID+NextFireAt.UTC() is identical across replicas (cron windows are absolute); controlapi messages dedup on (InstanceID, SenderKind, Sender, IdempotencyKey) and return the prior ID with replayed=true, so the second replica's POST enqueues nothing. multi_replica_test.go and replica_posture_test.go assert 2 envelopes against a dumb httptest server that does not dedup — false confidence.
verify_note: Window-deterministic idemKey (subID+NextFireAt) is identical across replicas, so control-API dedup collapses N replica POSTs to one enqueued message, contradicting the story's N-per-window posture; the tests count POSTs against a non-deduping httptest server so they pass falsely.

Rewrite the sensor-cron story's replica posture to match concept:sensor's single-replica invariant: multi-process servicing of one subscription (shared state DSN) is unsupported; if it occurs, the window-deterministic idempotency key deliberately collapses duplicate fires to one enqueued message per window (benign, not leader election). Distinct subscriptions keep distinct keys and are never collapsed. Replace multi_replica_test.go / replica_posture_test.go assertions: assert the same-subscription same-window key-equality (collapse) property and distinct-subscription key distinctness, not '2 envelopes' against a non-deduping fake.

summary: The idempotency key subscriptionID+bodyHash means an upstream whose body changes A->B->A produces the same key for the second A as the first, so the control API's persistent message-idempotency table silently swallows the legitimate change-back-to-A message.
evidence: idemKey = subscriptionID+hash; the change-detection gate is only against the immediately-previous hash so A->B->A passes locally, but MessageIdempotencies keeps keys durably and replays the original ID; the key needs a monotonic component. No test covers alternating content.
verify_note: idemKey=subID+bodyHash with only a previous-hash local gate lets A->B->A pass locally but the durable idempotency table swallows the second A, dropping legitimate change-back (up->down->up recovery) events.
remediation: Include a monotonic/sequence component in the sensor-http idempotency key so a body reverting to a prior value is not silently deduped by the persistent message table.

summary: io.ReadAll on the polled response body has no size cap, so a large or fast-streaming upstream can balloon sensor memory and produce an oversized message payload.

summary: The watermark is advanced in memory and persisted to the state DB before postMessage, so a failed send permanently drops the object's message with only a Warn log.
evidence: pollOne sets cur.WatermarkName/WatermarkTime and calls state.UpdateWatermark before postMessage; the postMessage error path only logs. After rimsky is unreachable past publisherkit's 3 attempts or returns 4xx, the next poll computes isNew=false and restart restores the already-advanced watermark — the object is never sent, violating the story's exactly-one acceptance (zero are sent).
verify_note: pollOne sets watermark and calls UpdateWatermark before postMessage and only logs send failure, so a failed send permanently drops the object (next poll computes isNew=false), violating the story's exactly-one acceptance — data loss.
remediation: Advance and persist the watermark only after postMessage succeeds so a failed send does not drop the object.

summary: With watermark_field=last_modified, strictly-after comparison drops every object sharing a LastModified with the watermark, including siblings in the same poll batch.
evidence: isNew = o.LastModified.After(cur.WatermarkTime); within one poll the batch is sorted ascending and the first object of a timestamp sets WatermarkTime=T, so the second object with LastModified==T fails After(T) and is skipped forever. Object stores commonly have second-granularity mtimes.
verify_note: isNew=LastModified.After(watermark) with ascending sort means the second object sharing a timestamp in the same batch fails After() and is silently skipped forever under last_modified watermarking.
remediation: Track already-seen keys at the watermark timestamp so equal-LastModified siblings are not dropped by strictly-after comparison.

summary: The default watermark_field=name only discovers objects sorting lexicographically above the high-water mark, so a new object with a lower-sorting name is never discovered.
evidence: isNew = o.Name > cur.WatermarkName; after b.json is watermarked, a later-dropped a.json is permanently invisible. The story promises discovery of a new object dropped after the last poll with no monotonic-naming precondition, and nothing documents/warns about the requirement.
verify_note: Default name watermark uses o.Name>WatermarkName, so a newly-dropped object sorting lexicographically below the watermark is never discovered, and nothing documents the monotonic-naming precondition the story omits.
remediation: Do not rely on lexicographic name ordering as a high-water mark; discover objects independent of sort position.

summary: The message idempotency key is subscriptionID+ETag with no object name, so two distinct objects with identical content produce the same key and rimsky's durable dedup silently discards the second object's message.
evidence: idemKey = subscriptionID+o.ETag; the filesystem lister's ETag is an FNV-64a content hash and S3 ETags are content MD5s, so identical bytes under different names collide; MessageIdempotencies.InsertOrLookup dedupes durably, dropping the second discovery.
verify_note: idemKey=subID+ETag omits object name; FS ETag is an FNV content hash and S3 ETags are content MD5s, so two distinct same-content objects collide and durable dedup drops the second discovery.
remediation: Include the object name in the idempotency key (subscriptionID+object+ETag) so two distinct objects with identical content are not deduped to one message.

summary: AttachStateDB only stores the DB handle and never reloads persisted subscriptions, so after a sensor restart all path bindings are gone and inbound webhooks 404 until rimsky itself restarts.

remediation: Have AttachStateDB reload persisted subscriptions/path bindings on startup so inbound webhooks resolve after a sensor restart without a full rimsky restart.

summary: The inbound idempotency key is recorded in memory and the state DB before postMessage, so a retry after a failed delivery matches LastIdempotency and is acknowledged 200 OK without the message ever reaching rimsky.

verify_note: serveWebhook sets LastIdempotency and persists it before postMessage, so a sender retry after a 502 hits the early return and gets 200 OK though the message never reached rimsky — the story's explicit falsifier, a silent drop-and-false-ack.
remediation: Record the idempotency key only after postMessage succeeds so a retry after failed delivery is not falsely acked.

summary: MakeLeafRunEvent keys the OpenLineage runId on the instance ID (or instanceID+/+childKey), so every node-run in an instance collides on one runId, the childKey form is not a UUID (OpenLineage requires a UUID; Marquez rejects it), and it disagrees with claim-terminal events which use the node-run UUID, breaking cross-event correlation.

verify_note: MakeLeafRunEvent keys runId on instanceID (fallback unreachable) so all node-runs collide and disagree with claim_terminal's NodeRunID runId, and instanceID/childKey is not the UUID OpenLineage requires.
remediation: openlineage emitter.go: key the OpenLineage runId on the node-run UUID (as claim-terminal events do), not the instance id, to fix per-node collisions and non-UUID childKeys.

summary: The rimsky metadata block is placed in a top-level Event.Facets field that does not exist in the OpenLineage RunEvent schema (facets live under run.facets/job.facets), and the custom facets lack the required _producer/_schemaURL envelope — spec-conformant backends silently drop all of it.

remediation: Place custom facets under run.facets/job.facets with the required _producer/_schemaURL envelope instead of a nonexistent top-level Event.Facets field.

summary: fetchSince advances a strictly-greater (observed_at, id) cursor over writer-assigned Go-side timestamps inserted inside transactions, so a lineage row whose transaction commits after the poller read past its observed_at (slow tx or clock skew between writer processes) is permanently skipped — silent loss with no detection.
evidence: WHERE (observed_at,id) > ($1,$2); writer sets row.ObservedAt = time.Now().UTC() in Go and inserts via the caller's tx, so visibility order is commit order not observed_at order; no lag window or txid-based fencing.
verify_note: The lineage writer assigns observed_at via Go time.Now() inside the caller's tx while the poller advances a strictly-greater (observed_at,id) cursor, so a row committing after the poller passed its timestamp is silently and undetectably skipped.
remediation: openlineage subscriber.go fetchSince: use a cursor that cannot skip a lineage row whose transaction commits after a later observed_at was read (silent loss).

summary: RIMSKY_OPENLINEAGE_BACKEND_URL is optional and an empty BackendURL makes Send a silent no-op while tick still advances and persists the cursor, so a subscriber started before the backend is configured permanently discards every lineage record produced in the window.
evidence: config.go reads the env with no requiredness check; emitter.go:60-62 returns nil on empty URL; subscriber.go treats nil as success and persists the advanced cursor; TestEmitter_EmptyBackendIsNoOp bakes it in.
verify_note: BackendURL is optional and empty makes Send a nil no-op that tick treats as success and persists the advanced cursor, permanently discarding every lineage record produced before the backend is configured.
remediation: Do not advance/persist the cursor when RIMSKY_OPENLINEAGE_BACKEND_URL is empty (fail or block) so records are not permanently discarded before the backend is configured.

summary: A permanently-rejected event (HTTP 422 for the non-UUID childKey runId, or any 4xx) halts the cursor forever with no transient-vs-permanent distinction, retry budget, or dead-letter — the entire export wedges head-of-line while only logging a Warn each tick.
evidence: on any Send error the loop breaks and the cursor never passes the row; the same row is retried every PollInterval indefinitely; contrast decode failures which skip-and-advance — opposite policies with no way to unstick a rejected-forever event.
verify_note: tick breaks on any Send error with no transient/permanent distinction or dead-letter, so a permanently-rejected row (the non-UUID runId 422) wedges the entire export head-of-line forever while only logging Warn.
remediation: Distinguish transient vs permanent (4xx/422) failures with a retry budget and dead-letter so a single rejected event (e.g. non-UUID childKey runId) cannot halt the cursor head-of-line forever.

summary: No test validates emitted events against the OpenLineage JSON schema or a real backend — every test uses a permissive httptest stub that accepts anything, so the story's well-formed-lineage-event acceptance has no proof and the runId/facet non-conformances ship untested.
evidence: the test stubs json.Unmarshal into the subscriber's own Event type; subscriber_openlineage_e2e_test.go uses httptest returning 200 and only checks strings; the repo vendors jsonschema but never applies it to the OpenLineage spec.

summary: The confirmed watermark-advanced-before-delivery bug in sensor-http cannot fail this test — it only checks the hash advanced after delivery already succeeded and never induces a post failure or crash between mark and deliver.

summary: preRestartPolls is captured before sensor.Stop, so a 1s-interval poll landing during the capture-to-termination window increments pollHits and trips the polled-while-stopped fatal as a false failure.

summary: Four near-identical deploy-template helpers, four near-identical create-instance helpers, and three identical state-postgres struct/connect pairs are copy-pasted across the sensor tests instead of sharing the existing deployScenarioTemplate/createScenarioInstance idiom.

summary: handleGetNode discards the errors from the holdings, events, and run-summary/attributes transactions, returning HTTP 200 with fabricated-empty data when the reads fail — which the test's polling helpers then misdiagnose as 'no dispatch yet'.

summary: The 'declared error class agent/rate_limited routes verbatim' subtest asserts only that the node settles failed and never inspects the delivered error class, so any failure mode passes (duplicate of the C086 finding, re-confirmed from the fake side).

verify_note: The rate_limited subtest's sole assertion is waitNodeSettledClaudeAgent(...,failed,...) which any failure mode satisfies; no error-class inspection proves 'routes verbatim', and this is the only guard for claude-agent error-class routing.

summary: requireSwapCollidedAndLeftStaging sleeps an unconditional 30s (the loop body is only time.Sleep) and asserts staging-intact BEFORE the swap_failed event is awaited, so the collided-swap-rolls-back invariant can pass vacuously before any swap attempt ran.

verify_note: requireSwapCollidedAndLeftStaging is a pure 30s time.Sleep with no exit condition, and its pinned-exists/staging>0 checks pass vacuously if the swap runs after the window, never rechecked after the collision is proven by the later requireEventKind.
remediation: Await the swap_failed event before asserting staging-intact (replace the unconditional sleep with an event wait) so the collided-swap-rolls-back invariant cannot pass vacuously.

summary: The pick-vs-scope contention test's only assertions are waitForNodeTerminal calls that accept failed as terminal, so the test passes even if both workers fail to acquire or execute.

remediation: Add success assertions to the fs pick-vs-scope and cross-queue contention tests so they fail when workers cannot acquire/execute.

summary: The cross-queue contention test (two ring policies over the same root and one seeded folder) asserts only failed-or-fresh terminal-ness, proving nothing about the load-bearing cross-queue claim behavior.
evidence: Same shape as fs_pick_vs_scope: waitForNodeTerminal treats FailedCount>0 as success, and there is no assertion on acquisition, exclusivity, or success — both workers failing their claims is a passing run.
verify_note: Same failed-as-terminal helper; the two ring policies over one seeded folder are only awaited for terminal-ness, proving nothing about cross-queue claim behavior — both workers failing is a passing run.

summary: The top-level overlap case never proves the contender attempted acquisition — it only counts claim rows for 30s — so a contender that never schedules yields the same pass as one correctly held off (distinct from the already-reported fan-out vacuousness).
evidence: runTopLevelOverlapCase waits for acquirer/verifier terminal then polls countAcquiredClaimScopeRows hoping it stays 1. No check of the contender's run_summary (pending/blocked with an acquisition attempt) and no observability-event check that Open was ever called with the contended selector.

remediation: Strengthen scopes_conflict and claim_scope_conflict_race tests to prove the contender attempted acquisition and was held off (no serial double-win).

summary: No scripted scenario ever exits non-zero with classifiable stderr or exits zero without reporting, so ClassifyAgentError (agent/refused), agent/subprocess_exit/before_complete, and the clean-exit resume-reminder path have zero cross-stack coverage.

summary: The fake emits a single {type:system, subtype:fake-claude} stdout line and no assistant/user tool_use stream-json, so the executor's CliStreamParser progress tracking and tool_use/silence timeout machinery run against an empty stream cross-stack.

summary: Doc claims in-place retry sees the row-persisted scratch, but the retry loop carries in-memory terminal scratch instead, dropping mid-dispatch/persisted scratch when the terminal outcome is empty.
evidence: scratch-recovery.md:11 asserts 'retries loop in-process on the same dispatch row, so the scratch persisted on that row is already available to the retry attempt without any copy.' Code at runner.go:220 does acq.Scratch = terminal.Scratch (in-memory) before re-dispatch, never re-reading the row. An empty terminal scratch is a persist no-op (runner_terminal_scratch.go:20 if len(scratch)==0 return), so a mid-dispatch callback-written scratch survives on the row but the retry executor is handed empty scratch via runner_dispatch.go:881 Scratch: acq.Scratch — the confirmed scratch-lost-on-retry bug; session tokens ride this channel.
verify_note: scratch-recovery.md:11 claims row-persisted scratch is available to retry 'without any copy'; runner.go:220 sets acq.Scratch=terminal.Scratch (in-memory), runner_dispatch.go:881 hands that, row never re-read; runner_terminal_scratch.go:20 empty terminal = persist no-op while callback.go:598 persists mid-dispatch scratch. Mid-dispatch scratch survives on row but empty terminal hands retry empty. Reachable bug -> major (needs empty terminal after mid-dispatch write, so not critical).
remediation: The retry loop must carry the row-persisted scratch, not the in-memory terminal scratch, so persisted scratch isn't dropped on an empty terminal outcome (per decision:scratch-recovery).
phase1_note: Intent (two independent transcript sources) is that in-place retry copies the terminal event's scratch into the next acquisition in-memory -- the doc's 'without any copy' framing understated this and was corrected in the same edit as 2285. But the copy is unconditional even when terminal.Scratch is empty, silently discarding whatever the row already carried, which violates the well-established empty-terminal-is-a-no-op invariant (scratch-protocol.md) on the one path that never re-reads the row. Queued fix-code: the retry-copy must skip the assignment when terminal.Scratch is empty.
